title: Preface
summary: This text chunk presents the front matter and contents of 'Basic Computer Architecture,' Version 3.09, by Smruti R. Sarangi (October 8, 2025), licensed under Creative Commons Attribution-NoDerivs 4.0. It lists numerous trademarks from AMD, Arm, AutoCAD, Facebook, Formula 1, Google, HP, IBM, Intel, Microsoft, NVIDIA, SPARC, SPEC, Tejas Simulator, and Qualcomm. The table of contents covers an introduction to computer architecture, including ISA design, theoretical foundations (Turing machines, universal ISA), practical machines (Harvard, Von Neumann), and future topics. It then details bit representation, assembly languages (SimpleRisc, ARM, x86, RISC-V), processor design (logic gates, arithmetic, pipelining), memory systems, multiprocessors, I/O and storage, plus appendices on real processors (ARM, AMD, Intel) and graphics processors (NVIDIA Tesla, CUDA).

title: Introduction to Computer Architecture

nodes.title: Introduction to Computer Architecture (intro)
nodes.summary: The text introduces computer architecture as the study of computer design principles, technologies, algorithms, and trends. It highlights the field's rapid evolution and ubiquity. Two perspectives are explained: architecture (software view) and organization (hardware implementation). The importance for software designers and writers to understand hardware is stressed. A computer is defined as a general-purpose device that processes information via programs, with examples like embedded systems. The chapter aims to provide an academic overview of major principles behind modern computers.

nodes.title: What is a Computer?
nodes.summary: The text defines computer architecture as an amalgam of software and hardware, with architecture being the software view and organization the hardware implementation. It defines a computer as a general-purpose, programmable device that processes information to yield meaningful results, illustrating this with a C program example. It notes computers can be built from various materials and discusses the structure of a typical desktop computer, including the CPU, main memory, and hard disk, along with peripherals like keyboard, mouse, monitor, and printer.

nodes.title: Structure of a Typical Desktop Computer
nodes.summary: The text describes a typical desktop computer's structure, identifying CPU, main memory, and hard disk as core components. It explains their functions: CPU executes programs, main memory stores temporary data, and hard disk provides permanent storage. Peripheral components like keyboard, mouse, monitor, printer, and network are also covered, highlighting their roles in input, output, and connectivity. The processor is emphasized as the only active unit, while others are passive. Finally, it discusses that computers are fundamentally dumb machines that execute programs without independent thought, but excel at this task.

nodes.title: Computers are Dumb Machines
nodes.summary: The text presents block diagrams of a simple computer with and without peripherals, noting the processor's central role in executing programs and communicating with memory, hard disk, and peripherals, while others are passive. It argues computers are dumb, lacking abstract thought, but powerful due to fast program execution, comparing them to the brain. It asks how to make dumb machines do intelligent things, concluding that humans must write detailed programs with basic instructions. Finally, it discusses the language of instructions, explaining that computers need simple commands, and programmers use high-level languages like C or Java.

nodes.title: The Language of Instructions
nodes.summary: This text compares computers (dumb, ultra-fast, tireless) to human brains (intelligent, slow, creative, get bored). It asks how to make dumb machines do intelligent things: by using human creativity to write detailed computer programs that specify basic instructions. It covers the need for compilers to translate high-level languages (C, Java) into machine-readable executables, and defines instruction set architecture (ISA) as the semantics of a processor's instructions. It then discusses ISA design principles: completeness (ability to implement all user programs, e.g., loops, arithmetic), conciseness (limited instruction count, 64-1000), and genericity (capturing common operations like add, subtract, logical and/or, avoiding rare functions like sin⁻¹).

nodes.title: Instruction Set Design
key_items: Complete - The ISA should be able to Implement all User Programs; Concise – Limited Size of the Instruction Set
Complete - The ISA should be able to Implement all User Programs
Concise – Limited Size of the Instruction Set
Generic – Instructions should Capture the Common Case
nodes.summary: The text discusses instruction set design, emphasizing the ISA as a contract between software and hardware. It covers necessary property: completeness (ability to implement all user programs), and desirable properties: conciseness (limited instruction count, e.g., MIPS 64, x86 ~1000), genericity (capturing common cases like arithmetic/logical ops, not rare functions), and simplicity (RISC vs CISC debate, favoring simple instructions; definitions of RISC and CISC). It includes Important Point 1 and Way Point 1 summarizing key concepts. It then poses how to ensure ISA completeness, introducing theoretical questions about representing all programs, with an example of add/multiply lacking subtract, and mentions universal machines, noting casual readers can skip to summary.

nodes.title: How to Ensure that an ISA is Complete?
Towards a Universal ISA*
nodes.summary: The text covers key computing concepts: computers are fast but dumb; instructions are basic commands; compilers translate high-level code to machine instructions; ISA defines instruction semantics and should be complete, concise, generic, and simple. It questions ISA completeness, introduces universal machines as equivalent to complete ISAs, and discusses Alan Turing's theoretical Turing machine—its infinite tape, tape head, state register, and transition function—as the foundation for modern ISAs.

nodes.title: Turing Machine*
nodes.summary: This text defines a universal machine and relates ISA completeness to designing universal machines. It introduces the Turing machine's structure: infinite tape, tape head, state register, and action table. Examples show Turing machines incrementing numbers, recognizing a^n b^n strings, and checking palindromes. The Church-Turing thesis is stated, and the text notes Turing machines can solve complex problems. Finally, it describes a universal Turing machine that simulates any other Turing machine using an encoded action table, simulated state register, and work area on its tape.

nodes.title: Universal Turing Machine*
nodes.summary: The text explains universal Turing machines (UTMs), which simulate any other Turing machine using a generic action table, symbols, and states. It details encoding the simulated machine's action table as decimal entries with delimiters, and dividing UTM's tape into three areas: simulated action table, simulated state register, and work area. The UTM matches state and symbol to execute actions. It defines Turing completeness—systems equivalent to a Turing machine—and notes universal machines and ISAs are Turing complete. Finally, it describes a modified UTM variant: semi-infinite tape, state as table pointer, unique entry per state ignoring symbol, and actions computing new values via simple arithmetic functions.

nodes.title: A Modified Universal Turing Machine*
nodes.summary: The text explains universal Turing machines (UTMs), which simulate other Turing machines by matching simulated states and symbols to an action table, performing actions with many tape head movements. It defines Turing completeness as equivalence to a Turing machine, covering universal machines and ISAs. A modified UTM is detailed with a semi-infinite tape, state as a pointer to an action table, arithmetic actions, and conditional state changes. This suggests a practical machine organization: program (instruction array), program counter, data area, and memory as a semi-infinite array. A CPU computes arithmetic functions and jumps. A single-instruction ISA, 'sbn' (subtract and branch if negative), is shown to be Turing complete.

nodes.title: Single Instruction ISA*
nodes.summary: This text describes a basic instruction processing machine (CPU) with control, arithmetic, program counter, instruction, program, data, and memory, equivalent to a Turing machine and similar to Von Neumann architecture. It introduces a single-instruction ISA: 'sbn a, b, c' (subtract and branch if negative), proven Turing complete, with an example adding two numbers and a loop summing 1 to 10 using initialization and exit conditions. It mentions other single-instruction ISAs. Finally, it advocates for multiple instruction ISAs, categorizing necessary instructions into arithmetic, move, and branch types.

nodes.title: Multiple Instruction ISA*
nodes.summary: The text explains using the sbn instruction to add two numbers, then provides a loop to sum 1 to 10, noting exit and loop-back conditions. It lists other single-instruction complete ISAs. It introduces multiple instruction ISAs, categorizing needed instructions into arithmetic, move, and branch types, emphasizing at least these three are required. It summarizes theoretical results: designing a complete ISA equals designing a universal machine; universal machines relate to Turing machines; Turing completeness means equivalence to a Turing machine; and describes a modified Turing machine's structure with instruction table, program counter, and semi-infinite memory.

nodes.title: Summary of Theoretical Results
nodes.summary: The text outlines three essential instruction types: arithmetic, data transfer, and branch instructions. It summarizes theoretical results, linking ISA design to universal machines and Turing machines, including Turing completeness and a modified Turing machine with an instruction table, program counter, and memory. It describes a one-instruction ISA using sbn. Finally, it covers practical machine design, presenting the Harvard architecture with separate instruction and data memories, a control unit, ALU, and I/O devices, and introduces the Von Neumann architecture.

This section explores ISA completeness through theoretical and practical lenses. It starts with basic computing concepts and questions ISA completeness, introducing universal machines and Turing machines (infinite tape, state register) as foundations. It details Turing machines with examples, then universal Turing machines that simulate others via encoded action tables. Turing completeness is defined, and a modified UTM with semi-infinite tape and state-as-pointer is described, leading to a practical machine organization: program, program counter, data, memory, and CPU. A single-instruction ISA (sbn) is shown to be Turing complete, with programming examples. Finally, multiple instruction ISAs are advocated, categorizing required instructions into arithmetic, move, and branch types, and theoretical results are summarized, including Harvard and Von Neumann architectures.

nodes.title: Design of Practical Machines
Harvard Architecture
nodes.summary: The text discusses practical machine design, introducing the concept machine from Section 1.6.7 and Turing's 1936 influence. It details the Harvard Architecture (Harvard Mark-I), which separates instruction and data memory, with a CPU divided into control and ALU, plus I/O devices. It notes input/output evolution from switches and paper to keyboards and monitors. Then it introduces the Von Neumann Architecture for general-purpose Turing-complete computers, mentioning independent work by Mauchly and Eckert.

nodes.title: Von Neumann Architecture
nodes.summary: This text covers the evolution of practical computer architectures inspired by Turing's work. It introduces the Harvard Mark-I with separate instruction and data memories, and the Von Neumann architecture used in ENIAC and EDVAC, highlighting the stored-program concept where instructions are treated as data. It also discusses the limitations of finite memory compared to Turing machines and introduces register-based machines as extensions, explaining the role of registers for fast access and the use of load/store instructions.

nodes.title: Towards a Modern Machine with Registers and Stacks
nodes.summary: The text covers program representation in memory, including CPU program counter interpretation, program storage and dynamic modification, and compiler translation from high-level code. It notes finite memory limits compared to Turing machines. It then details Von Neumann extensions: register machines with fast small storage and load/store instructions, including an addition example; hardware stack machines using LIFO and operand-less operations, with an expression example and practical systems; and accumulator-based machines with a single register and memory operand, used in early computers and Intel x86. It concludes with a transition to building a modern register-augmented Von Neumann machine.

The section on Design of Practical Machines covers practical computer architectures inspired by Turing's work. It details the Harvard Architecture's separate instruction and data memory, CPU components, and I/O evolution. It introduces the Von Neumann architecture, emphasizing the stored-program concept and its use in ENIAC and EDVAC. The section discusses finite memory limits versus Turing machines and extends Von Neumann's design with register-based, stack-based, and accumulator-based machines, explaining registers, load/store instructions, LIFO stacks, and program representation, concluding with a transition to building a modern register-augmented Von Neumann machine.

nodes.title: The Road Ahead
The Road Ahead (intro)
nodes.summary: This text covers stack-based machines, including push/pop operations, an example computation, limitations like redundant loads/stores, and practical implementations (Burroughs, UCSD Pascal, HP 3000) plus Java's hypothetical stack machine and JVM conversion. It then describes accumulator-based machines, their single register, early use, and relevance in Intel x86 processors. Finally, it outlines the book's roadmap, including processor design, software interfaces, and representing information via bits, bytes, and words.

nodes.title: Representing Information
nodes.summary: The text outlines a computer architecture book's roadmap, contrasting software and hardware roles. It details chapters: introduction from software designers' perspective, processor design, and full system integration. It explains information representation via bits, bytes, and words, and the need for binary encoding. It previews Chapter 2 on bit language, Chapter 3 on assembly and SimpleRisc, Chapters 4-5 on ARM and x86 ISAs, Chapter 7 on logic gates, registers, and memories, and Chapter 8 on computer arithmetic for integers and reals.

nodes.title: Processing Information
nodes.summary: Text visualizes computer storage as switch arrays. It outlines upcoming chapters: bits, assembly language, SimpleRisc, ARM, and x86 ISAs. It details processor building blocks, logic gates, registers, memories, computer arithmetic, processor design, hardwired vs. micro-programmed styles, and pipelining. It covers optimizing designs and three subsystems: memory systems, multiprocessors, and I/O/storage (hard disks). It summarizes that a computer is a programmable device processing information via basic instructions, excelling at routine tasks quickly.

nodes.title: Processing More Information
nodes.summary: The text outlines the need to understand numerical operation implementation and design trade-offs before designing a simple processor in Chapter 9, covering hardwired and micro-programmed styles. It introduces pipelining for simultaneous instruction processing (Chapter 10). It then previews optimizing processor design into a full system via three subsystems: memory systems for performance (Chapter 11), multiprocessors (Chapter 12), and I/O and storage, especially hard disks for performance and reliability (Chapter 13). Finally, it summarizes that computers are dumb but fast at routine tasks, are programmable information processors, and execute basic instructions.

The Road Ahead covers stack-based machines (push/pop, example computation, redundant loads/stores, Burroughs, UCSD Pascal, HP 3000, Java's hypothetical stack machine and JVM) and accumulator-based machines (single register, early use, Intel x86 relevance). It then outlines the book's roadmap: bit, byte, and word representation; binary encoding; the bit language, assembly and SimpleRisc, ARM and x86 ISAs, logic gates, registers, memories, and computer arithmetic. Further chapters address processor design, hardwired versus micro-programmed styles, pipelining, and optimizing designs across memory systems, multiprocessors, and I/O and storage. The section concludes that computers are programmable information processors that excel at routine tasks.

nodes.title: Summary and Further Reading
nodes.summary: This text covers processor design, including numerical operations, trade-offs, and a step-by-step simple processor design with hardwired and micro-programmed styles. It introduces pipelining, then describes memory systems, multiprocessors, and I/O/storage. A summary defines computers, programs, ISA, Turing completeness, and architecture types (Harvard vs. Von Neumann), registers, stacks, and accumulators. Further reading suggestions and exercises are provided on processor identification, I/O devices, ISA properties, designing instruction sets (add, subtract, load, store, divide, branch), Turing completeness proofs, and stack machine programming.

summary: This section introduces computer architecture as the study of design principles, contrasting architecture (software view) and organization (hardware). It defines computers, describes typical desktop structure, and emphasizes they are dumb but fast. It covers instruction set architecture (ISA) design principles: completeness, conciseness, genericity, and simplicity, including RISC vs. CISC. It explores theoretical completeness via Turing machines and universal machines, leading to practical designs like Harvard and Von Neumann architectures, and register, stack, and accumulator-based machines. It outlines the book's roadmap and concludes with a summary, further reading, and exercises.

title: I Architecture: Software Interface

nodes.title: I Architecture: Software Interface (intro)
nodes.summary: The text explains that computers process only binary sequences of 0s and 1s, unlike human language. Silicon transistors act as switches setting logical 0 or 1, forming the basis of modern electronic computers from mobile phones to supercomputers. Early mechanical computers processed decimal numbers. The chapter defines a bit as a variable with values 0 or 1, and a byte as a sequence of 8 bits. It states the chapter will explore expressing concepts in bits, questioning what bits can do, and noting bits can achieve everything decimal circuits could.

nodes.title: The Language of Bits
The Language of Bits (intro)
nodes.summary: The text explains that computers use binary (0s and 1s) because silicon transistors are compatible with this. It defines bit and byte, and notes early mechanical computers used decimals. It introduces binary representation for logical and arithmetic operations, outlines chapters on logical operations, positive and negative integers, floating point numbers, and text, with arithmetic in Chapter 8. It covers George Boole's Boolean algebra and Claude Shannon's application to digital circuits, defining Boolean variable and Boolean algebra.

nodes.title: Logical Operations
Logical Operations (intro)
nodes.summary: The text covers binary representation and Boolean algebra. It divides operations into logical and arithmetic types, then outlines sections on logical operations using bits, representing positive integers, negative integers, floating point numbers, and text in binary. It defines binary representation. It introduces George Boole and Boolean algebra, defines Boolean variables, and explains basic operators like NOT and OR with truth tables. It uses examples like traffic lights to illustrate logical conditions.

nodes.title: Basic Operators
nodes.summary: The text covers basic Boolean operators: NOT, OR, and AND, with definitions and truth tables, illustrated via light bulbs and traffic lights. It explains representing complex logical conditions using Boolean variables and operators. Derived operators NAND, NOR, and XOR are introduced, noting NAND and NOR as universal operators. It concludes by introducing Boolean algebra rules. All concepts are supported by truth tables and symbolic representations.

nodes.title: Derived Operators
nodes.summary: The text defines the AND operator with its truth table, uses it to express logical conditions like R.Y + R.G + G.Y = 0 for bulb states, and introduces NOT, AND, OR as basic operators. It then covers derived operators NAND and NOR, including their truth tables and universal property, and defines XOR with its truth table and equivalence A ⊕ B = A.B + A.B. Finally, it starts Boolean algebra rules.

nodes.title: Boolean Algebra
nodes.summary: This text covers Boolean logic fundamentals: the AND operator and its truth table, with an example of encoding bulb states; derived operators NAND, NOR (universal operators), and XOR with their truth tables; rules of Boolean algebra for NOT, OR, and AND (definition, double negation, identity, annulment, idempotence, complementarity, commutativity, associativity, distributivity); De Morgan's laws with an example; proofs of the consensus theorem and another theorem; and an introduction to logic gates as implementations of Boolean functions.

nodes.title: De Morgan's Laws
nodes.summary: The text covers De Morgan's laws, showing the NOT of (A + B) equals the AND of complements and the NOT of (A.B) equals the OR of complements, verified by truth tables. It includes examples proving the consensus theorem and another theorem using Boolean algebra steps. It also introduces logic gates as devices implementing Boolean functions, constructible from various materials.

nodes.title: Logic Gates
nodes.summary: The text covers De Morgan's laws with equations and explanations; Example 5 proving the consensus theorem X.Y + X.Z + Y.Z = X.Y + X.Z; Example 6 proving (X + Z).(X + Y) = X.Y + X.Z and referencing Example 5; definition of a logic gate as a device implementing a Boolean function; a figure listing logic gate symbols for NOT, AND, NAND, OR, NOR, XOR, and XNOR; and an introduction to implementing Boolean functions via truth tables to minimize gates for area, power, and time.

nodes.title: Implementing Boolean Functions
nodes.summary: The text defines logic gates implementing Boolean functions and lists gate symbols. It explains implementing Boolean functions via truth tables, minterms, and canonical sum-of-products representation, noting inefficiency. Karnaugh maps are introduced for simplification: constructing grids, numbering minterms, combining adjacent 1-cells to eliminate variables, and rules for rectangles. Examples reduce functions to minimal forms. The section ends with a waypoint.

nodes.title: The Road Ahead
nodes.summary: The text explains minimizing Boolean functions using Karnaugh maps: combining adjacent cells differing in one variable eliminates that variable (e.g., combining 110 and 111 yields A.B). It details rules for rectangles (power of 2 size, no 0 minterms, maximal size, no strict subset) and provides an example. A section 'The Road Ahead' reviews Boolean algebra basics, operators, De Morgan's laws, logic gates, minimization goals, and mentions future topics like number representation. It then introduces positive integers, starting with ancient number systems (Roman and Indian numerals), describing Roman numeral representation and its complications.

The section on Logical Operations covers binary representation, Boolean algebra, and their applications. It introduces George Boole's algebra, basic operators (NOT, OR, AND), and derived operators (NAND, NOR, XOR) with truth tables. It explains Boolean algebra rules, De Morgan's laws, consensus theorem, and logic gates as implementations of Boolean functions. It details implementing Boolean functions via truth tables, minterms, and canonical sum-of-products, followed by Karnaugh maps for minimization. The section concludes with a review and an introduction to number representation, starting with positive integers and ancient systems like Roman numerals.

nodes.title: Positive Integers
Ancient Number Systems
nodes.summary: The text introduces Boolean algebra, covering variables (0/1), operators (AND, OR, NOT, NAND, NOR, XOR), their properties (associative, commutative, reflexive), De Morgan's laws, logic gates, and minimizing gates using Karnaugh maps. It then shifts to number systems, discussing Roman and Indian numerals, place value, and bases. It defines decimal (base 10) and binary (base 2) systems, explaining representation and conversion, emphasizing binary's suitability for computers.

nodes.title: Binary Number System
nodes.summary: The text covers generalizing number bases, introducing notation like 3243₁₀, and detailing the binary system with definitions, examples, and conversions. It explains MSB, LSB, and introduces hexadecimal and octal systems for compact representation, providing conversion methods between binary, octal, and hex. It includes formulas and examples for these conversions and briefly introduces adding binary numbers.

nodes.title: Adding Binary Numbers
nodes.summary: This text covers binary-to-hexadecimal and binary-to-octal conversions using grouping of 4 or 3 bits, with examples. It explains binary addition, including 1-bit addition, truth tables for sum and carry, and n-bit addition with an example. Finally, it discusses sizes of unsigned integers in programming, detailing short (16-bit), int (32-bit), and long long int (64-bit) ranges, and provides a method to calculate the range of unsigned short integers.

nodes.title: Sizes of Integers
nodes.summary: The text explains adding n-bit binary numbers with an example, then covers unsigned integer sizes in C/C++ (short, int, long long int), their ranges, and calculating ranges for n-bit integers and bits needed for a decimal range. It introduces negative integers, discussing sign-magnitude representation, its range, two zeros, and arithmetic difficulties, and begins explaining the 1's complement approach, which flips bits for negatives and has the same range as sign-magnitude.

The section on positive integers covers ancient number systems including Roman and Indian numerals, place value, and bases like decimal and binary. It details binary representation, conversions between binary, octal, and hexadecimal, and binary addition. It also discusses Boolean algebra, logic gates, and Karnaugh maps. Finally, it explains unsigned integer sizes in programming (short, int, long long int), their ranges, and introduces negative integer representations like sign-magnitude and 1's complement.

nodes.title: Negative Integers
Sign-Magnitude-Based Representation
nodes.summary: The text introduces representing negative integers in binary. It defines the problem of mapping signed numbers to unsigned integers and the SgnBit function. It describes sign-magnitude representation, using the MSB for sign and remaining bits for magnitude, with range ±(2^(n-1)-1) and two zeros, and notes difficulties in arithmetic. It then introduces 1's complement, where positive numbers use a sign bit and negative numbers are formed by flipping all bits, also with range ±(2^(n-1)-1).

nodes.title: The 1's Complement Approach
nodes.summary: This text discusses representations of negative integers in binary systems. It introduces the general problem of mapping signed numbers to unsigned integers. It covers three methods: sign-magnitude representation, which uses a sign bit and magnitude bits but has two zeros and difficult arithmetic; 1's complement, which flips bits for negatives but also has two zeros and addition issues; and bias-based representation, which adds a constant bias, has a single zero and simpler addition but complicated multiplication. Each method's range, mapping function, examples, and arithmetic drawbacks are explained.

nodes.title: Bias-Based Approach
nodes.summary: The text defines the mapping function for 1’s complement, showing examples, deficiencies like dual zero representations and addition issues. It introduces the bias-based approach with formula F(u)=u+bias, examples, and discusses addition working with bias adjustment but multiplication being difficult. Finally, it motivates the 2’s complement method by listing lessons from previous approaches, explaining overflow and underflow definitions, and describing the number circle with a break point.

nodes.title: The 2's Complement Method
The 2's Complement Method (intro)
nodes.summary: The text explains the 2's complement method, starting from lessons learned from sign-magnitude, 1's complement, and bias-based approaches: need for simplicity, unified hardware for signed and unsigned arithmetic, and unique zero representation. It introduces the number circle using 4-bit examples, defines overflow and underflow, and describes the break point. It details the 2's complement system, its creation steps, and properties like unique zero, MSB as sign bit, negation rule, addition rule, and subtraction rule, using modulo arithmetic.

nodes.title: Properties of the 2’s Complement Representation
nodes.summary: The text covers properties of 2's complement representation: unique zero, MSB as sign bit, negation, unique representation range, and addition, subtraction, multiplication, and loop rules with proofs. It explains computing 2's complement via bit flip plus one, demonstrates a 4-bit addition example, and describes sign extension for converting between bit widths by replicating the sign bit.

nodes.title: Computing the 2’s Complement Representation
nodes.summary: The text demonstrates adding 4 and -3 in 4-bit 2's complement both graphically and via binary addition, noting discarded carry. It explains computing 2's complement for negative numbers as flipping bits and adding 1. Finally, it describes sign extension for converting a 16-bit number to 32-bit, showing that positive numbers are prefixed with zeros and negative numbers with ones, effectively copying the sign bit.

nodes.title: The Sign Extension Trick
nodes.summary: This text covers 2's complement representation, including an example of adding 4 and -3 using a 4-bit system, both graphically and via binary addition with overflow discard. It details computing 2's complement by inverting bits and adding 1, sign extension for converting bit-widths by replicating the sign bit, and the range from -2^{n-1} to 2^{n-1}-1. It presents a theorem for overflow detection: no overflow if operand signs differ; overflow if signs are same and result sign differs or is zero, with proof using the number circle. Finally, it offers an alternative interpretation: a signed n-bit number equals (A_{1...n-1} - A_n 2^{n-1}).

nodes.title: 2's Complement Range, Overflow Detection, and Alternative Interpretation
key_items: Range of the 2’s Complement Number System
Checking if a 2’s Complement Addition has Resulted in an Overflow
nodes.summary: The page covers the range of the 2's complement number system from -2^(n-1) to 2^(n-1)-1, including the extra negative number -2^(n-1). It presents a theorem for detecting overflow in 2's complement addition: overflow never occurs if operands have different signs; if operands have the same sign, overflow occurs if the result has an opposite sign or is zero. The proof uses the number circle and break point concept. Finally, an alternative interpretation theorem states that a signed n-bit number equals (A1...n-1 - An2^(n-1)), with bit indexing explained.

nodes.title: Alternative Interpretation of 2’s Complement
nodes.summary: The text covers the 2’s complement number system's range from −2^(n−1) to 2^(n−1)−1, including the extra negative number. It presents Theorem 2.3.4.1 for detecting overflow in addition: overflow cannot occur if operand signs differ, but can if signs are the same and the result has opposite sign or is zero. It proves this using the number circle and break point. Theorem 2.3.4.2 provides an alternative interpretation: an n-bit signed number equals A1...n−1 minus An*2^(n−1). It then introduces floating point numbers, defines fixed point numbers, and begins discussing generic floating point representation in base 10 and IEEE 754.

nodes.title: Number Systems: Two's Complement and Floating Point Representation
key_items: 2.4.2 Generic Form of Floating Point Numbers
nodes.summary: The page begins with a proof about two's complement representation for negative numbers, showing that A = A1...n − 2^n. It then introduces floating point numbers as numbers with a decimal point, noting integers are a subset, and mentions the IEEE 754 standard. To simplify, it discusses fixed point numbers, which have a fixed number of digits after the decimal point, giving monetary values as an example, and notes that addition and subtraction are easy but multiplication and division are difficult. Finally, it introduces the generic form of floating point numbers, which can have many digits after the decimal point, and begins discussing base-10 representation for positive numbers.

The 2's complement method is introduced, covering its motivation from sign-magnitude, 1's complement, and bias-based approaches, emphasizing unified hardware, unique zero, and modulo arithmetic. Properties include unique zero, MSB as sign bit, negation, addition, subtraction, multiplication, loop rules, and sign extension. Computation via bit flip plus one, addition examples, and sign extension for bit-width conversion are explained. Range is -2^(n-1) to 2^(n-1)-1, with overflow detection rules and proof using the number circle. An alternative interpretation equates signed n-bit numbers to A1...n-1 minus An*2^(n-1). The section transitions to floating point, defining fixed point, monetary examples, and generic base-10 floating point representation, leading to IEEE 754.

The section on negative integers covers binary representation methods: sign-magnitude, 1's complement, bias-based, and 2's complement. It details their mappings, ranges, examples, and arithmetic issues like dual zeros and difficult operations. The 2's complement method is emphasized for unified hardware, unique zero, modulo arithmetic, and properties such as negation, addition, subtraction, multiplication, loop rules, and sign extension. Overflow detection and number circle proof are included. The section transitions to floating point, defining fixed point, monetary examples, and base-10 floating point representation, leading to IEEE 754.

nodes.title: Floating Point Numbers
Fixed Point Numbers
nodes.summary: The text begins with a proof about 4-bit two's complement representation, showing -2 as 1110₂ and deriving A = A₁...ₙ − 2ⁿ for negative numbers. It then introduces floating point numbers with decimal point examples, notes integers as a subset, and mentions the IEEE 754 standard. Fixed point numbers are described with fixed decimal digits, using monetary values as an example, and their binary representation, ease of addition/subtraction, and difficulty in multiplication/division. Finally, it discusses the generic form of floating point numbers, contrasting them with fixed point, and starts explaining base-10 representation for positive floating point numbers.

nodes.title: Generic Form of Floating Point Numbers
nodes.summary: The text begins with a proof about 4-bit two's complement representation. It then covers floating point numbers, defining them and noting integers as a subset. Fixed point numbers are explained with monetary examples. The generic base-10 and binary forms for floating point numbers are derived, including expansions and examples. Normal form is introduced with significand, mantissa, and exponent, and definitions are provided. Finally, the IEEE 754 32-bit format is detailed, including bit allocation (sign, exponent, mantissa), biased exponent representation, bias value (127), and valid ranges for normal numbers.

nodes.title: IEEE 754 Format for Representing Floating Point Numbers
nodes.summary: The text describes normal form floating point representation with sign, significand, mantissa, and exponent, and introduces the IEEE 754 32-bit format, allocating bits for sign, biased exponent, and mantissa. It covers exponent bias (127), valid ranges, special values like infinity, NAN, zeros, and denormal numbers, with examples of smallest and largest normal values. Denormal numbers extend the range near zero, with a modified formula and default exponent -126.

nodes.title: Denormal Numbers
nodes.summary: The text covers IEEE 754 floating-point special cases: NANs from invalid operations and their propagation, positive/negative zeros, and denormal numbers. Denormals (E=0, implicit 0, exponent -126) extend representable values below normal numbers, with smallest positive 2^-149 and largest 2^-126 - 2^-149. They prevent underflow-to-zero but are slow and unsupported on some embedded processors, though common on laptops/desktops. Finally, double precision (64-bit) is introduced: 52-bit mantissa, 11-bit exponent, bias 1023, exponent range -1022 to 1023, for larger range and precision.

nodes.title: Double Precision Numbers
nodes.summary: The text defines smallest and largest positive denormal numbers and their ranges for positive and negative values, explaining their role as a buffer to avoid unexpected results, and noting that embedded processors often lack support. It introduces double precision numbers with 64 bits, detailing 52-bit mantissa, 11-bit exponent, bias 1023, and exponent range -1022 to 1023. It discusses floating point mathematics, covering inexact representation of rational and irrational numbers, non-associativity of operations, and commutativity, with a code example showing order effects.

nodes.title: Floating Point Mathematics
nodes.summary: The text covers floating point precision issues, including irrational number representation, limited mantissa bits, and non-associativity with examples like A+B-A, emphasizing operation order and bracket placement. It then introduces strings, describing ASCII as a 7-bit encoding for English characters, punctuation, and control codes, and UTF-8 as a variable-length (1-6 bytes) Unicode encoding compatible with ASCII, specifying byte structures and language byte requirements.

This section covers floating point numbers, starting with fixed point numbers, their binary representation, and operations. It explains the generic form with significand and exponent, then details the IEEE 754 32-bit format including bias, special values, and denormal numbers. It introduces double precision (64-bit) with larger range and precision. It discusses floating point mathematics, including precision issues, non-associativity, and commutativity, and briefly touches on string encoding with ASCII and UTF-8.

nodes.title: Strings
nodes.summary: The text covers floating point precision challenges and bracket placement. It details strings, starting with ASCII: 7-bit codes for 128 English characters, with control and printable characters. It introduces Unicode and UTF-8, which encodes over 1.1 million characters using 1-6 bytes, is ASCII-compatible, and dominates the web. It then mentions UTF-16 (2 or 4 bytes, used by Java and Windows) and UTF-32 (fixed 32 bits, rarely used). A table lists ASCII characters and codes. The summary reviews bits, bytes, Boolean algebra, canonical forms, Karnaugh maps, integer representation, four negative number methods, and details 2's complement properties and arithmetic.

nodes.title: Summary and Further Reading
nodes.summary: This text summarizes computer architecture fundamentals: bit/byte representation, Boolean algebra (OR, AND, NOT, NAND, NOR, XOR, De Morgan's laws, minterms, Karnaugh maps), integer number systems (binary, sign-magnitude, 1's complement, bias, 2's complement with properties like sign extension and overflow), IEEE 754 floating point (sign, significand, exponent, bias, denormal numbers, approximation issues), and character encoding (ASCII, Unicode). The section covers binary representation using bits/bytes, Boolean algebra (operators, laws, gates, Karnaugh maps), and integer systems (positive: Roman/Indian, bases, conversions; negative: sign-magnitude, 1's complement, 2's complement with arithmetic, overflow, sign extension). It explains floating point (fixed point, IEEE 754 32/64-bit, precision issues) and character encoding (ASCII, Unicode, UTF-8/16/32). It includes a summary, exercises, further reading, and introduces assembly language and SimpleRisc.

nodes.title: Assembly Language
Why Assembly Language
nodes.summary: Chapter 3 introduces assembly language as a textual representation of machine instructions, essential for understanding processor design and software development. It outlines the chapter's structure: discussing the need for assembly language from software and hardware perspectives, explaining generic semantics, designing the SimpleRisc assembly language, and encoding it. Section 3.1 covers why assembly is needed, including the compiler's role, challenges like performance and missing functionality, and definitions of assembler and cross-compiler. It also explains hardware designers' need to understand instruction semantics. Section 3.2 begins the basics, starting with the abstract machine model and assembly language's interaction with registers and memory.

nodes.title: The Basics of Assembly Language
Machine Model
nodes.summary: The text explains the importance of assembly language for processor design, using the GNU assembler format. It details the abstract Von Neumann machine model with registers, instruction memory, data memory, program counter, CPU, ALU, and I/O devices. It covers register views (ARM, x86, return address register, PC visibility), memory view (byte-addressable, 32/64-bit addresses, program storage), and little endian vs. big endian representations for multi-byte data types, including an example of storing a hexadecimal integer.

nodes.title: View of Memory
nodes.summary: This text covers registers and memory in assembly programming. It details register visibility for ARM, x86, and x86-64, including names, return address registers, and program counter visibility. Memory is explained as a byte-addressable array, with little and big endian representations for multi-byte data. Array storage is discussed, including row-major and column-major mapping for multidimensional arrays. Finally, assembly language syntax is introduced, focusing on the GNU assembler format and file structure.

nodes.title: Assembly Language Syntax
nodes.summary: This text covers multidimensional array mapping to 1-D arrays using row-major and column-major representations, with definitions. It then introduces GNU assembly language syntax, including file structure (sections like .text, .data, .bss), basic statement format (instruction and operands), immediate values, examples of add, sub, and mul instructions, and generic statement structure with labels, keys, directives, and comments. It classifies instructions by functionality (data processing, data transfer, branch, exception generating) and by number of operands (0-address to 3-address formats), noting that the book focuses on data processing, data transfer, and control instructions.

nodes.title: Types of Instructions
nodes.summary: The text outlines assembly language instruction types and formats. It classifies instructions by functionality into data processing, data transfer, branch, and exception generating, noting the book covers the first three. It then classifies instructions by operand count as n-address formats, compares ARM's 3-address and x86's 2-address formats with trade-offs, and provides examples. Finally, it defines addressing mode as the method of specifying and accessing an operand, transitioning to operand types.

nodes.title: Types of Operands
nodes.summary: The text defines n-address instruction formats, comparing 3-address ARM and 2-address x86 instructions, and discusses trade-offs between operand count, instruction size, and flexibility. It defines addressing modes as methods to specify operands, covers immediate addressing, and introduces register transfer notation for instruction semantics. It lists common addressing modes: immediate, register, register-indirect, base-offset, base-index, base-index-offset, memory-direct, memory-indirect, and PC-relative, and defines effective memory address. It introduces SimpleRisc, a 21-instruction RISC ISA for teaching and processor design, and surveys real instruction sets (ARM, x86, MIPS, etc.), comparing their types, years, vendors, registers, bits, and endianness.

This section introduces the fundamentals of assembly language. It begins with the Von Neumann machine model, detailing CPU components, register views for ARM, x86, and x86-64, memory as a byte-addressable array, and endianness. It covers multidimensional array mapping via row-major and column-major order, then presents GNU assembler syntax, including file structure, instruction formats, directives, and comments. Instruction classification by functionality and operand count (n-address formats) is explained, comparing ARM and x86. Addressing modes and operand types are discussed, including immediate, register, indirect, base-offset, and PC-relative modes, along with effective address calculation. Finally, SimpleRisc and real ISAs like ARM, x86, and MIPS are surveyed.

nodes.title: SimpleRisc
Different Instruction Sets
nodes.summary: This text introduces SimpleRisc, a RISC ISA with 21 instructions, used for teaching assembly and processor design. It surveys instruction sets including ARM, x86, MIPS, and others, with a table of popular ISAs. Details of the SimpleRisc machine model are given: 16 registers (r0-r15), with r14 as stack pointer and r15 as return address, 32-bit registers, flags register, 32-bit instructions, Von Neumann memory, and little-endian format. Specific instructions are described: the mov instruction for register transfer with a 16-bit signed immediate, and six arithmetic instructions: add, sub, mul, div, mod, and cmp.

nodes.title: SimpleRisc Machine Model, mov, and Arithmetic Instructions
nodes.summary: The page discusses processor families (IBM PowerPC, Sun UltraSparc, HP PA-RISC) and their RISC instruction sets, noting shared simple instructions and specialized ones. It introduces the SimpleRisc ISA, similar to ARM and MIPS. The model has 16 registers (r0-r15): 14 general-purpose, r14 as stack pointer (sp), r15 as return address (ra), each 32 bits. A hidden flags register holds E and GT bits. Instructions are 32-bit, memory is Von Neumann with little-endian multibyte data. The mov instruction (2-address) transfers register or 16-bit signed immediate to a register. Six arithmetic instructions are listed: add, sub, mul, div, mod, cmp, with destination as first operand.

nodes.title: Arithmetic Instructions
nodes.summary: This text covers instruction set architectures (ISAs) for server processors (IBM PowerPC, Sun/Oracle UltraSparc, HP PA-RISC), noting they are RISC-based with common simple instructions and specialized ones, and mentions SimpleRisc ISA. It details the SimpleRisc machine model: 16 registers (r0-r15, with r14 as stack pointer, r15 as return address), 32-bit width, internal flags (E, GT), 32-bit instructions, Von Neumann memory model with little-endian format. It specifies SimpleRisc instructions: mov (register transfer), arithmetic (add, sub, mul, div, mod, cmp), logical (and, or, not), and shift (lsl, lsr, asr), including semantics, formats, examples, and usage in code snippets.

nodes.title: Logical Instructions
nodes.summary: The text covers SimpleRisc instructions: the cmp instruction compares operands via subtraction, setting flags.E and flags.GT for equality and greater-than conditions. It details three logical instructions (and, or, not), including formats, bitwise operations, and an example computing (a ∨ b). It also describes three shift instructions (lsl, lsr, asr), their 3-address format, source operands, shift amount types, and differences between logical and arithmetic right shifts, referencing tables for semantics.

nodes.title: Shift Instructions – lsl, lsr, asr
nodes.summary: This text covers SimpleRisc instructions: comparison (cmp) setting flags for branches; logical instructions (and, or, not) with semantics and examples; shift instructions (lsl, lsr, asr) including logical vs arithmetic shifts; data transfer instructions (ld, st) detailing memory address computation and little-endian representation; and unconditional branch instruction (b) that jumps to a label.

nodes.title: Data Transfer Instructions: ld and st
nodes.summary: The text covers the semantics of shift instructions (lsl, lsr, asr) in SimpleRisc, including register/immediate operands, examples, and explanations. It describes data transfer instructions (ld, st), detailing memory address computation using register plus immediate offset, little-endian byte storage, and corresponding load/store operations with examples and semantics. It also introduces the unconditional branch instruction (b), which jumps to a labeled address, with its semantics and a brief example reference.

nodes.title: Unconditional Branch Instructions
nodes.summary: The text covers SimpleRisc instruction semantics: shift instructions (lsl, lsr, asr) with examples and explanations; data transfer instructions (ld, st) for loading/storing values between registers and memory, including address calculation, little-endian representation, and diagrams; unconditional branch instruction (b) for jumping to labels, with an example; and conditional branch instructions (beq, bgt) that branch based on E and GT flags from a preceding cmp instruction.

nodes.title: Conditional Branch Instructions
nodes.summary: The text covers SimpleRisc load/store operations with a figure, unconditional branching example, and conditional branch instructions beq and bgt with semantics table. It provides assembly examples: factorial using loop and bgt, primality test using mod, cmp, and beq, and LCM computation. Finally, it introduces functions (subroutines/procedures) as modular code constructs, with a C example for adding two numbers.

nodes.title: Functions
nodes.summary: The text covers assembly programming examples for prime checking and LCM calculation, then explains functions: return addresses, the call instruction and return address register, passing arguments and return values, problems of limited registers and overwriting, solutions via register spilling, caller-saved and callee-saved registers, the stack and activation blocks, stack pointer, function call/return instructions (call and ret) in SimpleRisc, and the LIFO nature of the stack.

nodes.title: Function Call/Return Instructions
nodes.summary: The text covers function call mechanics: copying arguments, initializing local variables, spilling registers, and destroying activation blocks via stack pointer adjustments. It explains stack-based variable and register protection using caller-saved and callee-saved schemes, and passing arguments and return values through the stack. It details SimpleRisc's call and ret instructions, including semantics, examples (adding, function invocation, recursive factorial), and the caller-saved register restoration. Finally, it introduces the nop instruction and poses a question about its purpose.

nodes.title: The nop Instruction
nodes.summary: The text covers converting a factorial program to SimpleRisc assembly, showing stack usage for saving/restoring registers with caller-saves convention. It introduces the nop instruction, explaining it does nothing but is needed for correctness in pipelining (Chapter 10). It then addresses loading 32-bit constants, demonstrating a 6-instruction sequence, and proposes modifiers ('u' or 'h') on ALU instructions to load constants in two operations, noting default sign extension for 16-bit immediates.

nodes.title: Modifiers
nodes.summary: The text justifies the nop instruction for correctness, then addresses loading 32-bit constants into registers using modifiers. It explains suffixes 'u' for unsigned immediates and 'h' for loading into upper half, reducing constant loading from six to two instructions. It also introduces encoding the SimpleRisc instruction set, defining opcodes and detailing the encoding of 0-address instructions like ret and nop.

nodes.title: Encoding the SimpleRisc Instruction Set
Encoding 0-Address Instructions
nodes.summary: The text explains sign extension for 16-bit immediates, introducing 'u' and 'h' suffixes for unsigned and upper-half loading, and their use in ALU instructions except shifts to reduce constant loading from six to two instructions and create byte-setting routines. It then details encoding the SimpleRisc instruction set into 32-bit values, defining opcodes with 5 bits for 21 instructions. It covers encoding 0-address instructions (ret, nop) with just opcodes, and 1-address instructions (call, b, beq, bgt) using 27-bit PC-relative offsets, optimized by assuming 4-byte alignment to effectively cover 29-bit byte offsets.

nodes.title: Encoding 1-Address Instructions
nodes.summary: The text presents instruction opcodes for add, sub, mul, div, mod, cmp, and, or, not, mov, lsl, lsr, asr, nop, ld, st, beq, bgt, b, call, and ret, along with a diagram for encoding the ret instruction. It describes the branch format (op and offset fields). Finally, it covers 3-address instructions (add, sub, mul, div, mod, and, or, lsl, lsr, asr), explaining the I bit for immediate vs. register operands, the register format fields (op, I, rd, rs1, rs2), and the immediate format with an 18-bit immediate split into a 2-bit modifier and 16-bit constant.

nodes.title: Encoding 3-Address Instructions
nodes.summary: The text details instruction encoding for a SimpleRisc processor, covering branching, 3-address instructions, and special cases. It explains handling rare branch targets over 228 bytes via chaining and describes the 1-address branch format. It then presents 3-address instruction encoding, distinguishing between register and immediate formats, including field definitions (op, I, rd, rs1, rs2/imm) and immediate modifier bits. An example encodes a sub instruction. Finally, it outlines encoding for cmp, not, and mov instructions, reusing the 3-address formats with empty fields for regularity and easy decoding.

nodes.title: Encoding cmp, not, and mov
nodes.summary: The text covers instruction encoding in SimpleRisc, including an example binary-to-hex conversion (0x0C480003). It details encoding for cmp (using 3-address format with empty destination), not, and mov (using 3-address format with empty first source). It discusses load and store instructions: ld uses 3-address immediate format with base register and offset; st reuses immediate format with rd holding the source register, accepting a design trade-off to avoid a new format. Figure 3.16 shows cmp, not, mov formats; Figure 3.17 shows ld/st formats. Example 36 encodes st r8, 20[r2].

nodes.title: Load and Store Instructions
nodes.summary: The text discusses SimpleRisc load and store instructions, which are 2-address instructions using base-offset addressing. It explains encoding load instructions with the three-address immediate format, setting the I bit. For store instructions, it addresses Question 5 about whether to define a new format, deciding against it for efficiency and instead reusing the immediate format with rd as the source register. Example 36 demonstrates encoding 'st r8, 20[r2]' into binary and hex. It includes Figure 3.17 showing load/store encodings, and Table 3.11 summarizing instruction formats. It concludes with a summary of instruction formats, emphasizing fixed 4-byte instructions, the decoder's role, and design trade-offs between elegance and efficiency.

nodes.title: Summary of Instruction Formats
nodes.summary: The text covers encoding load/store instructions with an example, summarizes instruction formats including branch, immediate, and register types with field definitions and a table, explains decoding logic based on opcode and I bit, and outlines lessons for designing an ISA: studying workload, limiting instruction count (64-128), choosing instruction types and distribution, and optimizing common cases.

nodes.title: Lessons Learned
nodes.summary: The text explains branch, immediate, and register instruction formats, detailing branch opcodes, nop detection, and using the I bit to distinguish immediate/register formats. It outlines six ISA design lessons: studying workload, limiting instruction count to 64-128, choosing instruction types based on workload (example distribution), defining common-case-fast instructions and operand formats, selecting addressing modes weighing hardware tradeoffs, and designing simple encoding for easy decoding. A chapter summary notes assembly language as textual machine instruction representation, assemblers converting to machine code, ISA-specific assembly, and its use for efficient programming, OS routines, and hardware designers.

nodes.title: Instruction Format, Addressing Modes, Encoding, and Assembly Summary
nodes.summary: Instruction design decisions include handling divisional operations, choosing formats (3-address, 2-address, 11-address), selecting addressing modes (register-indirect vs. register-only) with hardware and register tradeoffs, and encoding for simple decoding. nodes.title: ARM® Assembly Language
The ARM® Machine Model

It introduces the ARM machine model, noting 16 programmer-visible 32-bit registers (r0-r15), with special roles for r11 (frame pointer), r12 (scratch), r13 (stack pointer), r14 (link register), and r15 (program counter), using little-endian GNU syntax. nodes.title: Basic Assembly Instructions
Simple Data Processing Instructions
nodes.summary: The text covers ARM registers, distinguishing generic (r0-r12) from special (sp, lr, pc), and describes basic and advanced assembly instructions. It details data processing instructions like mov, mvn, arithmetic (add, sub, rsb), logical (and, eor, orr, bic), multiplication (mul, mla, smull, umull), and division (sdiv, udiv), with examples and semantics. nodes.title: Advanced Data-Processing Instructions
nodes.summary: The text covers ARM assembly language details: multiply instructions producing 64-bit results with register constraints; division instructions sdiv and udiv with quotient/remainder semantics; advanced data-processing instruction formats; shifter operands including lsl, lsr, asr, ror, and rrx, with examples; addressing modes: register, immediate, scaled-register; compare instructions cmp, cmn, tst, teq; and the CPSR register's condition flags N, Z, C, V, including how they are set by arithmetic, logical, and comparison operations.

nodes.title: Compare Instructions
nodes.summary: The text covers ARM addressing modes (immediate, scaled-register), compare instructions (cmp, cmn, tst, teq) in 2-address format that update CPSR flags. It details the CPSR register, a 32-bit register with N, Z, C, V condition flags at bits 29-32, explaining flag-setting rules for negative, zero, carry, and overflow conditions, including carry for addition, subtraction, and shifts. nodes.title: Instructions that Set CPSR Flags – The `S' Suffix
nodes.summary: The text covers ARM's four compare instructions (cmp, cmn, tst, teq), their semantics, examples, and flag updates. nodes.title: Data Processing Instructions that use CPSR Flags
nodes.summary: The text covers ARM compare instructions (cmp, cmn, tst, teq) that update CPSR flags by performing subtraction, addition, AND, or XOR, with examples and semantics. nodes.title: Simple Branch Instructions
nodes.summary: This text covers ARM assembly instructions and programming examples. nodes.title: Branch and Link Instruction
nodes.summary: The text explains ARM assembly programming concepts: computing a factorial iteratively, and a program to check if a number is a perfect square using a loop and comparison. nodes.title: Conditional Instructions
nodes.summary: The text explains ARM assembly through an example of a function call and return, and introduces the bx instruction for returning from functions with its semantics. It details ARM condition codes, listing 16 codes with their suffixes, meanings, and associated CPSR flags, and discusses their use in branches and normal instructions like addeq, illustrated by a program counting 1s. Finally, it covers simple load-store instructions (ldr and str) and their base register usage, including brief mentions of offset addressing and base registers.

nodes.title: Load-Store Instructions
nodes.summary: This text explains ARM load-store instructions: basic ldr/str using register-indirect addressing, variants with immediate or register offsets (base-offset, base-index, base-scaled-index modes), and byte/half-word operations (ldrb, ldrh, ldrsb, ldrsh, strb, strh) that handle signed/unsigned data with sign extension on loads. nodes.title: Advanced Features
Advanced Features (intro)
nodes.summary: ARM load-store instructions for bytes and half-words (ldrb, ldrh, ldrsb, ldrsh, strb, strh) are detailed, covering semantics, examples, and sign extension. nodes.title: Functions

nodes.title: Encoding the Instruction Set
Data Processing Instructions
nodes.summary: The text covers ARM instruction encoding: generic 32-bit format with condition codes and instruction types; data processing instructions, including immediate value encoding via 4-bit rotation and 8-bit payload, and shifter operand encoding; load/store instruction bit fields (I, P, U, B, W, L) for addressing modes, transfer size, and operation; examples of encoding immediate values; and the need for assemblers to handle non-encodable immediates.

nodes.title: Load-Store Instructions
nodes.summary: The text covers ARM load-store and branch instructions. It explains load/store encoding, including handling a register as a shifter operand, and details the format with bits I, P, U, B, W, L and their semantics. It describes immediate encoding (0-4095) and the purpose of the U bit for negative offsets. Finally, it details branch and branch-and-link instruction formats, including the 24-bit signed offset, shifting by 2, sign extension, and target calculation as PC+8.

nodes.title: Branch Instructions
nodes.summary: This text covers ARM memory instruction immediates, explaining that the 12-bit immediate is unsigned (0-4095) and that the U bit enables negative offsets by signaling subtraction. Branch instruction encoding is detailed, with a 24-bit signed offset shifted, sign-extended, and added to PC+8 for target computation; the L bit distinguishes branch-and-link. A summary lists ARM ISA features: 32-bit RISC, 16 registers, lr, visible PC, 32-bit encoding, 3-address data processing, CPSR flags, conditional execution, two branch variants, addressing modes, byte/half-word support, and data processing encoding fields.

This section covers ARM instruction encoding, including the generic 32-bit format with condition codes. It details data processing instructions, immediate value encoding via 4-bit rotation and 8-bit payload, shifter operands, and assembler handling of non-encodable immediates. Load/store instructions are explained with bit fields I, P, U, B, W, L for addressing modes, transfer size, and operation, including register shifter operands, immediate encoding (0-4095), and the U bit for negative offsets. Branch instructions are described with 24-bit signed offset, shifting, sign extension, target calculation as PC+8, and L bit for branch-and-link. The section concludes with a summary of ARM ISA features: 32-bit RISC, 16 registers, lr, visible PC, 3-address data processing, CPSR flags, conditional execution, branch variants, addressing modes, byte/half-word support, and encoding fields.

nodes.title: Summary and Further Reading
nodes.summary: This text summarizes ARM ISA features: its 32-bit RISC design, 16 registers (lr, pc), 3-address data processing with immediate operands, flag-setting compare and conditional instructions, branch and branch-and-link variants, base-index/base-offset and pre/post-indexed addressing, byte/half-word load/store, instruction encoding for data processing, data transfer, and branch instructions. It also lists further reading on Thumb, VFP, SIMD, security, A64, and exercises on ARM assembly programming, encoding, and design, followed by an introduction to the x86 family history from 8086 to 80486.

The ARM assembly language section covers the ARM machine model, including its 32-bit RISC architecture, registers (r0-r15 with special roles), and basic instructions like mov and mvn. It details data processing, arithmetic, logical, multiplication, division, compare, branch, and load-store instructions, along with addressing modes, shifter operands, and CPSR flags. Advanced features include byte/half-word operations, array handling, structures, stack operations (ldmfd/stmfd), and instruction encoding formats for data processing, load/store, and branch instructions. The section concludes with a summary of ARM ISA features and further reading on Thumb, VFP, SIMD, security, A64, and exercises, followed by an introduction to x86 family history.

nodes.title: x86 Assembly Language
Overview of the x86 Family of Assembly Languages
key_items: Main Features of the x86 ISA
nodes.summary: Chapter 5 introduces the x86 assembly language family, detailing its history from Intel's 8086 to AMD's x86-64 and its market importance. It outlines main features: CISC design, variable instruction lengths, numerous instructions, memory operands, 2-address format, diverse addressing modes, stack-based returns, flags register, and segmented memory. It notes modern x86 processors internally translate instructions to RISC. The chapter also presents the x86 machine model, including integer registers of various sizes and segment registers, setting the stage for detailed study of the 32-bit ISA.

nodes.title: x86 Machine Model
Integer Registers
nodes.summary: The text covers x86 architecture details: flags register for conditional branches, segmented memory with separate instruction/data segments and access restrictions. It contrasts CISC x86 with RISC, noting modern x86 translates to RISC internally. It describes the register set evolution from 16-bit to 64-bit, including general-purpose registers (ax to r15), special registers (ip, flags), and naming conventions. It details the eflags register fields (OF, CF, ZF, SF). It explains floating-point registers st0-st7 as an 80-bit stack with a tag register, and memory views with segment registers. It also mentions the x86-64 extension with r8-r15 and rip/rflags.

nodes.title: Floating Point Registers
nodes.summary: The text covers the eflags register in 32-bit x86, listing common fields like OF, CF, ZF, and SF with their semantics. It then details x86 floating point registers, which are eight 80-bit registers (st0-st7) with a 64-bit mantissa and 15-bit exponent, viewed as a stack with a tag register indicating status. Stack operations, overflow, and typical instruction behavior are explained. Finally, it briefly introduces x86 memory views, noting the segment registers and a flat memory model like ARM and SimpleRisc, storing code and data.

nodes.title: View of Memory
nodes.summary: The text covers x86 architecture details: the eflags register fields (OF, CF, ZF, SF) and their semantics; floating point registers st0-st7 organized as a stack with an 80-bit format and a tag register tracking validity; linear vs. segmented memory models, including segment registers (cs, ds, ss, es, fs, gs), segment descriptor tables (LDT, GDT), and the segment descriptor cache; and addressing modes for immediates (no size restrictions, hex/binary/decimal formats) and registers (named access like eax, ebx).

nodes.title: Addressing Modes
nodes.summary: This text discusses x86 memory addressing and assembly language. It describes the segment descriptor cache, introduced to avoid GDT contention and shorten the critical path, which stores frequently used segment descriptors. It defines process, LDT (per-process segment table), and GDT (system-wide segment table). Addressing modes are then covered: immediates with no size restrictions but format limitations in 32-bit vs. 64-bit modes; registers addressed by name; and memory operand modes including register-indirect, base-offset, base-index, base-index-offset, and base-scaled-index-offset. Equation 5.1 combines optional base, index, scale, and displacement. Examples illustrate modes. Finally, x86 assembly language is introduced, focusing on NASM syntax, statement structure, labels, comments, and instruction format with opcodes and operands.

nodes.title: x86 Assembly Language
nodes.summary: The text defines displacement in x86 ISA, lists memory operand addressing modes with examples, and presents a table. It introduces x86 assembly language, covering assemblers (MASM, NASM, GNU), NASM's use, and the generic statement structure with labels, instructions, and comments. It describes instruction formats (0, 1, 2-address) with examples and operand rules. It then covers integer instructions, specifically data transfer, detailing the mov instruction's semantics, examples, and its versatility in replacing load/store instructions.

The x86 Machine Model section covers integer registers, floating point registers, memory views, addressing modes, and x86 assembly language. Integer registers include the eflags register, segmented memory, CISC vs. RISC, register evolution from 16-bit to 64-bit, general-purpose registers, and special registers. Floating point registers are eight 80-bit stack registers (st0-st7) with a tag register. Memory views discuss segment registers, descriptor tables, and flat memory model. Addressing modes include immediates, registers, and memory operands with base, index, scale, and displacement. Assembly language covers NASM syntax, statement structure, and integer instructions like mov.

nodes.title: Integer Instructions
Data Transfer Instructions
nodes.summary: The text covers x86 instruction formats (0, 1, and 2-address), operand rules, and integer instructions. It details data transfer operations: mov (register/memory/immediate transfers), movsx and movzx (sign/zero extension), xchg (atomic swap), and push/pop (stack operations with size modifiers). ALU instructions including add, subtract, adc, and sbb are introduced. Examples illustrate assembly syntax, operand restrictions, stack behavior, and atomicity.

nodes.title: ALU Instructions
nodes.summary: This text covers x86 assembly language concepts, including stack operations with examples on final ebx values. It details ALU instructions: add, subtract, adc, sbb for multi-byte arithmetic; inc, dec, neg; cmp; signed multiplication (imul) and division (idiv) with variants and examples; logical operations (and, or, xor, not); and shift instructions (sar, shr, sal/shl) with examples. It also introduces branch and function call instructions: unconditional jmp, conditional jumps with condition codes, and emphasizes learning assembly through practice.

nodes.title: Branch/ Function Call Instructions
nodes.summary: The text covers x86 assembly branch and function call instructions. It details conditional and unconditional branches using jmp and j-prefixed instructions with condition codes, and provides examples for loops, primality testing, and factorial calculation. It explains call and ret semantics, including stack-based return addresses and function examples using registers, stack arguments, push/pop, and ebp/esp management. It introduces enter and leave instructions for stack frame handling, and concludes with advanced memory instructions: lea, string operations (stos, lods, movs), and the direction flag with std and cld.

nodes.title: Advanced Memory Instructions
nodes.summary: This text covers x86 assembly instructions beyond basics: the nop instruction for alignment and correctness, and advanced memory instructions including lea (load effective address) and string instructions (stos, lods, movs) with their b/w/d/q variants, direction flag (DF) control via std/cld, and semantics with examples. It explains the rep prefix for repeating string operations, including repe/repne variants, with examples for array copying. Finally, it introduces floating point instructions, discussing historical x87 co-processor context, lack of direct integer-FP register communication, memory-only immediate loading, and the conceptual organization of integer and FP registers sharing memory.

The section covers x86 integer instructions, starting with instruction formats (0, 1, and 2-address), operand rules, and data transfer operations: mov, movsx, movzx, xchg, and push/pop with size modifiers. It then details ALU instructions including add, subtract, adc, sbb, inc, dec, neg, cmp, signed multiplication (imul) and division (idiv), logical operations (and, or, xor, not), and shifts (sar, shr, sal/shl). Branch and function call instructions are explained: jmp, conditional jumps with condition codes, call and ret semantics with stack frames, enter/leave, and examples like loops, primality, and factorial. Advanced memory instructions include nop, lea, string operations (stos, lods, movs) with variants, direction flag control (std/cld), rep prefixes, and an introduction to floating point instructions and x87 context.

nodes.title: Floating Point Instructions
Floating Point Instructions (intro)
nodes.summary: The text discusses string operations with rep instructions, including repe and repne variants that terminate based on ecx and zero flag conditions. It then shifts to x86 floating point instructions, providing historical context of the x87 co-processor and modern integrated FPU, and noting the lack of direct communication between integer and FP registers. It details floating point data transfer, particularly load instructions like fld and fild, with semantics and examples, including loading a constant from memory to the FP stack.

nodes.title: Data Transfer Instructions
nodes.summary: The text covers x86 floating-point (FP) instructions: load (fld, fild) with examples of pushing constants to the FP stack; exchange (fxch) to swap FP register contents; store (fst, fstp, fist, fistp) to transfer FP values to memory or registers, including integer conversion and stack popping; and arithmetic instructions, focusing on add (fadd, faddp, fiadd) with variants for memory, registers, and integers. It explains instruction semantics, addressing modes, and provides assembly examples using NASM syntax, including data section definition and stack operations.

nodes.title: Arithmetic Instructions
nodes.summary: The text covers x86 floating-point instructions: converting st0 to an integer with fist and fistp, arithmetic operations including fadd, faddp, and fiadd, with semantics and examples. It details subtraction, multiplication, and division instructions (fsub, fmul, fdiv) in the same format, and provides an example computing the arithmetic mean of two integers. Finally, it presents special function instructions—fabs, fsqrt, fcos, and fsin—with their semantics.

nodes.title: Instructions for Special Functions
nodes.summary: The text covers x86 floating-point instructions. Table 5.24 details fsub, fmul, and fdiv with memory operands, including semantics and an example computing an arithmetic mean. Section 5.4.3 presents special function instructions (fabs, fsqrt, fcos, fsin) in Table 5.25, with an example for geometric mean. Section 5.4.4 introduces the fcomi compare instruction in Table 5.26, which sets the eflags register, including both fcomi and fcomip variants.

nodes.title: Compare Instruction
nodes.summary: This text covers x86 ISA support for advanced math instructions like trigonometric functions and square root, detailing instructions such as fabs, fsqrt, fcos, and fsin that operate on st0. It includes an example computing geometric mean. It presents floating-point compare instructions (fcomi, fcomip) and their semantics, noting the need for unsigned condition codes like 'a' and 'b' to avoid errors, with an example verifying sin(2θ) equals 2sin(θ)cos(θ) using a threshold comparison. It also covers stack cleanup instructions ffree and finit. Finally, it briefly discusses x86 instruction encoding.

nodes.title: Stack Cleanup Instructions
nodes.summary: The text covers floating point comparison using fcomi and ja, setting eax to 0 or 1. It then details stack cleanup instructions: ffree to empty a specific FP register, and finit to reset the entire FP unit. Finally, it introduces x86 ISA encoding, noting its CISC nature and regular encoding process, and states that detailed encoding description is omitted.

The section covers x86 floating point instructions, starting with historical context and register communication limits. It details data transfer instructions: loads (fld, fild), exchanges (fxch), stores (fst, fstp, fist, fistp), and arithmetic operations (fadd, faddp, fiadd, fsub, fmul, fdiv). It includes special functions (fabs, fsqrt, fcos, fsin), compare instructions (fcomi, fcomip) with condition code considerations, and stack cleanup (ffree, finit). Examples illustrate computing arithmetic and geometric means and verifying trigonometric identities. It briefly notes x86 instruction encoding without detail. rep string instructions are mentioned but not central.

nodes.title: Encoding the x86 ISA
key_items: High Level View of x86 Instruction Encoding
nodes.summary: This text covers floating-point stack cleanup instructions (ffree, finit) with semantics and examples, followed by x86 instruction encoding: the high-level binary format with prefix, opcode, ModR/M, SIB, displacement, and immediate fields; detailed ModR/M byte fields (Mod, Reg, R/M) and their addressing mode semantics; register encoding; SIB byte structure for base-scaled-index addressing; rules for encoding memory operands; an encoding example; and a summary of x86 ISA evolution, basic registers, 2-address instruction format, and segmented memory model including segment registers, address calculation, and descriptor tables.

nodes.title: Summary and Further Reading
nodes.summary: The text summarizes the x86 ISA, covering its CISC nature, 16/32/64-bit evolution, registers, addressing, segmented memory model, integer and floating-point instructions, encoding format, and further reading on extensions like MMX, SSE, AVX. It then lists exercises on x86 assembly programming, encoding, and design problems. Finally, it introduces the RISC-V ISA, discussing its history, motivation, technical requirements, and the 2010 landscape that enabled its development.

The x86 Assembly Language section covers the evolution and features of the x86 family, including its CISC design, registers, memory model, and instruction formats. It details integer instructions (data transfer, ALU, branching, string operations) and floating-point instructions (loads, stores, arithmetic, comparisons). It explains x86 instruction encoding, including ModR/M and SIB bytes.
