The section concludes with a summary, further reading, exercises, and an introduction to RISC-V, including its history and motivation.

nodes.title: RISC-V Assembly Language
RISC-V Assembly Language (intro)
nodes.summary: This chapter introduces RISC-V assembly language, covering its history and rationale for a new RISC ISA in 2010, including legal and technical reasons. It details requirements for modern ISAs: 32/64/128-bit variants, more registers, and support for atomics and floating point. It discusses the 2010 context where simple RISC design became easy, fabs increased capacity, and fabless companies emerged. Legal restrictions and licensing costs of legacy ISAs like ARM and MIPS drove the need for a new ISA with lenient licensing. The RISC-V project began in 2010 at Berkeley, with documents released under Creative Commons in 2015. It also introduces RISC-V base ISAs (RV32, RV32E, RV64, RV64E, RV128) and extensions (E, I, M, A, F, D, V).

nodes.title: RISC-V Machine Model
nodes.summary: This text covers RISC-V: its motivation (licensing issues with ARM/MIPS led to a new ISA in 2010), development, and maintenance. It details RISC-V's modular design, including base ISAs (RV32/64/128 and embedded 'E' variants) and extensions (like I, M, A, F, D, V, and 'G' for general-purpose, as well as 'Z' series). It explains compressed 16-bit 'C' instructions, variable instruction lengths (up to 176 bits), register file organization (32 registers, x0 hardwired to zero, calling conventions), and basic integer instructions like addi/add, noting the lack of a dedicated mov instruction.

nodes.title: Integer Instructions
Moving Values to Registers
nodes.summary: The text covers RISC-V registers and their mnemonics, then introduces integer instructions in RV32I. It explains loading values using addi and add with the zero register, since there's no dedicated mov. For 32-bit immediates, it describes lui and the li assembler directive, with examples. It also details add, addi, and sub instructions, including swapping values and arithmetic examples. Conventions for rs1, rs2, rd, and imm are defined.

nodes.title: Add and Subtract Instructions
nodes.summary: This text covers RISC-V assembly programming examples and instruction semantics. It includes examples for adding two numbers using li, computing a sequence of add and subtract operations, swapping register values with add instructions, and multiplying numbers. Tables define add, addi, sub, mul, div, and rem instructions, with explanations and register effects. The text also explains the M extension for multiplication and division, covering 64-bit product handling via mulh and mulhu, and dynamic fusion of consecutive multiplication instructions.

nodes.title: Multiplication and Division Instructions
nodes.summary: This text covers RISC-V multiplication and division instructions in the M extension. It details mul, div, and rem semantics, examples, and register usage. It explains that mul produces a 64-bit product, requiring mulh and mulhu for upper bits, which microarchitectures can fuse. Division uses 32-bit operands, rounds toward zero, and can fuse div and rem. Examples include multiplying 3 and -17, computing 123+1, and dividing -50 by 3. It also introduces logical and shift instructions with an i suffix.

nodes.title: Logical and Shift Instructions
nodes.summary: The text covers RISC-V arithmetic and logical instructions. It details multiplication and division, including rounding toward zero and remainder sign, noting that division and remainder instructions are fused by hardware. It presents an example dividing -50 by 3. It then lists logical (and, or, xor) and shift (sll, srl, sra) instructions with immediate variants, providing examples for OR, division via shift, and multiply-add. Finally, it introduces control transfer and memory instructions, focusing on conditional branches and the slt family of set-less-than instructions, with an example.

This section covers integer instructions in RV32I and the M extension. It starts with moving values to registers using addi and add with the zero register, plus lui and li for 32-bit immediates. It then details add, addi, sub, mul, div, and rem instructions with examples like swapping values, arithmetic sequences, and multiplication. The M extension is explained, covering mul's 64-bit product with mulh and mulhu for upper bits, and division rounding toward zero with dynamic fusion. Logical (and, or, xor) and shift (sll, srl, sra) instructions with immediate variants are introduced, followed by control transfer and memory instructions, focusing on conditional branches and the slt family.

nodes.title: Control Transfer and Memory Instructions
Conditional Branches
nodes.summary: The text provides RISC-V assembly examples: computing arithmetic expressions, adding 64-bit values with carry, factorial, summing 1–10, primality testing, counting ones in a 32-bit number, and perfect square checking. It introduces control transfer instructions, explaining conditional branches (beq, bne, bge, blt, bgeu, bltu) and the slt family (slt, slti, sltu, sltui) for comparisons without a flags register. It also covers unconditional jumps (jal, jalr) for function calls and returns, with examples like setting a register based on comparison.

nodes.title: Unconditional Branches
nodes.summary: The text covers three RISC-V assembly topics: a perfect square checking program, unconditional branch instructions (jal and jalr) with semantics, examples, and jump encoding details, and a function call example; a power computation program; and load/store instructions (lw, sw, la) with semantics, mentioning la as an assembler directive and load/store formats, including an incomplete example.

nodes.title: Load and Store Instructions
nodes.summary: This text covers RISC-V assembly programming: a power function implementation, load/store instructions (lw, sw, la) with examples for memory access, array copying, summation, and recursive factorial; the la assembler directive for loading constants; floating point instructions including the F and D extensions, 32 floating point registers with usage conventions, and the floating point control and status register (fcsr) with fflags and rounding mode bits.

This section covers RISC-V control transfer and memory instructions. It details conditional branches (beq, bne, bge, blt, bgeu, bltu), the slt family for comparisons, and unconditional jumps (jal, jalr) for calls and returns. Load/store instructions (lw, sw, la) are explained with examples like array copying, summation, and recursive factorial. The la assembler directive is covered. Floating-point instructions are introduced, including the F and D extensions, 32 floating-point registers, usage conventions, and the fcsr with fflags and rounding mode bits. Assembly examples include arithmetic expressions, 64-bit addition with carry, factorial, summing 1-10, primality testing, counting ones, perfect square checking, and power computation.

nodes.title: Floating Point Instructions
View of Registers
nodes.summary: The text covers RISC-V assembly with an example loading constant 17 into integer register s0. It introduces floating point instructions, the 2017 F/D extensions, IEEE 754 format, 32 floating point registers f0-f31, their usage convention, inability to load immediates directly, and the fcsr with fflags (NV, DZ, OF, UF, NX) and rounding modes (RNE, RTZ, RDN, RUP, RMM, DYN). It details load/store instructions flw and fsw, and examples loading constants into floating point registers via memory.

nodes.title: Load and Store Instructions
nodes.summary: This text covers RISC-V floating-point rounding modes (RNE, RTZ, RDN, RUP, RMM, DYN), single-precision load/store instructions (flw, fsw), and arithmetic instructions (fadd.s, fsub.s, fmul.s, fdiv.s, fmin.s, fmax.s, fsqrt.s). It explains that floating-point immediates cannot be loaded directly, requiring memory storage and flw, with pseudoinstruction la for constants. Examples demonstrate loading constants and computing expressions. It notes the lack of immediate source operands in floating-point arithmetic and mentions type conversion via fcvt, contrasting this with the more powerful integer ISA while noting minor practical performance impact.

nodes.title: Floating Point Arithmetic Instructions
nodes.summary: The text covers RISC-V floating point instructions, starting with single-precision arithmetic (fadd.s, fsub.s, fmul.s, fdiv.s, fmin.s, fmax.s, fsqrt.s) using .s and .d suffixes, noting no immediate operands and that immediates must be loaded via flw or converted. Example 116 shows computing sqrt(pi + e + pi*e) in fa0. It then introduces fused multiply-add/subtract (fmadd.s, fmsub.s) for dot products/matrix multiplication, and floating point-integer conversion (fcvt.s.w, fcvt.w.s). Example 117 computes pi*e+4 using fcvt for the integer 4 and converts the result to integer. Tables 6.15, 6.16, and 6.17 summarize semantics and examples.

nodes.title: Floating Point Conversion Instructions
nodes.summary: The text covers RISC-V floating-point instructions: fused arithmetic (fmadd.s, fmsub.s) with semantics, examples, and a usage example computing π×e+4; floating-point to/from integer conversion (fcvt.s.w, fcvt.w.s) with semantics, examples, and a conversion example; and floating-point comparison (flt.s, fle.s, feq.s) storing results in integer registers, with semantics, examples, and an example initializing a0 and setting a0=17 if e<π. Includes tables and code snippets.

nodes.title: Floating Point Comparison Instructions
nodes.summary: This text covers RISC-V floating point comparison instructions (flt.s, fle.s, feq.s), including their semantics, examples, and an example program comparing e and pi. It then introduces RISC-V instruction encoding, detailing the four core non-branch 32-bit formats (R, I, S, U), with visual representation and tables mapping instruction types to formats.

The section covers RISC-V floating-point instructions, including the 2017 F/D extensions and IEEE 754 format. It details 32 floating-point registers (f0–f31), usage conventions, and the fcsr with fflags (NV, DZ, OF, UF, NX) and rounding modes (RNE, RTZ, RDN, RUP, RMM, DYN). Load/store instructions flw and fsw are explained, noting that immediates cannot be loaded directly and require memory access via la. Arithmetic instructions (fadd.s, fsub.s, fmul.s, fdiv.s, fmin.s, fmax.s, fsqrt.s) are presented, with no immediate operands. Fused multiply-add/subtract (fmadd.s, fmsub.s) are introduced for dot products. Conversion instructions (fcvt.s.w, fcvt.w.s) and comparison instructions (flt.s, fle.s, feq.s) are covered. Examples demonstrate computing expressions, and instruction encoding formats (R, I, S, U) are briefly mentioned.

nodes.title: Instruction Encoding
Arithmetic and Data Transfer Instructions
nodes.summary: This section explains RISC-V 32-bit instruction encoding, covering arithmetic, data transfer, and control flow instructions. It details four core non-branch formats—R, I, S, and U—including their bit-level structures, opcode placement, register fields, immediate storage, and the roles of funct3 and funct7. Examples of instructions for each format are provided. The text emphasizes design goals like decoder simplicity, consistent opcode positioning, sign-extension of immediates, and hierarchical grouping via funct fields. It also introduces the B and J formats for control flow, referencing figures and tables for visual and example clarity.

nodes.title: Control Flow Instructions
nodes.summary: The text details RISC-V ISA instruction formats. It explains decoding simplicity via fixed opcode positions across R, I, S, and U formats, covering register fields, immediates, funct3/funct7 for instruction grouping, and sign-extension. It describes control flow B and J formats, including their special immediate encoding for PC-relative offsets with assumed zero LSB and sign extension. Finally, it outlines floating-point instruction encodings: I-format for flw, S-format for fsw with width fields, and R-format variants for arithmetic, conversion, and comparison operations, using rm, fmt, and funct5 fields.

nodes.title: Floating Point Instructions
nodes.summary: This text describes RISC-V floating point instruction encodings and summarizes the ISA. It details flw and fsw using I and S formats with a width field replacing funct3. Floating point arithmetic, conversion, and comparison instructions use a modified R format with rm (rounding mode), fmt (precision), and funct5 fields. Fused multiply-add (fmadd/fmsub) uses rs3 instead of funct5. The summary covers RISC-V ISA variants (RV32/64/128), modular extensions (integer, embedded, atomic, floating point, vector, compressed), 32 integer registers with x0 hardwired to zero, and register usage conventions (temporary, callee-saved, arguments, ra, sp, gp, zero), including mnemonics like t3 for x28.

The section on Instruction Encoding covers RISC-V instruction formats: arithmetic, data transfer, and control flow. It details R, I, S, and U formats with opcodes, registers, immediates, and funct fields, emphasizing decoder simplicity and sign-extension. B and J formats for PC-relative branches and jumps are explained. Floating-point instructions include flw/fsw using I/S formats with width fields, and R-format variants for arithmetic, conversion, and comparison with rm, fmt, and funct5 fields; fused multiply-add uses rs3. The ISA variants (RV32/64/128), modular extensions, and register conventions with x0 hardwired to zero are also summarized.

nodes.title: Summary and Further Reading
Summary
nodes.summary: The text details RISC-V instruction encoding for fused multiply-add (fmadd/fmsub), then summarizes the RISC-V ISA: RV32/64/128 variants, modular extensions (integer, embedded, atomic, floating-point, vector), compressed instructions, 32 integer registers with usage conventions (temporary, saved, arguments, ra, sp, gp, zero), immediate handling (12-bit arithmetic, 20-bit branches, lui/addi for loading), standard arithmetic/logical instructions, branch comparisons without flags, jal/jalr for calls/returns, assembler directives (li, la), 32 floating-point registers and fcsr, floating-point load/store (flw/fsw), arithmetic and conversion instructions, comparison instructions, and six instruction formats (R, I, S, U, B, J). It also lists further reading: official manuals, books, papers on history, critiques, formal specs, and performance aspects.

nodes.title: Further Reading
nodes.summary: The text covers RISC-V floating point comparison instructions and instruction formats: six formats (R, I, S, U, B, J) with usage details, immediate sizes, and branch/jump encoding. It lists further reading including official manuals, privileged/unprivileged specs, books, historical papers, critical analyses, formal specifications, simulators, and processors (BOOMv2, space-grade). Exercises include assembly programming, conceptual questions on mov, li, la, flags, rounding modes, floating-point immediates, field alignment, opcode fields, sign-bit extraction, plus design problems extending an assembler and cross-compiling C code for performance comparison.

The section summarizes RISC-V instruction encoding, fused multiply-add, and the ISA's RV32/64/128 variants, modular extensions (integer, embedded, atomic, floating-point, vector), compressed instructions, 32 integer registers with usage conventions, immediate handling, arithmetic/logical instructions, branch comparisons without flags, jal/jalr, assembler directives, 32 floating-point registers and fcsr, floating-point load/store, arithmetic, conversion, comparison instructions, and six instruction formats (R, I, S, U, B, J). It also provides further reading: official manuals, books, historical papers, critiques, formal specs, simulators, processors (BOOMv2, space-grade), and exercises covering assembly, conceptual questions, and design problems extending an assembler and cross-compiling C code.

This section covers RISC-V assembly language, including its history and rationale, base ISAs (RV32/64/128 and embedded variants), and modular extensions (I, M, A, F, D, V, etc.). It details the machine model, register conventions, and integer instructions with examples. Control transfer and memory instructions are explained, along with floating-point instructions, the fcsr, and conversion/comparison operations. Instruction encoding formats (R, I, S, U, B, J) are described. The summary reinforces key points and provides further reading on manuals, books, simulators, and exercises.

summary: This section covers the software interface architecture, starting with how computers process binary bits and bytes, including binary representation, Boolean algebra, integer systems, floating point, and character encoding. It then introduces assembly language, detailing the Von Neumann model, CPU components, registers, memory, addressing modes, and SimpleRisc instructions. Subsequent subsections cover ARM assembly (32-bit RISC, registers, instructions, encoding), x86 assembly (CISC evolution, registers, integer and floating-point instructions, encoding), and RISC-V assembly (base ISAs, extensions, registers, integer/floating-point instructions, encoding). Each subsection includes summaries, exercises, and further reading.

title: II Organization: Processor Design

nodes.title: II Organization: Processor Design (intro)
nodes.summary: The text introduces computer design requirements: a CPU, registers, large memory, and a complete, concise, generic instruction set, with SimpleRisc as an example needing logical, arithmetic, register, and memory operations. It outlines a chapter plan: this chapter covers simple circuits for logical operations, registers, and basic memory cells; Chapter 8 covers arithmetic units (adders, multipliers, dividers); Chapters 9-11 cover advanced elements like the CPU and advanced memory. It warns the chapter is a brief, cursory introduction to digital logic, not rigorous, and references seminal texts.

nodes.title: Logic Gates, Registers, and Memories
Logic Gates, Registers, and Memories (intro)
nodes.summary: The chapter introduces designing a computer, outlining requirements like a CPU, registers, memory, and a simple instruction set such as SimpleRisc. It presents a plan for upcoming chapters covering logical operations, registers, memory, arithmetic units, CPU, pipelined processors, and memory systems. The chapter offers a brief digital logic introduction for two reader types: those refreshing knowledge and beginners. It notes historical computer construction from mechanical parts to vacuum tubes to silicon transistors, and discusses silicon's abundance, properties, and molecular structure as a substrate for circuits.

nodes.title: Silicon-Based Transistors
Silicon-Based Transistors (intro)
nodes.summary: The text outlines a plan for chapters on computer architecture, covering registers, memory, logical and arithmetic operations, CPU, pipelined processors, and memory systems for two reader types: those with digital logic background and beginners. It discusses the evolution of computing from mechanical to vacuum tube to silicon-based circuits, then focuses on silicon transistors, including silicon's properties, semiconductor definition, and doping with n-type (phosphorus, arsenic) and p-type (boron, gallium) impurities, leading to p-n junctions and charge carriers (electrons and holes).

nodes.title: Doping
nodes.summary: The text explains silicon's tightly packed lattice and poor conductivity, classifying it as a semiconductor. It covers doping to modify conductivity: n-type with group V elements like phosphorus or arsenic adding free electrons, and p-type with group III elements like boron or gallium creating holes. Definitions describe these semiconductors and p-n junction formation. At the junction, diffusion and drift currents create a depletion region with balanced currents. Forward bias conducts current, while reverse bias does not, forming a diode that conducts in one direction.

nodes.title: P-N Junction
nodes.summary: The text explains the p-n junction, detailing diffusion of holes and electrons, the depletion region, drift and diffusion current balance at steady state, and behavior under forward and reverse bias, defining a diode as a one-directional conductor. It then introduces the NMOS transistor, describing its p-type substrate with n-type source and drain regions, the channel, SiO2 insulating layer, gate terminal, and operation as a switch controlled by gate voltage, where high voltage attracts electrons to form a conducting path, allowing current flow.

nodes.title: NMOS Transistor
nodes.summary: The text covers the structure and operation of NMOS and PMOS transistors, including their p-n junctions, substrate, source, drain, channel, gate, and terminals. It explains NMOS behavior with gate voltages, threshold voltage, conducting path, resistance, current flow, and switch analogy. Similarly, PMOS operation is described with reversed logic for holes and gate voltages. Finally, it introduces CMOS logic and a basic CMOS inverter circuit connecting NMOS and PMOS transistors between ground, output, and Vdd, with input to gates.

nodes.title: PMOS Transistor
nodes.summary: The text explains NMOS transistor off-state behavior and its circuit symbol. It introduces the PMOS transistor, describing its p-type source/drain, reverse operation where logical 0 attracts holes to conduct and logical 1 repels them, its switch behavior (on at 0, off at 1), and its circuit symbol. Finally, it presents a basic CMOS-based inverter circuit using both NMOS and PMOS transistors, with an NMOS connected between ground and output, a PMOS between Vdd and output, and input fed to both gates.

nodes.title: A Basic CMOS-Based Inverter
nodes.summary: The text explains NMOS and PMOS transistors, their operation as switches, and circuit symbols. It describes a CMOS inverter, noting that input 0 turns on PMOS and off NMOS, outputting 1, and vice versa, implementing NOT with low steady-state power dissipation. It also covers constructing NAND and NOR gates in CMOS technology, using inputs A and B to control NMOS-PMOS pairs.

nodes.title: NAND and NOR Gates
nodes.summary: The text explains CMOS inverter operation, where input 0 turns on PMOS and output 1, input 1 turns on NMOS and output 0, enabling NOT logic with low steady-state power dissipation. It then details CMOS NAND and NOR gate construction, their truth tables, and universal gate properties for building any logic function. AND and OR gates are derived by combining NAND/NOR with NOT. Finally, it introduces combinational logic, focusing on the XOR gate, its truth table, Boolean expression, and circuit implementation.

The section on silicon-based transistors begins with an introduction that outlines a computer architecture plan covering registers, memory, operations, CPU, pipelining, and memory systems for two reader types, and traces computing evolution from mechanical to vacuum tube to silicon circuits. It then focuses on silicon transistors, explaining silicon's properties, doping with n-type and p-type impurities, and the formation of p-n junctions and charge carriers. Subsections detail doping, p-n junction behavior including depletion region and diode action, and the structure and operation of NMOS, PMOS, and CMOS transistors as switches. It further covers CMOS inverter, NAND, and NOR gates, their truth tables, universal gate properties, and introduces combinational logic with XOR gates.

nodes.title: Combinational Logic
XOR Gate
nodes.summary: The text covers logic gates and combinational logic structures. It explains constructing AND from NAND and OR from NOR via NOT gates, and defines combinational logic as computing functions on Boolean inputs, exemplified by XOR. It details XOR with truth table and equation A⊕B = A.B' + A'.B. It describes decoders, specifically a 2×4 decoder using AND gates on input complements, and introduces multiplexers, which use select bits to choose one of n inputs based on unique binary identifiers.

nodes.title: Decoder
nodes.summary: This text covers digital logic components. It details a decoder's function: taking a log(n)-bit input to activate one of n outputs, including a 2×4 decoder example with Boolean combinations and AND gates. It also introduces the multiplexer (mux), which uses log(n) select bits to choose one of n inputs as output, highlighting its use in processors.

nodes.title: Multiplexer
nodes.summary: The text covers four combinational logic components. First, decoders: log(n)-bit input to n outputs, using AND gates from NOTs, with a 2x4 example. Second, multiplexers (mux): n inputs and log(n) select bits choose one output; design uses a decoder, AND gates, then OR gate, illustrated with a 4-input mux. Third, demultiplexers: log(n)-bit select and 1-bit input route to one of n outputs via decoder and AND gates, used in memory. Fourth, encoders: n inputs (one active) to log(n)-bit output encoding, reverse of decoder, with an 8-to-3 example. Includes figures for each.

nodes.title: Demultiplexer
nodes.summary: The text explains multiplexer operation, covering how a decoder enables AND gates to select one input based on select bits, with an OR gate yielding the final output, illustrated in Figure 7.12. It then describes demultiplexers, which route a single input to one of n outputs using a decoder and AND gates, noting their use in memory cells. Finally, it introduces encoders, which perform reverse logic by converting one active input among n into a log(n)-bit binary output, with an 8-to-3 encoder example.

nodes.title: Encoder
nodes.summary: The text explains multiplexer-based circuits: a demultiplexer routes one input to one of n outputs using a decoder and AND gates, used in memory cells; an encoder converts n inputs to log(n) outputs, with a 4-2 example and equations; and a priority encoder handles multiple active inputs by encoding the highest-index line, illustrated with 4-2 priority encoder equations. Circuit diagrams and examples are referenced.

nodes.title: Priority Encoder
nodes.summary: The text covers priority encoders and sequential logic. It begins with equations for a 4-2 priority encoder, explaining priority handling and circuit design. Then it provides equations for an 8-3 priority encoder. Next, it introduces sequential logic, focusing on storing bits, with requirements for self-sustaining memory, non-destructive read, and settable values. Finally, it analyzes the SR latch using cross-coupled NAND gates, detailing its set, reset, and hold operations.

This section covers combinational logic components. It explains constructing AND from NAND and OR from NOR, defines combinational logic, and details XOR with truth table and equation. It describes decoders (2×4 example using AND gates), multiplexers (select bits choose one of n inputs), demultiplexers (route one input to one of n outputs), encoders (n inputs to log(n)-bit output), and priority encoders (highest-index input encoded, with 4-2 and 8-3 examples). It also introduces sequential logic for storing bits, including SR latch analysis with cross-coupled NAND gates and set, reset, and hold operations.

nodes.title: Sequential Logic
SR Latch
nodes.summary: The text presents an 8-3 priority encoder example with equations. It then introduces sequential logic, explaining its purpose to store bits using feedback, with requirements for self-sustaining storage, readable values, and settable states. It details the SR latch using cross-coupled NAND gates, analyzing its behavior for various S and R inputs, including the invalid state and race condition, and provides a state transition table. Finally, it discusses the need for a clock to synchronize circuit operations due to varying delays, defining clock signal, clock cycle, and clock frequency, and includes a diagram.

nodes.title: The Clock
nodes.summary: The text explains the need for a global clock in processors to synchronize circuits with varying delays, defining clock signal, cycle, frequency, and period. It describes using integer time units, clock-based computation sequencing, and I/O communication. It then introduces the clocked SR latch (flip-flop), detailing its NAND gate augmentation and operation based on clock input, and concludes with the definition of a flip-flop as a clocked latch storing one bit.

nodes.title: Clocked SR Latch
nodes.summary: The text defines clock cycle, period, and frequency, relating clock frequency to processor specs. It describes a computation model where actions take clock cycles, using latches for synchronization to sequence computation, handle I/O, avoid races, and aid debugging. It then details the clocked SR latch (flip-flop), explaining its NAND gate operation and level sensitivity, before introducing edge-sensitive latches. Finally, it presents the master-slave SR flip-flop construction for edge-sensitive operation.

nodes.title: Edge Sensitive SR Flip-flop
nodes.summary: The text covers synchronization using clocks, defining level-sensitive and edge-sensitive latches. It explains the master-slave SR flip-flop design, where two SR flip-flops connected with complementary clocks create edge sensitivity at the downward clock edge. However, it notes a race condition when S and R are both 1. To fix this, it introduces the JK flip-flop, detailing its circuit and case analysis: for J=0, K=0 outputs are maintained; J=1, K=0 sets Q=1; J=0, K=1 sets Q=0, with Q and Q-bar fed back to input NAND gates.

nodes.title: JK Flip-flop
nodes.summary: The text explains master-slave flip-flops, which use two flip-flops triggered by opposite clock signals to create edge sensitivity, but notes race conditions with S=R=1. It introduces JK flip-flops, detailing their operation with J and K inputs and Q feedback, including a state transition table for maintain, set, reset, and toggle actions without race conditions. It also covers D flip-flops, where R=S, reflecting input at clock edges without maintain logic, and master-slave D flip-flops, which avoid race conditions by eliminating the (1,1) input.

nodes.title: D Flip-flop
nodes.summary: The text discusses JK flip-flop behavior when J and K are both 1, resulting in toggled outputs without race conditions, and presents its state transition table. It then introduces the D flip-flop, which uses complementary S and R signals, reflects input at negative clock edges, and maintains previous values when Clk is 0. Finally, it describes the master-slave D flip-flop, which avoids race conditions by not needing Q and Q feedback or the (1,1) input.

nodes.title: Master-slave D Flip-flop
nodes.summary: This text covers the behavior of a JK flip-flop when J and K are both 1, explaining output toggling and race condition avoidance, accompanied by its state transition table. It introduces the D flip-flop, a simplified SR flip-flop where R=S, reflecting input at each negative clock edge, and the master-slave D flip-flop, which avoids race conditions and uses 8 NAND gates, 1 inverter, and 34 transistors, compared to 38 for JK. It notes flip-flops are fast but inefficient for storage, suggesting SRAM/DRAM. Finally, it discusses metastability, setup/hold times, keep-out regions, and practical design precautions.

nodes.title: Metastability
nodes.summary: The text details master-slave D and JK flip-flops, noting their transistor counts and trade-offs between speed and efficiency compared to SRAM/DRAM. It explains metastability, where inputs near clock edges cause non-deterministic outputs, requiring setup and hold times within a keep-out region to ensure stability. The section on registers describes parallel in–parallel out registers built from n master-slave D flip-flops, enabling simultaneous loading and reading of n bits per clock edge. Figures illustrate the master-slave D flip-flop, the keep-out region timing, and the register structure.

nodes.title: Registers
nodes.summary: The text covers timing concepts like clock edge, setup/hold times, and keep-out regions. It describes registers: parallel-in–parallel-out using master-slave D flip-flops for n-bit storage, and serial-in–parallel-out shift registers that load serially over n cycles and output in parallel, used in high-speed I/O. It then introduces static RAM (SRAM), explaining the basic cell with two cross-coupled inverters (four transistors) for bit storage, contrasting with flip-flops using NAND gates, and noting additional read/write circuitry overhead, with access transistors W1 and W2.

The section on Sequential Logic covers storage elements built from feedback, starting with the SR latch using cross-coupled NAND gates, including its invalid state and race condition. It introduces the need for a clock to synchronize operations, defining clock signal, cycle, frequency, and period. Clocked SR latches (flip-flops) are explained, followed by edge-sensitive designs: master-slave SR, JK, and D flip-flops, detailing their operation, state transition tables, and race condition avoidance. Metastability, setup/hold times, and keep-out regions are discussed. Finally, registers are covered: parallel-in–parallel-out and serial-in–parallel-out, along with SRAM cells and their read/write circuitry.

nodes.title: Memories
Static RAM (SRAM)
nodes.summary: The text explains serial in–parallel out shift registers (Figure 7.25), loading n bits serially over n cycles then reading in parallel, used in high-speed I/O buses. It details SRAM: a 6-transistor cell with cross-coupled inverters and access transistors controlled by word line and bit lines (Figure 7.26). SRAM arrays use decoders, column mux/demux, write drivers, and sense amplifiers with precharging to Vdd/2 for fast reads (Figure 7.27); SRAM suits register files and on-chip memories, not small bit storage. It then introduces CAM cells (10 transistors, Figure 7.28) extending SRAM with match logic to address rows by content, used for hardware hash tables.

nodes.title: Content Addressable Memory (CAM)
nodes.summary: The text explains SRAM read operations using pre-charging and sense amplifiers to speed up reading, noting SRAM's suitability for register files and on-chip memories but not for small storage. It then introduces Content Addressable Memory (CAM), covering a 10-transistor CAM cell that compares stored values with input bits via match lines, and describes CAM arrays with priority encoders for locating rows by content. Finally, it briefly introduces Dynamic RAM (DRAM) as a dense, area- and power-efficient but slower memory technology suitable for large off-chip memories, showing a basic one-transistor DRAM cell.

nodes.title: Dynamic RAM (DRAM)
nodes.summary: The text covers CAM cell arrays with decoders, priority encoders, and match lines. It then details DRAM: a one-transistor, capacitor-based cell, its read/write operations, charge leakage, and refresh requirements. DRAM array design includes single bit lines, refresh circuits, sense amplifiers caching rows, and synchronous operation (SDRAM, DDR1-DDR5) with double-pumped data rates. Finally, ROM is introduced: replacing the DRAM capacitor with a direct connection to Vdd or ground, lacking write drivers and refresh circuitry, used for unmodifiable data like BIOS or security information.

nodes.title: Read Only Memory (ROM)
nodes.summary: The text explains DRAM refresh needs, then details DRAM array construction with single bit lines, refresh circuits, and sense amplifiers that cache rows for fast access. It covers synchronous DRAM (SDRAM) and DDR1-3 evolution. Next, it describes ROM cells using direct Vdd/ground connections, PROM with antifuses (including dielectric and amorphous silicon types), and mentions EPROM/EEPROM/flash. Finally, it introduces programmable logic arrays (PLAs) for flexible combinational logic, comparing them to hardwired circuits and illustrating with a minterm example.

nodes.title: Programmable Logic Arrays
nodes.summary: The text covers antifuse operation and PROM cell arrays, including dielectric and amorphous silicon antifuses. It explains EPROM, EEPROM, and their supersession by flash memory. A major focus is Programmable Logic Arrays (PLAs): their design using PLA cells, the AND plane for generating minterms, the OR plane for combining them, and advantages like flexibility and multiple outputs versus performance cost. An example implements a Boolean function. The section ends with Way Point 4 and a chapter summary of semiconductor basics, transistors, logic gates, and flip-flops (SR, JK, D) used in registers.

The section covers memory technologies. It begins with SRAM, detailing 6-transistor cells, read operations via precharging and sense amplifiers, and its use in register files and on-chip memories. CAM is introduced as an extension of SRAM with match logic for content-based addressing. DRAM is described as a dense, one-transistor cell requiring refresh, with array design, SDRAM, and DDR evolution. ROM variants include PROM with antifuses, EPROM, EEPROM, and flash. Finally, PLAs are explained for implementing combinational logic using AND and OR planes, with an example. The section concludes with a chapter summary of semiconductor basics, transistors, logic gates, and flip-flops.

nodes.title: Summary and Further Reading
nodes.summary: The text covers semiconductor physics, logic gates, sequential logic, and memory technologies. It explains silicon doping, p-n junctions, and NMOS/PMOS transistors. It details combinational gates (inverter, NAND, NOR, AND, OR, XOR, multiplexer, decoder, encoder, priority encoder) and sequential elements (latches, flip-flops: SR, JK, D, master-slave, registers). Memory topics include SRAM, DRAM, ROM, PROM, and PLA arrays. Further reading references semiconductor physics, VLSI, and memory systems books. Exercises cover transistors, logic gates, combinational and sequential logic, memories, and design problems. The next chapter introduces computer arithmetic, starting with binary addition.

This section covers the fundamentals of digital logic and computer memory. It introduces silicon-based transistors, including doping, p-n junctions, and CMOS technology. Combinational logic gates (NAND, NOR, XOR, decoders, multiplexers, encoders) and sequential elements (SR latches, flip-flops, registers) are explained. Memory topics include SRAM, CAM, DRAM, ROM variants, and PLAs. The section concludes with a summary, further reading, and exercises, leading into computer arithmetic.

nodes.title: Computer Arithmetic
Addition
Addition of Two 1-bit Numbers
nodes.summary: This chapter covers hardware algorithms for arithmetic operations, building on basic circuits and binary number knowledge. It details integer arithmetic, starting with addition algorithms, including half adders and full adders for 1-bit numbers. It notes subtraction is handled via 2's complement addition, discusses multiplication's relation to multi-number addition, and mentions efficient integer division lacks optimal methods but presents two popular positive binary division algorithms. It then covers floating-point arithmetic, noting most integer algorithms adapt with minor modifications, and floating-point division is efficient.

nodes.title: Addition of Three 1-bit Numbers
nodes.summary: The text defines sum and carry for adding two or three 1-bit numbers, then introduces the half adder (truth table, boolean expressions, circuit) for two bits, followed by the full adder (truth table, derived boolean expressions, complex circuit) for three bits with input carry. It then describes the ripple carry adder for n-bit numbers, explaining carry propagation and timing, and introduces asymptotic time complexity.

nodes.title: Ripple Carry Adder
nodes.summary: This text explains binary addition using ripple carry adders, covering the process of adding n-bit numbers, carry propagation (rippling), and the use of half and full adders. It introduces asymptotic time complexity and big-O notation to analyze adder performance, showing ripple carry adders have O(n) time complexity. It then presents carry select adders as a faster alternative, describing their two-stage design with parallel adders per block and multiplexers to select results based on input carry, achieving O(√n) time complexity.

nodes.title: Carry Select Adder
nodes.summary: The text covers adder designs: Carry Select Adder reduces ripple carry adder time from O(n) to O(√n) by dividing bits into blocks, computing two results per block for input carry 0 and 1 in parallel, and using multiplexers for carry selection, with optimal block size √n. Carry Lookahead Adder achieves O(log n), the theoretical lower bound, using generate and propagate functions: gi = Ai·Bi, pi = Ai⊕Bi, with carry out Cout = gi + pi·Cin, based on carry absorption, propagation, and generation cases.

nodes.title: Carry Lookahead Adder
Generate and Propagate Functions
nodes.summary: The text discusses adder optimizations, starting with minimizing carry select adder time O(k + n/k) to optimal O(√n). It then introduces the carry lookahead adder, achieving O(log n) time, the theoretical lower bound. It defines generate (gi) and propagate (pi) functions, generalizes them to multi-bit blocks, and derives recursive relationships (G1,n, P1,n) for combining sub-blocks. Examples for 1- to 4-bit systems and a general n-bit formula are provided. The adder's two-stage operation is introduced, with Stage I computing generate/propagate functions for bit subsequences in blocks.

nodes.title: Carry Lookahead Adder – Stage I
nodes.summary: The text explains carry lookahead adder principles: equations for carry-out (C1out to C4out) using generate (g) and propagate (p) functions, and generalized n-bit formula Cnout = Gn + Pn.C1in. It defines block relationships with sub-blocks via G1,n and P1,n, showing the basis for carry lookahead. The two-stage adder operation is detailed: Stage I computes generate and propagate functions for bit ranges using a tree of (G,P) blocks with O(log n) levels and O(log n) time; Stage II uses these to compute sum bits and carry out, with input carry C1in, propagating carries from rightmost blocks to 2-bit ripple carry adders at level 0. Includes Table 8.3 and Figures 8.7, 8.8, 8.9.

nodes.title: Carry Lookahead Adder – Stage II
nodes.summary: The text details the Carry Lookahead Adder's two stages: Stage I builds a tree of (G,P) blocks to compute generate and propagate functions, achieving O(log n) time; Stage II uses these to compute sum bits and carry out via propagation to 2-bit ripple carry adders, also O(log n). Total CLA complexity is O(log n), compared with ripple carry O(n) and carry select O(√n). It then introduces multiplication, explaining decimal and binary methods, partial sums, and defines partial sum and partial product.

nodes.title: Binary Multiplication: Overview and Partial Sums
nodes.summary: The page covers binary multiplication, starting with an overview of the classic problem. It compares naive decimal multiplication (e.g., 13 × 9) with binary multiplication, illustrating both in Figure 8.10. It explains multiplying each multiplier bit from least to most significant, writing the multiplicand or zero, and shifting left for each bit. These shifted values are partial sums; adding m partial sums yields the product (117 decimal = 1110101 binary). It defines partial sum (shifted multiplicand or zero) and partial product (sum of contiguous partial sums).

The section covers Carry Lookahead Adder (CLA) optimizations, including generate (g) and propagate (p) functions, multi-bit block generalizations, and recursive relationships for combining sub-blocks. It details the two-stage CLA operation: Stage I computes generate and propagate functions in O(log n) time using a tree of (G,P) blocks, and Stage II computes sum bits and carry out via propagation to 2-bit ripple carry adders. CLA complexity is O(log n), compared to ripple carry O(n) and carry select O(√n). The section also introduces binary multiplication, explaining partial sums, partial products, and the classic multiplication algorithm with examples.

The section on Addition covers hardware algorithms for integer and floating-point arithmetic. It begins with half and full adders for 1-bit numbers, then details ripple carry adders (O(n) time), carry select adders (O(√n) time), and carry lookahead adders (O(log n) time), including generate/propagate functions and multi-bit optimizations. It also addresses subtraction via 2's complement, multiplication through partial sums and products, integer division algorithms, and floating-point arithmetic adaptations.

nodes.title: Multiplication
Overview
nodes.summary: The text covers binary multiplication, starting with an overview of the naive method using partial sums and partial products, illustrated with decimal and binary examples. It defines partial sum and partial product, discusses unsigned and signed 2's complement multiplication, and addresses overflow concerns, recommending 64 bits for 32-bit multiplication results. It then introduces the iterative multiplier design for signed 32-bit numbers, using registers U, V, and N, and explains the algorithm involving shifting and adding the multiplicand based on multiplier bits.

nodes.title: Iterative Multiplier
nodes.summary: The text discusses multiplication of signed 2's complement numbers, noting that unsigned multiplication logic applies if we ignore sign but overflows can occur, so 64 bits are recommended for 32-bit multiplication. It details an iterative multiplier design using registers U (33-bit), V (32-bit), and N (33-bit) to multiply signed 32-bit numbers for a 64-bit product. The algorithm iterates 32 times, adding or subtracting the multiplicand based on the multiplier's LSB and handling the sign in the final step. Overflow prevention via 33-bit U is justified. Two examples illustrate 4-bit multiplication. Time complexity is O(n log n). The text ends introducing the Booth multiplier as a faster practical alternative.

nodes.title: Booth Multiplier
nodes.summary: The text covers the iterative multiplier's O(n log n) complexity, introduces the Booth multiplier to speed up multiplication by handling runs of 1s, details Booth's algorithm with bit-pair actions, proves its correctness for positive and negative multipliers, discusses the need for a 33-bit U register to avoid overflow, provides worked examples for 2×3 and 3×(−2), and describes an O(log² n) time algorithm using parallel partial sum generation and an adder tree.

nodes.title: An O(log(n)2) Time Algorithm
nodes.summary: The text demonstrates binary multiplication steps with a specific example, then describes an O(log(n)^2) time algorithm for multiplying n-bit numbers, ignoring overflow detection. It explains parallel generation of partial sums via AND operations and their addition using a tree of adders with O(log(n)) levels, each taking O(log(n)) time, yielding O(log(n)^2) total time. The text also introduces carry save adders that add three numbers to produce two (A+B+C=D+E), setting the stage for the Wallace tree multiplier, which achieves O(log(n)) time.

nodes.title: Wallace Tree Multiplier
nodes.summary: The text explains parallel addition optimization using a tree of adders, reducing time from O(nlog(n)) to O(log(n)^2). It introduces the carry save adder, which adds three numbers to produce two, expressed as A + B + C = 2D + E, using full adders with O(1) time complexity. Using carry save adders, the Wallace tree multiplier reduces n partial sums by a factor of 2/3 per level, achieving O(log(n)) time, the fastest possible multiplier. The Dadda multiplier variant is mentioned. Finally, it introduces division, defining N = DQ + R, and notes division is slower than addition, subtraction, and multiplication, assuming positive operands and satisfying certain properties.

The section covers binary multiplication: naive partial sums/products, unsigned and signed 2's complement, and overflow (recommending 64 bits for 32-bit results). It details iterative multiplier design with registers U, V, N, handling signs and 33-bit overflow prevention, with O(n log n) complexity. The Booth multiplier improves speed by handling runs of 1s, with correctness proofs and examples. Faster algorithms are introduced: an O(log² n) parallel partial sum generation with adder trees, and the Wallace tree multiplier using carry save adders to achieve O(log n) time, the fastest possible, with the Dadda variant noted. Finally, division is introduced with N = DQ + R.

nodes.title: Division
Overview
nodes.summary: The text covers the Wallace Tree Multiplier, explaining its O(log n) time complexity using parallel carry save adders and a final carry lookahead adder, and mentions the Dadda multiplier variant. It then introduces integer division, defining N = DQ + R with properties R < D and Q maximal, and discussing negative number handling. An iterative division approach is derived by reducing the dividend, and the restoring division algorithm is illustrated for positive 32-bit numbers using registers D and U.

nodes.title: Restoring Division
nodes.summary: The text covers division algorithms for positive and negative numbers, including properties of quotient and remainder, handling negative numbers, and converting to positive. It details the iterative restoring division algorithm for 32-bit numbers, with a proof of correctness, overflow avoidance using a 33-bit register, and time complexity O(n log n). An example dividing 4-bit numbers is provided. It also introduces non-restoring division, which reduces add/subtract operations per iteration, noting similar hardware but improved efficiency.

nodes.title: Non-Restoring Division
nodes.summary: The text covers restoring and non-restoring division algorithms. It presents a 4-bit restoring division example (7/3) with step-by-step register states, then introduces non-restoring division, explaining its efficiency from using one add/subtract per iteration instead of up to two. A 32-bit non-restoring algorithm is given, followed by a correctness proof comparing it to restoring division and an overflow analysis proving U needs 33 bits. A 4-bit non-restoring example (7/3) is also shown. Finally, it introduces floating point addition and subtraction, noting subtraction as addition of the negation, and outlines upcoming sections on same-sign, opposite-sign, and generic addition.

The section covers multiplication and division algorithms. It begins with the Wallace Tree Multiplier and Dadda variant, then defines integer division with properties and negative number handling. Restoring division is detailed for 32-bit numbers, including proof, overflow avoidance, and complexity, followed by non-restoring division with examples and correctness proofs. Finally, it introduces floating point addition and subtraction, outlining upcoming topics.

nodes.title: Floating Point Addition and Subtraction
Floating Point Addition and Subtraction (intro)
nodes.summary: The text demonstrates non-restoring division of 4-bit numbers 7/3, detailing shift and subtract steps leading to quotient 0010 and remainder 0001. It then introduces floating point addition and subtraction as equivalent problems, recaps IEEE 754 format including normalized and denormalized forms, and outlines simple addition with same signs: unpacking fields, aligning exponents by assuming EA ≥ EB, and representing significands as unsigned integers with a leading sign bit in a 25-bit register W.

nodes.title: Simple Addition with Same Signs
nodes.summary: The text covers IEEE 754 32-bit floating-point representation, including normalized and denormalized forms, significand unpacking with a leading sign bit, and a simple addition algorithm for same-sign numbers involving exponent alignment, significand addition, normalization, and overflow handling. It provides two addition examples. It then discusses rounding after truncating extra bits, defining P and residue R, and introduces the four IEEE 754 rounding modes that determine when to increment P.

nodes.title: Rounding
nodes.summary: The text explains floating-point addition with an example, then covers rounding techniques after normalization. It defines terminology like P (integer significand), R (residue), and describes modifying P by truncation or incrementing. It details four IEEE 754 rounding modes: truncation, round to +∞, round to −∞, and round to nearest (ties to even), with conditions for incrementing the significand based on sign and residue. It discusses implementing rounding, requiring state for discarded bits and P. Decimal examples illustrate each mode, and a table summarizes increment conditions.

nodes.title: Implementing Rounding
nodes.summary: The text covers IEEE 754 rounding modes with a table defining increment conditions for significand based on result sign and rounding mode. It details truncation, round to +∞, round to −∞, and round to nearest (including even rounding), explaining hardware implementation using round and sticky bits, and updating them during shifts and normalization. It addresses renormalization after rounding, including exponent overflow checks. Finally, it discusses adding numbers with opposite signs, including 2's complement, arithmetic shifting, sign determination, normalization, and the use of guard, round, and sticky bits.

nodes.title: Addition of Numbers with Opposite Signs
nodes.summary: The text details floating-point arithmetic, focusing on rounding using round and sticky bits to evaluate residue conditions, renormalization after rounding, and handling exponent overflow. It covers addition of numbers with opposite signs, including 2's complement, shifting, normalization, and the use of a guard bit with round and sticky bits for precision. A generic addition algorithm flowchart handles zero values and overflow/underflow. Finally, it briefly introduces multiplication of floating-point numbers, noting its similarity to addition.

nodes.title: Generic Algorithm for Adding Floating Point Numbers
nodes.summary: The text covers floating-point addition details: managing guard, round, and sticky bits during shifts, including left-shift optimization; rounding and possible re-normalization; and a generic addition algorithm shown in a flowchart that handles zero values, swaps operands based on exponents, manages signs, normalizes, checks overflow/underflow, rounds, and constructs the result. It also introduces floating-point multiplication as similar to generic addition but with fewer steps.

The section covers floating point addition and subtraction, starting with IEEE 754 format basics, including normalized and denormalized forms and significand unpacking. It details simple addition algorithms for same-sign numbers, involving exponent alignment, significand addition, normalization, and overflow handling. Rounding techniques are explained, defining P, residue R, and the four IEEE 754 rounding modes with increment conditions. Hardware implementation using guard, round, and sticky bits is discussed, along with renormalization and overflow checks. Addition of opposite signs using 2's complement and arithmetic shifting is covered. A generic addition algorithm flowchart handles zero values, sign management, rounding, and overflow/underflow. Multiplication is briefly introduced as similar to addition.

nodes.title: Multiplication of Floating Point Numbers
nodes.summary: The text details floating point addition, multiplication, and division algorithms. It covers guard, round, and sticky bits during shifting, and a generic addition algorithm handling zero values and exponent alignment. Multiplication involves adding exponents minus bias, multiplying significands, normalizing, and rounding, with O(log n) complexity. Division computes the quotient without remainder, initializing W with the dividend's significand and E as exponent difference plus bias. It discusses simple division with O(n log n) complexity and introduces Goldschmidt division, which computes the reciprocal of the divisor before multiplying, leveraging faster multiplication.

nodes.title: Division of Floating Point Numbers
nodes.summary: The text covers floating point division algorithms. It contrasts integer and floating point division, noting no remainder. Simple division involves exponent subtraction, significand division, normalization, and rounding, with O(n log n) complexity. Goldschmidt division computes reciprocal via series expansion, taking O(log^2 n) time. Newton-Raphson method iteratively refines reciprocal using error squaring, also O(log^2 n). It includes mathematical derivations, error analysis, and complexity comparisons, concluding that floating point division is asymptotically faster than integer division due to approximation. A summary of earlier topics like adders and multipliers is also included.

nodes.title: Summary and Further Reading
nodes.summary: This text covers computer arithmetic, including half and full adders, ripple carry, carry select, and carry lookahead adders with complexities; iterative, Booth, and Wallace tree multipliers; restoring and non-restoring division; floating-point addition, multiplication, and division algorithms; further reading on arithmetic algorithms; and exercises on adders, multipliers, dividers, floating-point, and design problems. It also introduces processor design, comparing hardwired and microprogrammed styles, and describes a basic processor design using an assembly line analogy.

The section covers computer arithmetic, starting with hardware algorithms for integer addition: half/full adders, ripple carry, carry select, and carry lookahead adders with generate/propagate functions, plus subtraction via 2's complement. Multiplication topics include partial sums, iterative multipliers, Booth encoding, Wallace tree and Dadda multipliers, and division algorithms like restoring and non-restoring. Floating-point arithmetic covers IEEE 754 format, addition/subtraction algorithms with alignment, normalization, rounding modes, guard/round/sticky bits, and overflow handling. Floating-point multiplication and division, including Goldschmidt and Newton-Raphson methods, are analyzed with complexity comparisons. A summary and further reading, including processor design styles, concludes the section.

nodes.title: Processor Design
Design of a Basic Processor
nodes.summary: This text discusses designing a basic processor for the SimpleRisc instruction set, starting with the required background. It outlines the five stages of instruction processing: instruction fetch, operand fetch/decode, execute, memory access, and register write. It contrasts hardwired and microprogrammed design styles, noting their modern relevance. The text details each stage, including fetching instructions, decoding and reading registers, executing via the ALU, accessing memory for load/store, and writing back results. It also introduces the fetch unit and the program counter, and compares processor design to a car assembly line, while covering the register file and the need for control signals.

nodes.title: Units in a Processor
Instruction Fetch – Fetch Unit
nodes.summary: The text details instruction processing stages: decoding involves operand extraction, immediate extension, and control signal generation. It covers the SimpleRisc register file, ALU operations including address and branch computation, memory unit for load/store, and write-back. It then explains the fetch unit: using the program counter (pc) to fetch 32-bit instructions from memory, computing the next PC via adder or branch target with multiplexer and isBranchTaken signal, and distinguishing PC from pc. It describes fetch unit inputs, branch conditions, and introduces data path versus control path elements.

nodes.title: Data Path and Control Path
nodes.summary: The text covers instruction fetch (IF) stage details: multiplexer selection between branchPC and default PC using isBranchTaken signal, instruction memory options (Von Neumann vs. Harvard), SRAM-based instruction memory, and fetch unit external inputs. It lists isBranchTaken conditions for non-branch, call, ret, b, beq, and bgt instructions, noting conditional branches require flags register analysis and a dedicated branch unit. It then defines data path (registers, memories, ALU) and control path (control unit generating multiplexer control signals), illustrated with a traffic analogy. Finally, it introduces the operand fetch unit, recapping SimpleRisc instruction formats (branch, register, immediate) and lists opcodes for various instructions.

nodes.title: Operand Fetch Unit
Operand Fetch Unit (intro)
nodes.summary: The text describes a processor's division into data path (storing/processing elements like memories, register file, ALU) and control path (control unit generating signals), with a city traffic analogy. It defines both paths. It recaps SimpleRisc instruction formats (branch, register, immediate) and opcodes. It details the operand fetch unit's functions: calculating immediate operands (immx) by extracting and modifying bits, and computing branch targets via PC-relative addressing, including the ret case using the ra register. It notes both fields are computed for all instructions, though only one is needed.

nodes.title: The Operand Fetch Unit
nodes.summary: The text explains instruction decoding, covering the I bit's role in distinguishing register/immediate formats, and noting that cmp, mov, and not have specific operand constraints. It then details the operand fetch unit's functions: calculating immediate operands and branch targets, and reading source registers. For immediate operands, it extracts imm18, uses modifiers to create a 32-bit immx. For branch targets, it extracts a 27-bit offset, shifts left by 2, sign-extends, and adds to PC for PC-relative addressing; for ret, the target is the ra register. It notes that both immx and branchTarget are computed for all instructions, though only one is typically needed, and the other contains junk.

nodes.title: Computation of the Immediate Operand and the Branch Target
nodes.summary: The text explains the operand fetch unit, covering immediate operand and branch target calculation from instruction bits: imm18 extraction with modifiers (sign extension, u/h), and 27-bit offset shifting/sign extension for PC-relative branchTarget, plus ret using ra. It describes reading source registers via two read ports from a 16-register file, prioritizing simplicity over power, and defines ports (read, write, read-write). Figures 9.5 and 9.6 illustrate these circuits.

nodes.title: Reading the Registers
nodes.summary: The text explains pre-computing values for speed, then details reading source registers using a register file with multiple ports. It covers operand selection via multiplexers controlled by isRet and isSt signals, defining ports, and discussing instruction decoding. It presents the operand fetch unit circuit and the branch unit, which chooses between return address and branch target, computes branch outcomes using flags (E and GT), and outlines the overall flow to the execute unit.

nodes.title: Operand Fetch, Execute, and Branch Units
nodes.summary: The page covers sending opcode and immediate bit to the control unit and the operand fetch circuit, with outputs passed to execute. It divides instructions into branch and non-branch: non-branch handled by ALU, branch by a dedicated branch unit. The branch unit circuit uses a multiplexer to select between return address (op1) and branchTarget based on isRet, outputting branchPC to fetch. It computes branch outcomes using flags (E and GT) from the last compare, illustrated with the beq instruction.

The section covers the processor's division into data and control paths using a traffic analogy, and recaps SimpleRisc instruction formats and opcodes. It details the operand fetch unit's functions: computing immediate operands (imm18 extraction, modifiers, 32-bit immx) and branch targets (27-bit offset, shift, sign-extend, PC-relative; ret uses ra). Source registers are read via two ports from a 16-register file, with multiplexers controlled by isRet and isSt. Both immx and branchTarget are computed for all instructions. The branch unit selects between return address and branch target, computes branch outcomes using E and GT flags, and passes results to the execute unit.

nodes.title: Execute Unit
nodes.summary: This text details the execute and memory access units of a processor. It covers the execute unit's division into branch and ALU handling. The branch unit uses a multiplexer for return address or branch target and logic gates to compute branch outcomes based on flags and control signals. The ALU selects between register and immediate operands, uses control signals for operations, and includes modules like adder, multiplier, divider, shifter, logical unit, and mov, enabled via transmission gates. The memory access unit uses the ALU result as address for load and store instructions.

nodes.title: Memory Access Unit
nodes.summary: This text describes the execute unit, focusing on the ALU and branch logic, including a multiplexer for output selection. It then details the memory access unit, covering address calculation, load and store instruction operations, MAR and MDR registers, and control signals (isLd, isSt). Finally, it explains the register writeback unit, including source selection (ALU result, load result, or return address), control signals (isLd, isCall), write port operation, destination register selection, and the enable signal (isWb).

nodes.title: Register Writeback Unit
nodes.summary: The text details the register writeback (RW) unit, which writes back ALU results, load results, or call return addresses (PC+4) to the register file. A multiplexer selects the source using isLd and isCall signals. The write port receives an address (destination register rd or return address register 15) and data via multiplexers, enabled by isWb, which is false for store, nop, compare, and branch instructions. Figure 9.14 shows the RW circuit. Section 9.2.7 describes the complete data path, composed of five units (IF, OF, EX, MA, RW), with two memories (instruction and data), state elements (pc, flags, register file, optional mar/mdr), and exceptions in wire orientation. Section 9.3 introduces the control unit, which generates 22 control signals (isBranchTaken from the branch unit) based on a 6-bit input (5 opcode bits and 1 immediate bit).

nodes.title: The Data Path
nodes.summary: This text covers processor design details: register writeback signal isWb conditions (false for branch instructions, true for ALU, mov, ld), the data path unifying five units (IF, OF, EX, MA, RW), clock cycle operations, two memory elements (data and instruction memory), state elements (pc, flags, register file, optional mar/mdr), wire orientations with two exceptions (branch target/outcome to fetch, writeback data to register file), interplay of data and control paths, and the control unit generating 22 control signals from 6-bit input (5 opcode, 1 immediate), with isBranchTaken from branch unit.

The section covers the processor's units: instruction fetch (PC, adder, branch target, PC vs pc, inputs, branch conditions), data path vs control path (multiplexer, memory types, branch conditions, traffic analogy), operand fetch (immediate and branch target computation, register file, multiplexers, branch unit), execute unit (branch unit, ALU operations, modules), memory access unit (address calculation, load/store, MAR/MDR, control signals), register writeback (source selection, control signals, write port, enable), data path integration (five units, memories, state elements, control unit generating 22 signals from 6-bit input).

nodes.title: The Control Unit
nodes.summary: The text covers processor design, detailing the data path that combines five units: instruction fetch, operand fetch, execution, memory access, and register writeback. It describes state elements like pc, flags, and register file, and notes top-down wire orientation with exceptions for branch and writeback data. It then explains the control unit, listing 22 control signals and their conditions, including isWb, aluSignals, and isBranchTaken. It contrasts hardwired control (fast but inflexible) with microprogram-based control (flexible via microinstructions) for modifying or adding instructions, and summarizes the hardwired SimpleRisc ISA processor design.

nodes.title: Microprogram-Based Processor
nodes.summary: This text covers CISC instructions, hardwired processor design (five stages, data path elements, control signals), and introduces microprogrammed processors. It defines microprogramming, discusses its flexibility benefits like fixing bugs, implementing complex instructions, SOC customization, and BIST routines. Firmware is defined, and the efficiency-flexibility tradeoff is highlighted. The design of a microprogrammed data path using a bus-based structure is introduced, with a bus definition and simplified unit design.

nodes.title: Microprogrammed Data Path
Microprogrammed Data Path (intro)
nodes.summary: The text defines firmware as microcode in modern devices and introduces microprogrammed processor design for post-fabrication flexibility, noting the efficiency-flexibility tradeoff. It describes modifying a hardwired data path to use a bus-based interconnect for flexible unit communication, defining a bus with one writer and multiple readers. It outlines simplified units: the fetch unit with PC and IR registers, where PC reads/writes to the bus and IR is not bus-connected, and the decode unit that decodes instructions into fields like rs1, rs2, and immediate, similar to an operand fetch unit but without the register file.

nodes.title: Fetch Unit
nodes.summary: The text covers the design philosophy of a microprogrammed processor, emphasizing independent units with input/output registers connected to a shared bus, each performing actions in about one cycle. It details the fetch unit, including its pc and ir registers, bus connections, and the need for instruction decoding. It also describes the decode unit, which breaks down instructions into fields like rd, rs1, rs2, immediate, and branch target, excluding the register file, and references figures for both units.

nodes.title: Decode Unit
nodes.summary: This text describes the design of key units in a microprogrammed processor. It explains the fetch unit, which uses pc and ir registers connected to a shared bus, with ir not connected. The decode unit breaks down instructions into fields like I, rd, rs1, rs2, immx, and branchTarget, extracting specific bits from ir, and computes branch targets. The register file is kept separate, with regSrc, regData, and regVal registers, and supports read, write, and nop operations via args values from the bus. Each unit operates independently with input/output registers, performing one-cycle computations.

nodes.title: Register File
nodes.summary: The text describes components of a microprogrammed processor's datapath. It details the decode unit extracting instruction fields (I, rd, rs1, rs2, immx, branchTarget) from the instruction register, including branch target calculation, and notes that extracting all fields simplifies datapath design. It then covers the register file, which is separate from decode (unlike hardwired), with regSrc, regData, regVal, and args for read, write, and nop operations. Finally, it describes the ALU with input registers A and B, args-specified operations like add and subtract, flag updates (flags.E and flags.GT) for comparisons, and result storage in aluResult, assuming 1-cycle operation for both register file and ALU.

nodes.title: ALU
nodes.summary: The text describes the components of a microprogrammed processor's data path. It details the register file, accessed via regSrc, regData, and args, with read results in regVal after one cycle. The ALU takes inputs A and B, performs operations specified by args, updates flags.E and flags.GT for comparisons, and stores results in aluResult, also in one cycle. The memory unit uses mar and mdr for addresses and data, executes load/store via args, and places loaded data in ldResult. Finally, an overview integrates these units with a microprogrammed control unit that executes microinstructions to orchestrate data flow.

nodes.title: Memory Unit
nodes.summary: The text covers the memory unit and data path in a microprogrammed processor. Section 9.5.5 describes the memory unit (Figure 9.21), which includes mar and mdr registers, arguments for load/store operations, and the ldResult register for loaded data. Section 9.5.6 provides an overview of the data path (Figure 9.22), integrating all units and adding the microprogrammed control unit (μcontrol unit) that executes microinstructions and orchestrates data flow. The data path includes components like instruction memory, register file, ALU, and flags.

nodes.title: Overview of the Data Path
nodes.summary: Describes the memory unit in a microprogrammed processor, including mar, mdr, ldResult registers, and load/store arguments. Presents the complete data path with the microprogrammed control unit (μcontrol unit), which executes microinstructions, orchestrates data transfers, and updates the PC. Notes an extra connection from ir to the μcontrol unit for the opcode. Defines the μcontrol unit, microprogram memory, and micro PC (μpc). Introduces the microassembly language: its machine model, internal registers of varying widths (1-bit, 4-bit, 32-bit), and the start of microinstructions for a program instruction's life cycle.

The section on Microprogrammed Data Path defines firmware as microcode and explains the microprogrammed processor design for post-fabrication flexibility, highlighting the efficiency-flexibility tradeoff. It details a bus-based interconnect with one writer and multiple readers, and describes key units: the fetch unit with PC and IR registers; the decode unit extracting instruction fields and computing branch targets; the register file with regSrc, regData, regVal, and args for read/write/nop; the ALU with inputs A and B, operations, flags, and aluResult; and the memory unit with mar, mdr, ldResult, and load/store arguments. It concludes with an overview integrating all units with a microprogrammed control unit that executes microinstructions, orchestrates data flow, updates the PC, and introduces the microassembly language and microinstruction lifecycle.

nodes.title: Microassembly Language
Machine Model
nodes.summary: The text discusses the microcontrol unit (μcontrol unit) in a microprogrammed processor, responsible for executing microinstructions, managing data transfers, and updating the PC. It highlights an extra connection from the ir register to the μcontrol unit for opcode transfer, ensuring only this unit accesses the opcode. Definition 63 defines the μcontrol unit as hardware that fetches and executes microinstructions from a dedicated microprogram memory, using a micro PC (μpc) to point to the current microinstruction. It also introduces Section 9.6 on microassembly language, covering the machine model with internal registers (1-bit, 4-bit, 32-bit) visible to microassembly instructions, and notes that microinstructions do not access memory. Section 9.6.2 begins discussing microinstructions and the life cycle of a program instruction, starting with fetching from instruction memory.

nodes.title: Microinstructions
nodes.summary: The text describes a microcontrol unit (μcontrol) for a microprogrammed processor, responsible for executing microinstructions, data transfers, and PC updates. It details a microprogram memory storing microinstructions per program instruction, a micro PC (μpc) pointing to the current microinstruction, and an opcode connection from the instruction register (ir) to μcontrol. It introduces the microassembly language, including the machine model (internal registers of various sizes), and eight microinstructions (mloadIR, mdecode, mswitch, mmov, mmovi, madd, mbeq, mb). It also covers the preamble (common microinstructions) and the design rationale, such as using PC-direct addressing and allocating 10 bits for microinstruction addresses to support up to 1024 microinstructions.

nodes.title: Implementing Instructions in the Microassembly Language
nodes.summary: The text explains microinstructions and their implementation. It lists 8 microinstructions with semantics, encoded in 3 bits. It introduces a 4-instruction preamble common to all program instructions for fetching, decoding, incrementing PC, and jumping to instruction-specific microcode. It details implementing 3-address ALU instructions, including reading operands, combining register transfers with ALU operations, and handling register vs. immediate operands via conditional branching.

nodes.title: 3-Address Format ALU Instructions
nodes.summary: The text describes microcode implementation for instruction processing, including fetching the PC, decoding, incrementing PC (or overwriting for branches), and executing mswitch to jump to instruction-specific microcode. It details 3-address format ALU instructions (add, sub, mul, div, mod, and, or, lsl, lsr, asr) with microcode handling operand reads, immediate checks, ALU operations, result write-back, and branching to .begin. It also covers 2-address format ALU instructions (not, mov, cmp), focusing on mov with similar immediate/register handling and write-back. The text emphasizes fusing register transfers with ALU operations for efficiency, and notes the total microinstruction count per program instruction.

nodes.title: 2-Address Format ALU Instructions
nodes.summary: The text describes microcode implementations for several instructions, starting with a snippet that writes the ALU result to the register file and notes the overhead of 14 microinstructions per program instruction, emphasizing flexibility. It then details 2-address ALU instructions: mov, not, and cmp, including handling of register and immediate operands, and the write-back process. It describes the nop instruction as a simple branch. Finally, it explains the ld instruction, covering effective address calculation, memory load, and writing the loaded value to the register file.

nodes.title: The nop Instruction
nodes.summary: The text covers implementing compare operations where the second operand is an immediate by transferring rs1 to ALU register A, checking if the operand is an immediate, then transferring immx to register B and issuing a compare, or if a register, reading from the register file and transferring to ALU, then branching. It details the trivial nop instruction via branching. For ld and st instructions, it describes transferring rs1 to ALU, adding the immediate to compute the effective address in aluResult, moving it to mar, initiating load, and writing ldResult to rd over two cycles, with corresponding assembly code.

nodes.title: ld and st instructions
nodes.summary: The text details microcode implementations for SimpleRisc instructions: ALU operations handling immediate or register operands and compare; trivial nop via branch; ld calculating effective address, loading to mar, and writing ldResult to rd; st computing address and storing rd value via mdr; branch instructions including unconditional b setting PC to branchTarget, conditional beq and bgt checking flags, and call (combining branch with writing PC+4 to return address register 15) and ret.

nodes.title: Branch Instructions
nodes.summary: Microcode implementations for SimpleRisc store, branch (b, beq, bgt, call, ret), and examples (stack-based call/ret, factorial, Armstrong number, prime test) are provided.
