The store instruction's microcode calculates the effective address then stores data. Branch instructions handle unconditional and conditional branches, with call saving the return address. Examples show stack-based call/ret and custom instructions. A shared bus design with write and read buses, a transfer multiplexer, and a μadder is described, where registers connect to both buses, the PC connects to both, and the isMBranch signal is generated for conditional branches.

The section on Microassembly Language describes the microcontrol unit in a microprogrammed processor, its role in executing microinstructions, managing data transfers, and updating the PC, with a dedicated micro PC and microprogram memory. It covers the machine model with internal registers of various sizes, eight microinstructions, and their encoding. It details implementing instructions, including a common preamble for fetching, decoding, and jumping to instruction-specific microcode. It explains 3-address and 2-address ALU instructions, nop, ld, st, and branch instructions (b, beq, bgt, call, ret), with examples and a shared bus design featuring write/read buses, transfer multiplexer, and microadder.

nodes.title: Shared Bus and Control Signals
nodes.summary: The text presents microcode for divisibility and comparison, then details a shared bus design with write and read buses, a transfer multiplexer, and a microadder, connecting registers, PC, and functional units. It describes control signals for register read/write, functional unit arguments encoded with unit ID and opcode, and introduces the microcontrol unit with vertical and horizontal microprogramming paradigms, including a 45-bit vertical microinstruction encoding.

nodes.title: The Microcontrol Unit
Vertical Microprogramming
nodes.summary: The text details encoding processor operations using binary, with a special zero value indicating no operation, and a 10-bit args bus split into 3-bit unit ID and 7-bit opcode, supporting 128 operations per unit. It then covers the microcontrol unit design, comprising a μfetch unit and μpc, which increments or branches each cycle. Two microinstruction encoding paradigms are presented: vertical microprogramming, which uses a 45-bit encoding with a dedicated decode unit to generate control signals, and horizontal microprogramming, which uses a 65-bit encoding with control signals embedded, eliminating the decode stage. The text includes figures and tables illustrating encodings, unit designs, and multiplexer control rules.

nodes.title: Horizontal Microprogramming
nodes.summary: The text explains horizontal microprogramming by removing the decode stage and embedding control signals directly in microinstructions. It details the microinstruction encoding with fields for control signals (33 bits), immediate (12 bits), branch target (10 bits), and args (10 bits), totaling 65 bits, derived from register control signals, transfer multiplexer, and μfetch multiplexer controls. It describes the simplified μcontrol unit and modified μfetch multiplexer with rules in Table 9.9. Finally, it contrasts horizontal and vertical microprogramming: horizontal needs more storage but eliminates signal generation logic and requires processor-specific microassemblers, while vertical is more portable.

nodes.title: Trade-offs between Horizontal and Vertical Microprogramming
nodes.summary: The text details horizontal microprogramming using a μcontrol unit, where decode is eliminated and signals are embedded in instructions, with an execute unit generating isMBranch and a 4-input μfetch multiplexer. It contrasts horizontal and vertical microprogramming trade-offs: storage, signal logic, and microassembler specificity. A summary covers processor design with five stages (IF, OF, EX, MA, RW), their roles, data vs. control paths, hardwired control, and microprogrammed processor with 8 microinstructions and 19 registers on a shared bus.

The section covers the microcontrol unit, including processor operation encoding with a 10-bit args bus and 45-bit vertical or 65-bit horizontal microinstruction formats. It describes the μfetch unit, μpc, and two encoding paradigms: vertical microprogramming uses a decode unit for control signals, while horizontal embeds signals directly, eliminating decode but requiring more storage and processor-specific microassemblers. Trade-offs are contrasted. A processor design summary includes five stages (IF, OF, EX, MA, RW), data vs. control paths, hardwired control, and a microprogrammed processor with 8 microinstructions and 19 registers on a shared bus.

nodes.title: Summary and Further Reading
nodes.summary: The text summarizes processor design, focusing on a five-stage SimpleRisc pipeline (IF, OF, EX, MA, RW) and the roles of each stage. It distinguishes data and control paths, and covers hardwired control units versus microprogrammed processors. Microprogramming details include eight microinstructions, a shared bus data path with 19 registers, microcode for all SimpleRisc instructions, and vertical versus horizontal microprogramming trade-offs. It also provides further reading suggestions and a series of exercises on hardwired design, microprogramming, and design problems like Logisim and VHDL implementations. The section ends with an introduction to pipelining principles.

This section covers processor design for a SimpleRisc instruction set. It details the five stages: instruction fetch, operand fetch/decode, execute, memory access, and register writeback. It contrasts hardwired and microprogrammed control, explaining units like fetch unit, ALU, register file, and control signals. It introduces microprogramming, microinstructions, microassembly language, and shared bus data paths. It discusses vertical versus horizontal microprogramming trade-offs. The section concludes with a summary, exercises, and an introduction to pipelining.

nodes.title: Principles of Pipelining
A Pipelined Processor
The Notion of Pipelining
nodes.summary: The text reviews a five-stage hardwired processor (IF, OF, EX, MA, RW) with data and control paths, and mentions a microprogram-based alternative. It then addresses the inefficiency of a single-cycle processor, where most units are idle because each instruction completes sequentially. Using a car factory analogy, it introduces pipelining: overlapping the execution of multiple instructions so that different stages work concurrently. It describes how instructions move through the pipeline one stage per cycle, keeping all units busy, and notes the five-stage pipeline organization shown in a figure.

nodes.title: Overview of Pipelining
nodes.summary: The text explains the inefficiency of single-cycle processors due to idle units, using a car factory analogy, and introduces pipelining as a solution. It defines pipelining, describes its five stages (IF, OF, EX, MA, RW), and how instructions move through them simultaneously to keep all units busy. It outlines the instruction lifecycle and presents the performance benefit: a 5x increase in instruction throughput because the cycle time is reduced to τ/5, allowing one instruction to finish every τ/5 nanoseconds instead of every τ nanoseconds.

nodes.title: Performance Benefits
nodes.summary: This text defines pipelining as dividing a processor into ordered stages to process instructions concurrently, assuming equal stage times. It illustrates a five-stage pipeline (IF, OF, EX, MA, RW) and its performance benefits: with balanced stages, cycle time reduces to τ/5, yielding a five-fold throughput increase over a single-cycle processor. It notes limitations to arbitrarily increasing pipeline stages. It then introduces the design of a simple pipeline, focusing on splitting the data path into the five stages to process five instructions simultaneously without considering dependencies or correctness issues.

This section introduces pipelining as a technique to improve processor efficiency. It begins by reviewing a five-stage hardwired processor (IF, OF, EX, MA, RW) and contrasts it with a single-cycle processor's inefficiency, where units sit idle because instructions execute sequentially. Using a car factory analogy, it explains how pipelining overlaps instruction execution, keeping all units busy by moving instructions through stages one per cycle. The overview reiterates this, detailing the five stages and the instruction lifecycle. Performance benefits are quantified: with balanced stages, cycle time reduces to τ/5, yielding a five-fold throughput increase. The section also notes limitations on increasing pipeline stages and introduces the design of a simple pipeline, focusing on splitting the data path into five stages to process five instructions simultaneously, without addressing dependencies or correctness issues.

nodes.title: Design of a Simple Pipeline
Splitting the Data Path
nodes.summary: The text covers pipelining advantages, noting a 5-stage pipeline gives a five-fold speedup, but limitations prevent unlimited stage increases. It then details designing a simple pipeline by splitting the data path into five stages (IF, OF, EX, MA, RW), ensuring all instructions traverse in the same order with balanced stage delays. Exceptions like division are noted. Timing is managed via a global clock and pipeline registers (latches) inserted between stages to enable simultaneous instruction advancement each cycle.

nodes.title: Timing
nodes.summary: The text discusses pipelining a data path, covering rules for splitting circuits: distinct subparts with minimal connections, uniform data flow order, and balanced work. It notes div/mod operations as exceptions causing imbalance, often handled by stalling. Timing is addressed using a global clock and pipeline registers (latches) inserted between five stages (IF, OF, EX, MA, RW), transferring instructions at clock edges. It defines pipeline registers and explains instruction transfer. The instruction packet concept is introduced to hold all instruction details, intermediate results, and control signals, ensuring no overlap between instructions, with all pipeline registers sized uniformly. The data path design mirrors the single-cycle processor with added registers and connections.

nodes.title: The Instruction Packet
nodes.summary: The text defines pipeline registers/latches, which transfer instructions between stages on the clock's negative edge. It illustrates an instruction moving through IF, OF, and EX registers. It introduces the instruction packet, containing all details, intermediate results, and control signals for an instruction, to prevent overlap between concurrent instructions and ensure state cleanup. It specifies packet contents (PC, instruction, operands, control signals) and notes uniform register sizing. It then describes designing the pipelined data path, adding registers after each stage except RW, and begins detailing the IF and OF stages.

Design of a simple pipeline involves splitting the data path into five stages (IF, OF, EX, MA, RW), ensuring balanced delays and uniform data flow, despite exceptions like division. Timing uses a global clock and pipeline registers between stages to advance instructions each cycle. Pipeline registers, or latches, transfer instructions on clock edges, and the instruction packet holds all instruction details, intermediate results, and control signals to prevent overlap and ensure uniform register sizing. The pipelined data path adds registers after each stage except RW, mirroring the single-cycle processor with added registers and connections.

nodes.title: Pipeline Stages
IF Stage
nodes.summary: The text covers Section 10.3 on Pipeline Stages, specifically 10.3.1 IF Stage and 10.3.2 OF Stage. For the IF stage, it explains the addition of a pipeline register to save the PC and instruction, with Figure 10.4 illustrating the design and noting minimal data path changes. For the OF stage, it introduces Figure 10.5 showing the operand fetch stage design, highlighting extra additions such as the pipeline register and control unit components like isImmediate.

nodes.title: OF Stage
nodes.summary: The text describes three pipeline stages in a processor. The IF stage adds a pipeline register to save the PC and instruction. The OF stage extracts fields, uses control signals, and saves intermediate results and control signals in the OF-EX register. The EX stage uses the ALU, computes branch outcomes and targets, and saves results in the EX-MA register.

nodes.title: EX Stage
nodes.summary: The text details the OF, EX, MA, and RW stages of a pipelined processor. The OF stage extracts instruction fields, sends them to register file and control units, and saves control signals and intermediate results in the OF-EX pipeline register. The EX stage uses the ALU for operations, computes branch targets and outcomes, and stores results in the EX-MA register. The MA stage accesses data memory for load/store using ALU result and op2, saving load results in MA-RW. The RW stage writes data back to the register file using control signals like isWb, finalizing instruction execution.

nodes.title: MA Stage
nodes.summary: This text describes the branch unit's role in determining isBranchTaken and the default PC fetching. It then details two pipelined processor stages: the MA stage, where the ALU result provides the effective memory address, store data comes from the op2 field connected to the MDR, control signals isLd and isSt go to the memory unit, and the load result is saved in ldResult; and the RW stage, illustrated in Figure 10.8, showing the register file write-back with fields like ldResult, aluResult, isLd, isCall, rd, and isWb.

nodes.title: RW Stage
nodes.summary: The text details the MA and RW stages of a pipelined processor, describing how the MA stage uses ALU results as memory addresses and op2 for store data, with control signals isLd and isSt routed to memory, outputting ldResult. The RW stage multiplexes aluResult, ldResult, and PC+4 for write-back into the register file, with no pipeline register at the end. It then summarizes the full pipeline datapath with registers, introducing abstraction for advanced pipelines, and notes assumed multiplexers for register operands. Finally, it introduces pipeline hazards, starting with the pipeline diagram tool for analyzing instruction dependencies and execution stages.

nodes.title: Putting it All Together
nodes.summary: The text explains the RW stage's inputs (aluResult, ldResult, and PC+4) and multiplexer for write-back, noting no pipeline register at the end. It summarizes the complete pipeline datapath with registers (Figure 10.9), then shifts to an abstracted block-diagram version (Figure 10.10) for advanced pipelines, omitting operand-selection multiplexers as part of the register file. It introduces pipeline hazards as a correctness concern, and describes the pipeline diagram as a tool for analyzing instruction dependencies, clock cycles, and stage execution.

The section covers pipeline stages in a processor: IF stage adds a pipeline register to save PC and instruction with minimal data path changes; OF stage extracts fields, uses control signals, and saves intermediate results and control signals in the OF-EX register; EX stage uses ALU, computes branch outcomes and targets, and saves results in the EX-MA register; MA stage accesses data memory for load/store using ALU result and op2, saving load results in MA-RW; RW stage writes data back to the register file using control signals like isWb, with no pipeline register at the end. nodes.title: Pipeline Hazards
The Pipeline Diagram
nodes.summary: The text describes the RW stage of a pipeline, including inputs from ALU and load results, multiplexer selection, and lack of a pipeline register. It summarizes the full pipelined data path, introduces abstraction for advanced pipelines, and omits certain multiplexers for simplicity. It then covers pipeline hazards, focusing on pipeline diagrams to analyze correctness, provides rules for constructing them, and gives an example. It introduces data hazards with an example of a dependency between add and sub instructions, and begins a pipeline diagram for that case.

nodes.title: Data Hazards
nodes.summary: The text explains pipeline diagrams, showing how instructions move through IF, OF, EX, MA, RW stages, can stall, and cannot have duplicate entries. It defines hazards as potential erroneous execution, focusing on data hazards like RAW, WAW, and WAR, noting RAW is critical in in-order pipelines while WAW/WAR affect out-of-order processors, mitigated by register renaming. An example pipeline diagram shows a RAW hazard. It also introduces control hazards from branch instructions, with an example.

nodes.title: Control Hazards
nodes.summary: This text defines in-order and out-of-order pipelines, explaining WAW, WAR, and RAW hazards, with examples showing how register renaming prevents wrong values in modern processors. It then covers control hazards from branch instructions, describing wrong-path execution and pipeline diagrams, and defines control hazards. Finally, it defines structural hazards, provides an example of conflicting memory access, and argues that the SimpleRisc pipeline avoids structural hazards due to sufficient fetch unit and register file capacity, concluding that focus should be on eliminating RAW and control hazards.

nodes.title: Structural Hazards
nodes.summary: The text discusses control hazards and the need to nullify wrong-path instructions to prevent register/memory commitment. It defines structural hazards as resource constraints causing stalls, provides an example with memory access conflicts, and argues SimpleRisc avoids them due to adequate fetch and register file capacity. Software solutions for RAW hazards are explored, including compiler-inserted nops and instruction reordering, with an example problem on reordering code and adding nops for correct SimpleRisc execution.

The Pipeline Hazards section covers pipeline diagrams for analyzing correctness, including construction rules, examples, and the full pipelined data path with RW stage details. It defines data hazards (RAW, WAW, WAR), emphasizing RAW in in-order pipelines and register renaming for out-of-order processors. Control hazards from branches are explained via wrong-path execution and nullification. Structural hazards are defined, with an example of memory access conflicts, but SimpleRisc avoids them due to sufficient resources. Software solutions for RAW hazards, such as compiler-inserted nops and instruction reordering, are also discussed.

nodes.title: Solutions in Software
nodes.summary: The text explains software and hardware solutions for pipeline hazards. It details avoiding RAW hazards via nop insertion and compiler reordering, and control hazards using delay slots and delayed branches, with examples. It introduces hardware interlocks, specifically Data-Lock and Branch-Lock conditions, to ensure correctness by stalling the pipeline. It defines pipeline stalls and compares software and hardware approaches.

nodes.title: Pipeline with Interlocks
Pipeline with Interlocks (intro)
nodes.summary: This text discusses hardware-level pipeline interlocks as a solution to RAW and control hazards, contrasting them with limited, non-portable software solutions. It defines two key conditions: Data-Lock (stalling instruction issue until correct operands are available) and Branch-Lock (preventing wrong-path execution). Pipeline stalls, or interlocks, enforce these conditions. A comparison table outlines trade-offs: software solutions offer potential performance benefits but lack portability and depend on program characteristics, while hardware interlocks are generic but slower due to stalls. The text also suggests combining approaches by reordering code to reduce stalls. It ends by introducing pipeline diagrams for interlocks, starting with a data hazard example.

nodes.title: A Conceptual Look at a Pipeline with Interlocks
nodes.summary: This text compares software and hardware approaches for pipeline correctness, detailing trade-offs in portability, branch handling, RAW hazards, and performance. It explains using a combination of code scheduling and hardware interlocks. It defines pipeline bubbles for dynamically stalling pipelines to resolve data and control hazards, including detailed pipeline diagrams for RAW and branch hazards. It describes implementing bubbles via a bubble bit or opcode change, and the need to disable affected stages to avoid redundant work. It also covers handling slow instructions like div/mod using multiple T states and stalling fetch and operand fetch stages.

nodes.title: Ensuring the Data-Lock Condition
nodes.summary: This text covers pipeline hazard management. It details ensuring the Data-Lock condition with conflict detection hardware comparing OF stage instructions against EX, MA, and RW stages to identify RAW hazards. It outlines stalling mechanisms by disabling PC and IF-OF registers and inserting nops (bubbles). Algorithm 5 provides pseudocode for conflict detection. It also addresses the Branch-Lock condition, comparing predict-not-taken (fetching and canceling on taken branches) with stalling, and notes a branch hazard unit modifies stages on taken branches. Finally, it introduces pipeline forwarding concepts.

nodes.title: Ensuring the Branch-Lock condition
nodes.summary: The text discusses ensuring the branch-lock condition in pipelines, covering branch instructions and delay slots, with pros and cons of software exposure. It presents two design options for avoiding delay slot exposure: predict not taken (fetching subsequent instructions and canceling if branch taken) and stalling. The predict-not-taken approach is preferred for performance, with details on canceling instructions and converting to bubbles, requiring a branch hazard unit. It includes Important Point 14 and mentions the augmented data path. Finally, it introduces a pipeline with forwarding and basic concepts.

This section covers hardware pipeline interlocks as a solution to RAW and control hazards, contrasting them with software approaches. It defines Data-Lock and Branch-Lock conditions, enforced by pipeline stalls or bubbles. It compares trade-offs between software scheduling and hardware interlocks, detailing conflict detection hardware for RAW hazards and mechanisms for stalling via disabling registers and inserting nops. It also addresses branch handling with predict-not-taken versus stalling, the role of a branch hazard unit, and introduces pipeline forwarding.

nodes.title: Pipeline with Forwarding
Basic Concepts
nodes.summary: The text covers ensuring the Branch-Lock condition in pipelines with delay slots versus not exposing them to software. Two design options are presented: predict not taken with cancellation, or stalling. It details the predict-not-taken approach, including a branch hazard unit, and references an augmented data path. Then it introduces pipeline forwarding as an alternative to interlocks, explaining basic concepts and forwarding paths like RW→MA, RW→EX, and MA→EX to resolve data dependencies without stalls.

nodes.title: Forwarding Paths in a Pipeline
nodes.summary: The text explains forwarding as a technique to avoid pipeline stalls by transferring operand values directly between stages. It details specific forwarding paths: RW→MA, RW→EX, MA→EX, and the tricky RW→OF, which requires canceling a register read. It notes that MA→OF, EX→OF, and paths to IF are unnecessary. The text also discusses data hazards: forwarding always works for ALU producers but fails for load instructions when the consumer needs the value too early, requiring a backward-in-time path.

nodes.title: Data Hazards with Forwarding
nodes.summary: The text discusses forwarding in pipelined processors, explaining that instructions in the OF stage receive operand values via forwarding paths rather than the register file, avoiding inconsistent register states. It argues against adding certain forwarding paths (MA→OF, EX→OF) as redundant, and notes that paths to IF are unnecessary since operands are unknown. The text then examines whether forwarding eliminates all data hazards, concluding it does not: load-use hazards require a stall cycle because a load's value is available too late for an immediately following instruction's EX stage. It defines load-use hazards, notes that store instructions after loads do not need stalls, and mentions compiler or bubble solutions. Finally, it introduces the implementation of forwarding, focusing on datapath changes using multiplexers before functional unit inputs.

nodes.title: Implementation of a Pipeline with Forwarding
Implementation of a Pipeline with Forwarding (intro)
nodes.summary: The text defines a load-use hazard as when a load instruction supplies a value to an immediately following instruction's EX stage, requiring a single stall cycle in a forwarding pipeline. It discusses elimination methods: inserting a bubble, compiler reordering, or using a nop. A store after a load does not need a stall because the value is needed in the MA stage, allowing forwarding from RW. Then, it describes implementing a pipeline with forwarding, focusing on data path changes: adding multiplexers before functional unit inputs. Specifically, the OF stage adds M1 and M2 to select between register file values and forwarded RW values, alongside baseline multiplexer M′. The IF stage requires no changes, and the text notes that all possible register operands are read due to timing constraints.

nodes.title: OF Stage with Forwarding
nodes.summary: The text explains hardware support for forwarding in a pipelined processor. It details modifications to the OF, EX, MA, and RW stages using multiplexers. In the OF stage, M1 and M2 select between register file values and forwarded RW values. The EX stage adds M3 and M4 for forwarding from MA and RW to ALU inputs, and M5 for RW-to-EX forwarding of the store value. The MA stage includes M6 to forward the store value from RW. The RW stage does not use forwarded values but sends its write value to earlier stages. It notes that the IF stage is unchanged, and explains design conventions and reasons for reading all register operands.

nodes.title: Pipeline Stages with Forwarding Support
nodes.summary: This page details forwarding in the EX, MA, and RW stages. The EX stage uses multiplexers M3, M4, and M5 to select between OF-stage values and forwarded values from MA and RW for operands A, B, and op2; MA-to-EX forwarding is omitted for op2 to save a path. The MA stage adds multiplexer M6 to choose between op2 and forwarded RW value for store data, with memory address from EX. The RW stage, as the last stage, does not use forwarded values but sends its write value to MA, EX, and other stages.

nodes.title: RW Stage with Forwarding
nodes.summary: The text details adding forwarding to EX, MA, and RW pipeline stages. In EX, multiplexers M3 and M4 select between OF values and forwarded MA/RW values for operands A and B; M5 forwards only RW for op2. In MA, M6 selects between op2 and forwarded RW for store values. RW forwards written values to MA, EX, and OF. The integrated pipeline requires six multiplexers, extra interconnections, and a forwarding unit for control signals, significantly complicating the data path.

nodes.title: Putting it All Together
nodes.summary: The text explains adding forwarding and interlock logic to a pipelined processor. It describes multiplexers and interconnections for forwarding, and a dedicated forwarding unit to generate control signals. Figures 10.27–10.30 illustrate stages and the full datapath. It covers interlock logic for data-lock (load-use hazards) and branch-lock conditions, noting load-store dependencies don't stall due to forwarding. Data-lock stalls one cycle with a bubble; branch-lock invalidates IF/OF on taken branches. Interlocks take precedence over forwarding. Finally, it introduces designing the control path and forwarding unit for multiplexer control.

nodes.title: Forwarding Conditions
nodes.summary: The text introduces Figure 10.31, a pipelined processor with forwarding, and discusses RAW hazard handling. It explains that for load-use hazards, only a 1-cycle stall is needed, simplifying the Data-Lock circuit by checking dependencies between load in EX and instruction in OF, excluding load-store dependence due to forwarding from RW to MA. Other data dependencies require a 1-cycle stall with a bubble. Branch-Lock conditions remain identical: if a taken branch is in EX, invalidate IF and OF. Interlocks always take precedence over forwarding. Finally, it transitions to designing the control path's forwarding unit for controlling forwarding multiplexers.

The section covers implementing forwarding in a pipelined processor to handle data hazards, especially load-use hazards that require a one-cycle stall via bubble, compiler reordering, or nop. It details datapath changes: adding multiplexers in OF (M1, M2), EX (M3, M4, M5), and MA (M6) stages to select forwarded values, while IF remains unchanged and RW forwards its write value. A forwarding unit generates control signals, with six multiplexers and extra interconnections. Interlock logic handles data-lock and branch-lock stalls, taking precedence over forwarding, and the control path design for multiplexer control is introduced.

nodes.title: Forwarding Conditions
Forwarding Conditions (intro)
nodes.summary: The text details a pipelined processor with forwarding, focusing on hazard handling and forwarding unit design. It explains that for RAW hazards except load-use, forwarding suffices; load-use requires a 1-cycle stall via a bubble. A load-store dependence needs no stall due to RW→MA forwarding. Branch-lock condition remains unchanged, invalidating IF and OF for taken branches. Interlocks take precedence over forwarding. The forwarding unit, using inputs from four pipeline registers, controls forwarding multiplexers. Four forwarding paths are discussed: RW→OF, RW→EX, MA→EX, RW→MA with distances 3,2,1,1. Distance-1 paths are necessary: MA→EX for consecutive ALU instructions, RW→MA for load-store. Sometimes both paths are possible, preferring RW→MA to forward late. The mov instruction is treated as a regular ALU instruction for simplicity, ignoring potential optimizations.

nodes.title: Forwarding Unit, Paths, and Distance Cases
key_items: Forwarding Paths with Distance Equal to 1
nodes.summary: The forwarding unit takes inputs from four pipeline registers (OF, EX, MA, RW) to compute control signals. nodes.title: Case of the mov Instruction

nodes.title: Conflicts with Multiple Instructions
nodes.summary: The text discusses handling conflicts with multiple instructions in forwarding paths. It explains that when an EX stage instruction has RAW dependence on both MA and RW stages, the MA stage value must be chosen due to its earlier position, using a priority circuit. It then presents pseudocode for forwarding conditions: Algorithm 6 detects first operand conflicts (rs1 or ra for ret), and Algorithm 7 detects second operand conflicts (rs2, rd for store, ra for call), ignoring ready-to-use hazards and interlocks, and only applying when forwarding paths exist.

nodes.title: Algorithms for Forwarding Conditions

nodes.title: Support for Interrupts/ Exceptions*
Interrupts
nodes.summary: The text discusses forwarding correctness in pipelines, including a special case where a call instruction forwards to a ret via the RW→OF path without issues. It then introduces interrupts and exceptions: interrupts are signals from I/O devices that make the processor stop and jump to a handler; exceptions arise from program errors and use the same handler mechanism. The text defines both terms and emphasizes precise exceptions, where the processor must resume exactly at the interrupted point after handling, treating interrupts and exceptions generically.

nodes.title: Exceptions
nodes.summary: The text explains interrupts and exceptions. It describes an interrupt as a signal from an I/O device to the processor, like a keyboard press, which causes the processor to stop execution and jump to an interrupt handler. Exceptions are interrupts generated by program actions, such as illegal memory access, and are handled by exception handlers, similar to Java exceptions. Precise exceptions refer to the processor stopping, handling, and resuming exactly where it left off, a term applied to both interrupts and exceptions.

nodes.title: Precise Exceptions
nodes.summary: This text covers interrupts and exceptions in computer architecture. It defines interrupts as signals from I/O devices to the processor, and exceptions as events triggered by erroneous program actions. nodes.title: Saving and Restoring Program State

nodes.title: Performance Metrics

nodes.title: Performance of an Ideal Pipelined Processor
nodes.summary: The text defines static and dynamic instructions, CPI, IPC, and the performance equation. nodes.title: Power and Temperature Issues
Overview
nodes.summary: The text discusses performance relationships involving compiler, architecture, and technology, noting power and complexity constraints limit pipeline depth. It covers power and temperature issues: high power dissipation in processors, server farms, and mobile devices; chip packaging with heat spreaders, TIM, heat sinks, and fans; temperature effects like reliability, aging (NBTI), and leakage. nodes.title: Dynamic Power
nodes.summary: The text discusses processor heat generation, reaching up to 120°C, and its negative effects: reduced reliability of copper wires and transistors, aging via NBTI, and temperature-dependent leakage power. It emphasizes reducing power and temperature for lower electricity bills, cooling costs, longer battery life, higher reliability, and slower aging. It reviews power dissipation mechanisms: dynamic power (from charging/discharging capacitances during transitions, proportional to activity factor, capacitance, supply voltage squared, and frequency) and leakage power (static power from sub-threshold and gate-induced drain leakage, accounting for 20-40% of processor power).

nodes.title: Leakage Power
nodes.summary: The text covers dynamic power, leakage power, and temperature modeling in processors. Dynamic power is resistive loss from input/output transitions, proportional to frequency and supply voltage squared. Leakage power, 20-40% of total power, arises from current flow across supposedly isolated terminals, including sub-threshold and gate-induced drain leakage. The BSIM3 model equation for leakage power is presented, with variables defined. Leakage depends on temperature, historically exponential but now approximately linear due to lower threshold voltages. Total power is dynamic plus leakage. Temperature modeling is noted as complex, requiring thermodynamics and heat transfer background.

nodes.title: Modeling Temperature*
nodes.summary: The text derives leakage power (Pleak) in Equation 10.22, defines its variables (A, thermal voltage νT, k, q, T, VGS, Vth, Voff, n, VDS) in Table 10.3, and simplifies to Equation 10.23 showing temperature dependence. It contrasts historical exponential versus modern linear leakage-temperature relationships, notes cumulative leakage across billions of transistors, and gives total power (Ptot = Pdyn + Pleak, Equation 10.24). Chip temperature modeling is described via a grid, thermal resistance matrix A, and linear equation T - Tamb = A × Ptot (Equation 10.25), forming a feedback loop with leakage. The ED2 metric is introduced to compare designs by normalizing performance or energy using dynamic voltage-frequency scaling (DVFS), where frequency and voltage scale together.

nodes.title: The ED2 Metric
nodes.summary: The text covers silicon die thermal modeling using a grid, power vector, temperature vector, ambient temperature, and thermal resistance matrix, with a linear equation relating power and temperature, noting a feedback loop with leakage power. It introduces the ED2 metric to compare processor designs by integrating performance and energy, using DVFS to equalize delay or energy, and deriving ED2 as a voltage- and frequency-independent design constant. Finally, it outlines advanced processor techniques, including branch prediction, speculative execution, and the need to cancel mispredicted instructions, with a waypoint summary of prior processor design concepts.

The section covers power and temperature issues in processors, including performance constraints from compiler, architecture, and technology. It details power dissipation mechanisms: dynamic power from charging/discharging capacitances (CV², related to activity factor, frequency, and supply voltage squared) and leakage power (20-40% of total power, from sub-threshold and gate-induced drain leakage). Temperature effects include reliability reduction, aging (NBTI), and temperature-dependent leakage. Chip packaging with heat spreaders, TIM, heat sinks, and fans is discussed. Leakage power modeling via BSIM3 and simplified equations, thermal modeling using a grid and thermal resistance matrix (T - Tamb = A × Ptot), and the feedback loop with leakage are presented. The ED2 metric for design comparison using DVFS is introduced, along with advanced techniques like branch prediction and speculative execution.

nodes.title: III Organization: System Design (intro)
nodes.summary: The text discusses refining the memory system abstraction beyond a simple byte array, noting that the 1-cycle access assumption for data and instruction memory is often unrealistic. It introduces caches and hierarchical memory to balance large capacity with low latency. It also covers multitasking, where processors switch between programs (e.g., every few milliseconds) without user perception due to human perceptual limits, and mentions the operating system's role (e.g., Windows, Linux) in managing this, requiring special memory support.

nodes.title: The Memory System
The Memory System (intro)
nodes.summary: The text introduces the need to refine the simple memory abstraction for faster systems. It discusses moving from a single-cycle memory assumption to a hierarchical system with caches to balance large capacity and low latency. It also covers supporting multiple time-shared programs, requiring operating system and memory support to prevent overwriting. Additionally, it addresses finite memory and introduces virtual memory for large programs. The overview details the tradeoffs between latches, SRAM, CAM, and DRAM cells in terms of area, latency, and power, highlighting the need for a fast, flexible memory system.

nodes.title: Overview
Need for a Fast Memory System
nodes.summary: The text argues for virtual memory to support multiple programs and large memory-intensive applications, requiring a fast, flexible memory system. It examines tradeoffs among latches, SRAM, CAM, and DRAM cells in speed, area, power, and capacity, showing latches are fastest but largest, DRAM smallest but slowest. On-chip memory is limited, off-chip is slow, and all-DRAM would cause unacceptable CPI increases. It then introduces memory access patterns, using an analogy of organizing books by access frequency, to motivate exploiting locality for both high capacity and low latency.

nodes.title: Memory Access Patterns
nodes.summary: The text addresses on-chip memory limits and the latency-storage tradeoff, noting that DRAM has high latency (100 cycles, increasing CPI by 34X) while SRAM has lower capacity. It then uses an analogy of organizing books to introduce temporal locality (reusing the same item frequently) and spatial locality (accessing similar items soon after). Examples include books, TV channels, and retail store layouts. The text defines both locality concepts and raises the question of whether memory accesses exhibit these patterns, proposing to measure locality in programs like SPEC benchmarks to potentially resolve the memory capacity and latency conflict.

nodes.title: Temporal and Spatial Locality of Instruction Accesses
nodes.summary: The text uses book and TV analogies to explain temporal and spatial locality: reusing the same items and accessing similar items. It defines both concepts, then applies them to instruction and data memory accesses, noting that instructions show strong locality due to loops, common code, and nearby branches. It mentions SPEC benchmarks and the 90/10 rule. Finally, it describes the stack distance method for characterizing temporal locality, including stack operations, bounded stack depth, and handling of new or evicted entries.

nodes.title: Characterizing Temporal Locality
nodes.summary: The text distinguishes instruction and data memory accesses, asserting instruction accesses show strong temporal and spatial locality due to loops, common code, and short branch targets. It introduces stack distance to measure temporal locality, describing its method, bounded stack handling, and a SPEC2006 Perlbench experiment showing skewed distribution with a heavy tail. Address distance is defined to quantify spatial locality, with K=10 as a suitable window, and a similar experiment showing most accesses within ±25. Both distributions indicate high locality, and methods for utilizing these localities are referenced.

nodes.title: Characterizing Spatial Locality
nodes.summary: The text discusses approximating stack distance with a log-normal distribution. It defines address distance as the difference between a memory access's address and the closest address among the last K accesses, used to quantify spatial locality. It explains that small average address distance indicates high spatial locality, and recommends K=10. An experiment on SPEC2006 Perlbench profiles address distance for 1 million accesses, showing that over a quarter fall between -5 and +5, over two-thirds between -25 and +25, tapering beyond ±50, with a heavy-tailed distribution. It concludes by noting similar experiments across thousands of programs.

nodes.title: Utilizing Spatial and Temporal Locality
nodes.summary: The text discusses approximating stack distance with a log-normal distribution, then defines address distance to characterize spatial locality as the difference between a memory access and the closest of the last K accesses, noting K=10 as effective and that small average address distance indicates high spatial locality. An experiment with SPEC2006 Perlbench shows most address distances are small but with heavy tails. It argues that temporal and spatial locality are common in real programs and should be assumed for performance design. Finally, it introduces hierarchical memory systems (cache, shelf, cabinet analogy) to exploit temporal locality.

nodes.title: Exploiting Temporal Locality – Hierarchical Memory System
nodes.summary: This text discusses temporal and spatial locality in programs, noting most exhibit high locality though exceptions exist. It introduces hierarchical memory systems (L1, L2, L3 caches, main memory) with inclusive/exclusive cache definitions, access protocols, and hit/miss concepts. It explains performance benefits via an example showing 33.3x speedup over flat memory, and begins spatial locality discussion referencing an address distance distribution.

nodes.title: Exploiting Spatial Locality – Cache Blocks
nodes.summary: The text covers average memory access latency calculations for hierarchical versus flat memory configurations, showing a 33.3x speedup, and discusses how hit rates, latencies, stack distance, cache policies, and technology affect performance. It explains exploiting spatial locality through cache blocks/lines, their definition, typical sizes, power-of-2 requirement, and differing L1/L2 block sizes. It summarizes temporal/spatial locality principles and hierarchical memory design. Finally, it introduces cache basics: black-box operation for loads/stores, SRAM-based implementation, block addressing, and basic operations like lookup, data read, and data write.

nodes.title: Caches

nodes.summary: This text discusses cache design fundamentals. It presents a cache as a black box with load/store inputs and hit/miss outputs. Using a 32-bit machine with 64-byte blocks and an 8 KB L1 cache as an example, it outlines basic cache operations: lookup, data read, data write, insert, replace, evict, and fill. It then explains cache implementation using separate tag and data SRAM arrays, and introduces fully associative (content addressable) caches where blocks can be placed in any entry, with entries containing tag (block address) and data fields.

nodes.title: Cache Lookup and Cache Design
11.2.2 Cache Lookup and Cache Design
nodes.summary: The text explains cache misses, fill operations involving load requests, insertion, eviction, and replacement, summarizing basic cache operations: lookup, data read, data write, insert, replace, evict. It describes designing an 8 KB cache with 64-byte blocks for a 32-bit system, splitting into tag and data SRAM arrays with a cache controller. It introduces fully associative (content addressable) caches, where any block can map to any entry, requiring tag (26-bit block address) and data (64 bytes) fields.

nodes.title: Fully Associative(FA) Cache
nodes.summary: The text explains cache miss handling, defining the fill operation as fetching a block from lower memory and inserting it into cache via atomic sub-operations: load request, insertion, space check, insert, replace, and evict. It summarizes basic cache operations: lookup, data read, data write, insert, replace, and evict, noting fill is a sequence of lookup, insert, and replace, and read is lookup or lookup plus fill. It then details cache design for an 8 KB cache with 64-byte blocks in a 32-bit system, splitting cache into tag and data SRAM arrays with a cache controller. It describes fully associative caches using CAM arrays for parallel tag comparison and encoding, noting scalability limits. Finally, it introduces direct mapped caches, which assign each block a fixed location via modulo operation on the block address.

nodes.title: Direct Mapped(DM) Cache
nodes.summary: The text covers fully associative, direct mapped, and set associative caches. It explains tag array implementation using SRAM or CAM, including comparators, encoders, and hit/miss detection. Fully associative caches are flexible but costly; direct mapped caches use index bits for a single location, optimizing tag storage. Set associative caches combine both, with sets and ways, balancing power, latency, and hit rate. Address division into tag, index, and offset is described, along with tradeoffs among the cache types.

nodes.title: Set Associative Cache
nodes.summary: The text explains cache designs: direct mapped (one entry per block, lower hit rate, efficient), fully associative (search all entries, high power, higher hit rate), and set associative (compromise). Set associative groups entries into sets, with associativity (ways per set). It covers address division into tag, set index, and ignored bits, tag size calculation, and implementation using parallel tag comparisons. It discusses the impact of index/ignored bit ordering (NON-CONT vs CONT) on conflict avoidance. Finally, it details data read and write operations, including write-through vs. write-back schemes and the modified bit.

nodes.title: Cache Data Read and Write Operations
key_items: 11.2.3 Data read and data write Operations
nodes.summary: This page details cache data read and write operations. It explains that data reads begin after a cache hit, fetching the block from the data array and using multiplexers to select bytes, with possible overlap between tag and data array reads. For writes, the entire block must be present in the cache to maintain atomicity and avoid extra state. Writing updates the data array using word and bit lines, with circuits based on demultiplexers. Two write methods are compared: write-through, which updates lower-level caches immediately for simplicity but increases traffic, and write-back, which uses a modified bit to track changes and delays updates until eviction.

The section covers cache operations including lookup, read, write, insert, replace, evict, and fill. It explains fully associative (CAM-based, parallel tag comparison, high flexibility but costly), direct mapped (fixed location via modulo, efficient tag storage), and set associative (compromise with sets and ways) caches. Address division into tag, index, and offset is described, along with tradeoffs. Data read/write operations are detailed, including byte selection and write-through vs. write-back schemes with modified bits.

nodes.title: Data read and data write Operations
nodes.summary: The text covers cache data read and write operations, and the insert operation. For reads, it explains starting after a hit or miss, reading the data array, selecting bytes with multiplexers, and overlapping lookup and data reads. For writes, it stresses the block must be present, describes writing via word/bit lines and demultiplexers, and contrasts write-through (simpler, more traffic) and write-back (modified bit, cheap writes, complex evictions). The insert operation involves finding an empty entry via valid bits, or invoking replace/evict, with valid and modified bits stored in the tag array.

nodes.title: The insert Operation
nodes.summary: The text covers cache replacement and insertion protocols. It discusses write-back vs. write-through tradeoffs, and the use of a modified bit in the tag array. It details the insert operation: checking valid bits for empty entries, using a valid bit to indicate empty/non-empty status, and invoking replace/evict if no empty entry exists. It then defines replacement policies as methods to choose an entry to evict. Two policies are described: random replacement (simple but suboptimal) and FIFO replacement (using a counter to track oldest block, with implementation details and drawbacks regarding temporal locality).

nodes.title: The replace Operation
nodes.summary: The text covers cache replacement and eviction operations. It defines replacement schemes, then details random, FIFO, and LRU policies, including implementation challenges. It introduces pseudo-LRU with small counters, explaining periodic decrementing and replacement candidate selection. The evict operation is described for write-through and write-back caches, noting modified bit handling. Finally, it summarizes the cache read operation, including lookup, hit/miss handling, data extraction, and block insertion with replacement when necessary.

nodes.title: The evict Operation
nodes.summary: The text explains replacement policies using least recently used blocks with counters, noting low overhead and parallel updates. It details the evict operation: write-through simply discards, while write-back checks the modified bit to write back if needed. It then describes the cache read process: lookup overlapping data read, hit returns value, miss cancels read and requests the lower cache block, extracts data, and invokes insertion, replacing an invalid entry or, if all ways are valid, selecting a replacement candidate.

nodes.title: Putting all the Pieces Together
nodes.summary: The text explains cache replacement using counters to track least recently used blocks, setting new blocks to high counters. It covers eviction: discard for write-through, write-back for modified write-back caches. It details read operation steps: lookup, hit returns data, miss fetches block from lower cache, then insert, replace if full, evict, and insert. It details write operations for write-back (hit writes and sets modified bit; miss writes to buffer then insert) and write-through (always writes to lower cache). It introduces the memory system hierarchy with i-cache, d-cache, L2, and main memory, noting L1 accesses take 1-2 cycles on hit.

nodes.title: Mathematical Model of the Memory System

It classifies cache misses into compulsory, capacity, and conflict (the three Cs) and discusses the working set. nodes.title: Cache Misses
nodes.summary: The text examines cache performance via Equation 11.1, focusing on reducing miss rate, miss penalty, and hit time. It classifies cache misses into compulsory, capacity, and conflict, defining working set. Reduction strategies include larger blocks, hardware prefetchers, bigger caches, higher associativity, victim caches, and cache-friendly code. Two rules of thumb are presented: Square Root Rule and Associativity Rule. Finally, it discusses reducing hit time with small caches and miss penalty using write buffers for write misses.

nodes.title: Reduction of Hit Time and Miss Penalty

It then covers reducing hit time via small, simple caches (increasing miss rate) and reducing miss penalty using write buffers for write misses and critical word first with early restart for read misses. Finally, it summarizes memory system optimizations, noting trade-offs between performance, power, area, and complexity.

nodes.title: Summary of Memory System Optimization Techniques

It includes a summary table of optimization techniques (large block size, prefetching, larger cache, associativity, victim cache, compiler techniques, small cache, write buffer, critical word first, early restart) with their benefits and disadvantages. It concludes that memory systems require careful design balancing performance with power, area, and complexity. It then introduces virtual memory, noting that multiple programs run simultaneously and data can exceed main memory size, and a small change to the memory system can address both requirements.

nodes.title: Process – A Running Instance of a Program
