nodes.title: The ``Overlap'' and ``Size'' Problems
nodes.summary: The text discusses two key problems in virtual memory: the overlap problem, where processes may corrupt each other's memory without isolation, and the size problem, where processes may need more memory than physical RAM, requiring disk storage. It then introduces address translation with paging as a solution, using a translator between virtual and physical addresses to satisfy programmer/compiler and processor/memory needs, illustrated by a Russian-Arabic translator analogy. Finally, it lists two virtual memory requirements: accessibility of any valid address (e.g., 3 GB in Linux) and the perception of contiguous memory.

nodes.title: Implementation of Virtual Memory with Paging
11.4.2 The “Overlap” and “Size” Problems
nodes.summary: The text discusses two key problems in virtual memory: the overlap problem, where concurrent processes may corrupt each other's memory without hardware-enforced isolation, and the size problem, where processes may need more memory than physical RAM, potentially using disk space. It then introduces virtual memory implementation via paging, describing an address translation system that converts virtual addresses to physical addresses, akin to a language translator. Finally, it lists requirements from programs and compilers: access to any valid virtual address (e.g., 3 GB in Linux) and perception of virtual memory as a single contiguous space.

nodes.title: 11.4.3 Implementation of Virtual Memory with Paging
nodes.summary: The text discusses virtual memory's overlap and size problems: preventing processes from corrupting each other's memory and allowing processes larger than physical memory via disk storage. It introduces address translation between virtual and physical addresses, comparing it to a language translator. Requirements from programs/compilers include accessible valid addresses, contiguous virtual space, and isolation; from the memory system: non-overlapping physical addresses, avoiding fragmentation, and additional storage for excess memory. A naive byte-level mapping satisfies requirements but is inefficient, large, slow, and ignores locality. Pages and frames are introduced as a more efficient solution.

nodes.title: Pages and Frames
nodes.summary: The text outlines memory system requirements: non-overlapping program addresses, avoiding large contiguous allocations to prevent fragmentation, and providing extra storage when physical memory is insufficient. It defines virtual and physical addresses and introduces translation systems. A basic byte-level mapping satisfies requirements but is inefficient due to large tables and lack of locality. It then introduces pages, frames, and page tables for block-level translation to reduce state and exploit spatial locality. Page tables can be hardware or software implemented, with hardware lookup logic. It describes 32-bit address splitting into page number and offset, and analyzes a single-level page table's size and memory overhead.

nodes.title: A Single Level Page Table
nodes.summary: The text defines pages and frames as equal-sized blocks in virtual and physical address spaces, and page tables as per-process mappings between them. It explains address translation: splitting a 32-bit address into a 20-bit page number and 12-bit offset for 4KB pages, then replacing the page number with a frame number. It describes single-level page tables (1M entries, 2.5MB per process) and their excessive memory waste. To reduce storage, it introduces two-level page tables, splitting the 20-bit page number into two 10-bit parts: a primary table pointing to secondary tables, only allocated when needed. This reduces storage to KBs per process, making it efficient for commercial systems.

nodes.title: Two-Level Page Table
nodes.summary: The text explains two-level page tables, splitting a 20-bit page number into two 10-bit parts: a primary page table indexing secondary page tables, each containing frame numbers. It calculates storage sizes, showing efficiency for typical programs due to spatial locality. It then describes inverted page tables, used by processors like Itanium, which map frame numbers to process IDs and page numbers, requiring hashing for lookups. Advantages include space savings; disadvantages include slow scans and hash collisions requiring verification.

nodes.title: Inverted Page Table
nodes.summary: The text explains inverted page tables, which address page tables by frame number, storing process ID and page number per entry. It highlights advantages like saving space with many processes and small memory, and challenges in lookup, solved via hashing and linear probing. It notes eviction and buffering of entries, and that commercial systems rarely use inverted tables due to overhead. It then describes the Translation Lookaside Buffer (TLB), a small fully associative cache storing page-to-frame mappings for fast virtual address translation, with high hit rates from locality. Finally, it introduces swap space for running programs larger than physical memory.

nodes.title: Inverted Page Tables, TLB, and Swap Space
nodes.summary: The page begins with inverted page table mechanics: using hash tables and linear probing to find page number/process ID pairs, with a search limit of K, eviction to main memory buffers, and the ability to disallow certain frame mappings, noting the overhead makes it impractical in commercial systems. It then covers the Translation Lookaside Buffer (TLB): a small fully associative cache of 32-64 entries indexed by page number, accessed in the EX stage, enabling physical address availability by the MA stage on a hit; on a miss, the pipeline stalls and the page table is accessed, with high hit rates due to temporal locality and working set size. Finally, it introduces swap space as the solution for running programs whose memory footprint exceeds physical memory.

This section covers virtual memory implementation with paging, addressing overlap and size problems. It explains address translation, requirements from programs and the memory system, and defines pages, frames, and page tables. It details single-level page tables, their inefficiency, and introduces two-level page tables for reduced storage. Inverted page tables and their trade-offs are described, followed by the Translation Lookaside Buffer (TLB) for fast address translation. Finally, swap space is introduced for running programs larger than physical memory.

nodes.title: Swap Space
nodes.summary: The text covers inverted page tables, including linear probing for matching page number and process ID pairs, eviction to swap space, hash table control, and their impracticality in commercial systems. It then explains the Translation Lookaside Buffer (TLB) as a small fully associative cache to reduce memory accesses, its operation in the pipeline, and high hit rate due to locality and coverage. Next, swap space is discussed as a solution for limited physical memory, detailing storage device characteristics, swap space types, and a valid bit in page table entries. Finally, the Memory Management Unit (MMU) is briefly introduced regarding page table management during process lifecycle and TLB misses.

nodes.title: Memory Management Unit (MMU)
nodes.summary: This text explains virtual memory using slower, larger storage devices like hard disks for swap space, augmenting page tables with bits to track frame locations and allowing multiple swap spaces. It details the MMU's role in page table access, TLB management, and handling page faults via frame allocation, eviction, and replacement policies. It includes an address translation process diagram and mentions advanced paging system features.

nodes.title: Advanced Features of the Paging System
nodes.summary: The text discusses page fault sensitivity to replacement policies like FIFO and LRU, referencing OS textbooks. It outlines address translation steps via a flowchart: TLB hit/miss, page table hit/miss, frame allocation, eviction, swap space, and TLB population. It covers advanced paging features: shared memory for inter-process communication by mapping pages to the same frame, protection by marking text pages read-only to prevent virus code modification, and segmentation in x86 systems using segment registers for text, data, and stack to handle address size and reserved memory issues. It concludes with a summary section.

Virtual memory is introduced to address overlap (memory corruption between processes) and size (programs larger than physical RAM) problems. It defines processes versus programs, the OS kernel, loader, and scheduling. Implementation via paging is detailed: pages, frames, single-level and two-level page tables, inverted page tables, and the Translation Lookaside Buffer (TLB). Swap space on disk supports larger programs, while the Memory Management Unit (MMU) handles address translation, page faults, and TLB misses. Advanced features include replacement policies (FIFO, LRU), shared memory, protection, and x86 segmentation.

nodes.title: Summary and Further Reading
Summary
nodes.summary: This text covers shared memory implementation via kernel mapping, protection by marking text pages read-only against viruses, and segmented memory using segment registers to layer on virtual memory for layout flexibility. It summarizes memory system design: SRAM/DRAM trade-offs, locality principles, cache hierarchies (L1, L2, L3, main memory), cache operations, mapping schemes, write and replacement policies, AMAT formula, miss types, and optimizations like prefetching and victim caches. Virtual memory topics include isolation, larger footprints, page tables, page faults, sharing, protection, segmentation, and further reading on advanced memory systems and phase change memory.

nodes.title: Further Reading
Further Reading (intro)
nodes.summary: The text covers average memory access time (AMAT) formula, three cache miss types, and optimization methods like prefetching and victim cache. It explains virtual memory's purposes: protection and larger footprints, and its implementation via page tables, page faults, and replacement algorithms, plus advanced features. Further reading lists key architecture and memory system textbooks and research on DRAM and phase change memory. Exercises include defining locality, verifying heavy-tailed distributions, address distance, exploiting locality, and cache simulation problems for fully associative LRU and FIFO, plus a two-level write-back cache example.

nodes.title: Cache Exercises on Locality and Replacement Policies
nodes.summary: The page includes exercises and an overview related to caches and the memory system. Exercises ask for definitions of temporal and spatial locality, experimental verification of log-normal distribution as heavy-tailed and its implications for stack distance and temporal locality, definition of address distance and why nearest match is in last K accesses, and how to exploit temporal and spatial locality in memory. Further exercises involve simulating fully associative caches with LRU or FIFO replacement for a given access sequence, and a two-level write-back cache with LRU for a sequence of reads and writes. An overview section also appears.

nodes.title: Caches and the Memory System
nodes.summary: The text comprises 18 exercises on computer architecture. It covers temporal and spatial locality, address distance, log-normal distributions, and cache design. Exercises involve simulating fully associative caches with LRU and FIFO, two-level write-back and write-through caches, and calculating cache size. It includes comparing sorting algorithms' cache performance, deriving tag and index bits, analyzing 2D array traversal misses, calculating IPC with miss rates, comparing cache designs, and recursive average memory access time. It also addresses experimentally determining cache parameters, and virtual memory page table calculations for single and two-level tables.

nodes.title: Virtual Memory
nodes.summary: The text covers cache performance exercises: comparing cache misses in traversals; calculating IPC with L1/L2 miss rates; analyzing designs with base CPI, local miss rates, hit times, and miss penalties; deriving average memory access time for n-level caches and as n→∞; and estimating cache size, block size, and associativity via timing programs with LRU. Virtual memory exercises include page table entries and sizes for single and two-level tables, indexing primary page tables, using paging for producer-consumer and fork, thread vs. fork memory addressing, copy-on-write optimization, inverted page tables, and CPI calculation with TLB and cache misses. Also covered are DLL loading/unloading via virtual memory and design problems: using CACTI to explore cache area/latency/power, and writing a cache simulator.

nodes.title: Design Problems
nodes.summary: The text presents two design problems: using CACTI to analyze cache area, latency, and power by varying read ports, associativity (4-way, 512 KB, 64B blocks), and size (256 KB to 4 MB); and writing a hierarchical cache simulator. It then introduces multiprocessor systems, noting processor performance limits: IPC gains under 50%, frequency capped near 3 GHz due to power/heat, with performance saturating from 2001-2010 per SPECint2006. Future improvement relies on transistor scaling rather than frequency increases.

This section provides further reading and exercises on memory systems and computer architecture. It covers average memory access time, cache miss types, optimization techniques like prefetching and victim cache, and virtual memory purposes and implementation via page tables, page faults, and replacement algorithms. Exercises address temporal and spatial locality, cache simulation with LRU and FIFO, two-level write-back caches, cache size derivation, sorting algorithm cache performance, IPC calculation, multi-level cache AMAT, and virtual memory page table calculations, including two-level tables, copy-on-write, and inverted page tables. Design problems involve using CACTI for cache analysis and writing a cache simulator, and the section introduces multiprocessor systems and future performance trends.

The section summarizes memory system design, covering shared memory via kernel mapping, read-only text page protection, segmented memory with segment registers, and virtual memory. It reviews SRAM/DRAM trade-offs, locality, cache hierarchies (L1/L2/L3), cache operations, mapping schemes, write/replacement policies, AMAT formula, miss types, and optimizations like prefetching and victim caches. Virtual memory topics include isolation, page tables, page faults, sharing, protection, and segmentation. Further reading and exercises cover AMAT, cache miss types, optimizations, virtual memory implementation, locality, cache simulation, multi-level caches, page tables, copy-on-write, inverted page tables, CACTI, cache simulators, multiprocessors, and future performance trends.

The section covers refining memory abstraction into a hierarchical system with caches to balance capacity and latency, supporting multiple programs and virtual memory. It details memory cell tradeoffs (latches, SRAM, CAM, DRAM), locality principles (temporal/spatial, stack/address distance), and cache design (associativity, operations, write/replacement policies). It presents a mathematical model for CPI and AMAT, miss classification, and optimizations (prefetching, victim caches, etc.). Virtual memory topics include paging, page tables, TLB, MMU, page faults, protection, segmentation, and shared memory. It concludes with a summary, further reading, and exercises.

nodes.title: Multiprocessor Systems
Multiprocessor Systems (intro)
nodes.summary: The text explains that single-processor performance is limited by power, temperature, and complexity, with frequencies plateauing around 3 GHz and IPC gains capped. It presents historical CPU frequency and Spec Int 2006 performance data from 2001–2010, showing saturation. The solution is multiprocessing: using multiple processors or cores per chip. It defines multiprocessing, multiprocessors, multicore processors, and cores. It traces multiprocessor history from the 1960s–70s, citing Burroughs 5000, IBM 370, PDP 11/74, VAX-11/782, and Univac 1108-II, and distinguishes symmetric (SMP) from asymmetric multiprocessors.

nodes.title: Background
Background (intro)
nodes.summary: Defines multiprocessing and multicore; traces multiprocessor evolution from 1960s mainframes (e.g., Burroughs 5000, IBM 370) to modern multicore chips; explains symmetric vs. asymmetric multiprocessing; notes motherboard integration and core count growth; discusses Moore's Law, transistor miniaturization, and historical transistor doubling trends.

nodes.title: Moore's Law
nodes.summary: The text covers asymmetric multiprocessing, where a master processor controls OS and I/O, assigns work to slaves, and traces hardware evolution from cables to multicore chips. It explains Moore's Law: transistor doubling every 1-2 years, shrinking feature sizes, and implications like power and temperature limits ending frequency scaling, leading to multicore processors with doubling cores, and many-core GPUs. It includes historical notes and a feature size table.

nodes.title: Implications of the Moore's Law
nodes.summary: The text covers Moore's Law, its history, and implications: transistor shrinkage, feature size reduction in Intel processors (2001-2011), power and temperature constraints ending clock frequency scaling, leading to multicore processors. It discusses future core counts, graphics processors, multithreaded processors, and references. Then it introduces multiprocessor software, defining loosely coupled (multicomputers, independent programs) and strongly coupled multiprocessing (shared memory, overlapping programs).

The Background section defines multiprocessing and multicore, tracing multiprocessor evolution from 1960s mainframes to modern multicore chips, and distinguishes symmetric and asymmetric multiprocessing. It details Moore's Law, including historical transistor doubling trends, feature size reduction in Intel processors (2001-2011), and the implications of power and temperature limits ending frequency scaling, which led to multicore processors, many-core GPUs, and future core counts. It also introduces multiprocessor software, defining loosely coupled (multicomputers, independent programs) and strongly coupled (shared memory, overlapping programs) multiprocessing.

nodes.title: Software for Multiprocessor Systems
Strong and Loosely Coupled Multiprocessing
nodes.summary: The text introduces multiprocessor design, including multithreaded processors and broad trends, while noting advanced architecture references. It contrasts loosely coupled multiprocessing, where unrelated programs run in parallel like a multicomputer cluster, with strongly coupled multiprocessing, where programs share memory, data, code, files, and network connections. The chapter's focus is on strongly coupled systems. It then explains shared memory versus message passing paradigms using a factory analogy, describing shared memory as immediate visibility of changes and message passing as explicit communication. Shared memory suits strongly coupled multiprocessors; the chapter will cover software requirements before hardware for multicore, multithreaded, and vector processors.

nodes.title: Shared Memory vs Message Passing
Shared Memory vs Message Passing (intro)
nodes.summary: The text defines loosely and strongly coupled multiprocessing, noting the book's focus on strongly coupled systems. It contrasts shared memory and message passing programming paradigms via a factory worker analogy, explaining shared memory suits strongly coupled multiprocessors while message passing suits loosely coupled ones, with distributed shared memory as a hybrid. An OpenMP example demonstrates parallel summation using shared memory, highlighting code structure with parallel and sequential sections.

nodes.title: Shared Memory
nodes.summary: The text contrasts shared memory and message passing paradigms. It presents a shared memory OpenMP example adding numbers in parallel, detailing thread creation via #pragma omp parallel, thread IDs, partial sums, and sequential aggregation. It defines threads as sub-programs sharing address space with private stacks, describes parent-child thread spawning, joining, and synchronization. It notes implementing shared memory on loosely coupled systems as distributed shared memory. Finally, it introduces message passing, defining a process as a running program instance that does not share address space.

nodes.title: Message Passing
nodes.summary: This text covers parallel programming concepts: a figure showing sequential initialization, spawning child threads, parallel execution, and joining; message passing with processes not sharing address space; definitions of process and send/receive functions (including ANYSOURCE); an MPI-like parallel sum example using partial sums and reduction; and Amdahl's Law deriving speedup from sequential fraction f_seq and P processors via equations for parallel time and speedup.

nodes.title: Amdahl’s Law
nodes.summary: The text begins with parallel code for summing partial results: non-root processes send their partial sum to the root, while the root aggregates all received sums, shuts down processes, and returns the total. It then introduces Amdahl's Law, explaining that programs consist of sequential and parallel parts. The sequential part includes initialization and reduction (aggregating results), while the parallel part is divided among processors. It derives equations for parallel execution time and speedup S = 1 / (f_seq + (1 - f_seq)/P), where f_seq is the sequential fraction and P is the number of processors.

This section contrasts shared memory and message passing paradigms. It defines loosely and strongly coupled multiprocessing, using a factory worker analogy. Shared memory, suitable for strongly coupled systems, is illustrated with OpenMP examples for parallel summation, detailing thread creation, IDs, partial sums, and synchronization. Message passing, for loosely coupled systems, is explained through processes not sharing address space, with send/receive functions and an MPI-like parallel sum example. Distributed shared memory is noted as a hybrid. Finally, Amdahl's Law is introduced, deriving speedup from sequential fraction and processor count.

nodes.title: Amdahl's Law
nodes.summary: The text presents parallel reduction code, derives Amdahl's Law (Tpar = Tseq × (fseq + (1 - fseq)/P) and speedup S = 1/(fseq + (1 - fseq)/P)), and notes speedup saturates at 1/fseq with diminishing returns. It discusses reducing sequential sections algorithmically and via fast processors. Flynn's 1966 classification is detailed: SISD (uniprocessor), SIMD (single instruction multiple data, e.g., SSE/GPUs), MISD (multiple instruction single data, rare, for fault-tolerant voting like aircraft), and MIMD (multiple instruction multiple data, dominant, including SPMD and MPMD types).

The section covers multiprocessor design, contrasting loosely coupled systems (like clusters running unrelated programs) with strongly coupled systems that share memory, data, code, files, and network connections. It explains shared memory versus message passing paradigms using a factory analogy, illustrating OpenMP for shared memory and MPI-like message passing, and noting distributed shared memory as a hybrid. Amdahl's Law is derived, showing speedup saturation and diminishing returns. Flynn's classification (SISD, SIMD, MISD, MIMD) is detailed, emphasizing MIMD's dominance with SPMD and MPMD types. The focus is on strongly coupled systems, covering software requirements before hardware for multicore, multithreaded, and vector processors.

nodes.title: Design Space of Multiprocessors
nodes.summary: The text covers Flynn's 1966 classification of multiprocessors: SISD (standard uniprocessor), SIMD (single instruction, multiple data, with examples like x86 SSE, GPUs, and vector processors), MISD (multiple instruction, single data, rare and used for high-reliability systems like aircraft with voting), and MIMD (multiple instruction, multiple data, prevalent in multicores and servers). It details MIMD subcategories SPMD (single program, multiple data, common in parallel programs) and MPMD (multiple program, multiple data, for heterogeneous systems). It transitions to discussing MIMD multiprocessors, focusing on shared-memory systems, distinguishing logical (software) and physical (hardware) perspectives, and begins describing the logical view where each processor connects to shared memory with its own program counter.

nodes.title: MIMD Multiprocessors
Logical Point of View
nodes.summary: The text discusses SPMD and MPMD paradigms, noting SPMD's advantage of running the same program on all processors versus MPMD's different programs for heterogeneous units. It focuses on SIMD and MIMD systems, excluding MISD. It details MIMD multiprocessors, distinguishing logical (software interface) and physical (hardware design) perspectives. The logical view covers shared memory, thread stacks, and data sharing challenges. Coherence is introduced, explaining how private caches must act as one, the need to update replicas on writes, and propagation delays affecting shared variable access, illustrated with examples.

nodes.title: Coherence
nodes.summary: The text covers memory coherence and consistency in multiprocessors. It defines coherence as handling multiple threads accessing the same memory location, noting complexities from caches and buffers. It provides examples of possible and disallowed outcomes, formalizes coherence with completion and order axioms, and explains they ensure writes complete and are seen in the same order by all threads. Then it introduces memory consistency for accesses to different locations, with an example showing possible outcomes (0,0), (0,1), (1,1) and questioning (1,0).

nodes.title: Memory Consistency
nodes.summary: The text covers memory consistency models in multiprocessors: the order axiom and coherence, program order, and sequential consistency (SC) requiring interleaving in program order. It introduces weak consistency (WC) allowing reordering, explains atomicity, completion, and issues with weak models. Examples show parallel summation using SC and WC with fences. It also discusses shared vs. private caches, and outlines physical memory design, noting SC's rarity and WC's prevalence in modern processors.

nodes.title: Physical View of Memory
nodes.summary: This text outlines multiprocessor memory system design, focusing on physical implementation. It compares shared caches (single, simple, but unscalable due to port and size constraints) with private caches (fast, low-power, but require cache coherence to appear unified). It introduces coherence and consistency, details cache banking to split large last-level caches for bandwidth, and overviews snoopy protocols for coherent private caches. It includes trade-off tables, design examples, and references to advanced topics like consistency models and interconnection networks.

nodes.title: Shared Caches
nodes.summary: The text covers shared caches in multiprocessors, explaining the drawbacks of a single cache (bandwidth, area, power, speed) and the need to split large last-level caches (LLC) into multiple cache banks. It details cache bank organization, addressing (bank address, offset, set index, tag), and benefits: reduced contention and improved power and speed. It then introduces coherent private caches and snoopy protocols, aiming to make private caches behave as a single shared cache, using an interconnection network, with software transparency.

nodes.title: Coherent Private Caches
Shared Cache Banking and Coherent Private Caches
nodes.summary: Section 12.4.5 explains that implementing a shared cache as a regular uniprocessor cache is inefficient due to multiple thread accesses causing bandwidth issues, larger area/power, and slow tag arrays. It defines last level cache (LLC) and proposes splitting a multi-megabyte LLC into multiple subcaches called cache banks (e.g., 4 MB into 8-16 banks), describing bank addressing and advantages: reduced contention and improved speed and power efficiency. Section 12.4.6 introduces coherent private caches and snoopy protocols, aiming to make private caches appear as one shared cache via an interconnection network, with a conceptual diagram and reference to Section 12.6 for network design.

nodes.title: Overview of a Snoopy Protocol
nodes.summary: The text discusses shared caches and coherent private caches in multiprocessors. It explains splitting a large last-level cache (LLC) into multiple cache banks to reduce contention and improve speed and power efficiency, detailing bank addressing. Then it covers snoopy protocols for cache coherence on a shared bus, including the completion and order axioms. It introduces write-update protocol design, where writes are broadcast, reads check sister caches, and describes the M, S, I states with an FSM for processor-generated events.

nodes.title: Write-Update Protocol
nodes.summary: The text describes the write-update protocol, where caches broadcast writes for consistency. It details read handling via cache checks, sister cache queries, or lower-level fetches. The protocol uses M, S, and I states, with a finite state machine diagram (Figure 12.11) showing transitions for processor events, including read/write hits and misses. State-specific actions for eviction and modification are explained. It introduces the bus arbiter (Figure 12.12) managing FIFO bus requests and describes sister cache responses to misses and writes. Finally, it contrasts the directory protocol, which sends messages only to sharers using a directory structure.

nodes.title: Directory Protocol
nodes.summary: This text covers cache coherence protocols: states I, S, M with transitions for read/write hits and misses, eviction, and broadcast requirements; bus arbiter with FIFO queue; snoopy protocol details; directory protocol maintaining sharer bit vectors to reduce messages; and definitions of snoopy vs. directory protocols. It explains why writes must wait for bus broadcast to maintain order, and introduces the write-invalidate protocol as a message-reduction optimization.

nodes.title: Write-Invalidate Protocol
nodes.summary: The text discusses cache coherence protocols: directory-based write-update, including maintaining sharer bit vectors, message forwarding, ordering, and scalability; why writes must wait for a bus broadcast to preserve order; and the write-invalidate protocol with snoopy and directory implementations. It details three block states (M, S, I), state transition diagrams for processor actions and bus messages, and message types (read miss, write miss, write). It explains the M state's exclusivity, read/write hits without messages, eviction write-backs, and directory operation for write-invalidate.

nodes.title: Write-Invalidate Protocol with a Directory
nodes.summary: The text explains cache coherence protocols, focusing on state transitions due to bus messages from S and M states, including read/write misses and evictions. It describes the write-invalidate protocol with a directory, detailing directory entry lifecycle and sharer management. It introduces the exclusive (E) state for optimization, noting E to M transition and eviction. Finally, it discusses implementing sequential consistency, covering write completion, concurrent read/write behavior, and a design where cores issue memory requests in program order using coherent memory, with an access graph for proof.

nodes.title: Implementing Sequential Consistency and Cache Coherence Protocols
key_items: Overview of an Implementation of Sequential Consistency*
nodes.summary: The page covers cache coherence protocols: write-invalidate/update, adding an exclusive state (E) where a block is read-only and exclusively owned, enabling seamless E-to-M transitions and eviction. It then addresses implementing memory consistency models, focusing on sequential consistency. A simple implementation is outlined: a coherent memory system where writes complete atomically, reads return the latest completed write, and concurrent read/write behavior is undefined but must be consistently observed. Cores issue memory requests in program order, waiting for completion before the next. This system is claimed to be sequentially consistent, with a proof planned using an access graph.

The section covers coherent private caches, beginning with shared cache banking to address bandwidth, area, and power issues by splitting the LLC into banks. It introduces snoopy protocols for cache coherence on a shared bus, detailing write-update and write-invalidate protocols. The write-update protocol broadcasts writes, uses M, S, I states, and involves a bus arbiter. Directory protocols reduce messages using sharer bit vectors, with write-invalidate optimizing further. The write-invalidate protocol with a directory manages state transitions and introduces an exclusive state. Finally, it discusses implementing sequential consistency, where cores issue requests in program order, ensuring a coherent memory system with a proof via access graph.

nodes.title: Implementing a Memory Consistency Model*
Overview of an Implementation of Sequential Consistency*
nodes.summary: The text covers cache coherence protocols, focusing on write-invalidate and update protocols, directory actions on writes and evictions, and the exclusive state for read-only ownership, enabling E to M transitions without bus messages. It then discusses implementing memory consistency, specifically sequential consistency, with a coherent memory system where writes complete instantaneously and reads return the latest completed write. Concurrent read/write behavior is addressed. The text introduces the access graph as a tool for reasoning about concurrent systems, defining nodes for memory accesses, edges for program order and read-write dependencies, and the happens-before relationship for completion ordering.

nodes.title: Access Graph*
nodes.summary: This text explains access graphs as a tool for reasoning about concurrent systems. It describes representing memory accesses as nodes, with four edge types: program-order, store-to-load (causality), and coherence edges (load-to-store, store-to-store). The happens-before relationship is defined via paths in the graph. The text explains using access graphs to determine adherence to memory models like sequential or weak consistency, with acyclic graphs indicating consistency. It outlines a proof that acyclic access graphs imply sequential consistency, involving topological sorting and completion times. Finally, it sketches a proof of sequential consistency for systems that wait for memory requests to complete.

nodes.title: Proof of Sequential Consistency*
nodes.summary: The text explains that an acyclic access graph implies consistency with a memory model, detailing a proof technique using induction and completion times. It proves sequential consistency (SC) by contradiction for a system that waits for memory requests, then describes an impractical SC machine using a shared L1 cache and in-order pipeline, noting scalability issues due to port requirements.

nodes.title: Design of a Simple (yet impractical) Sequentially Consistent Machine*
nodes.summary: The text proves sequential consistency (SC) by contradiction using an access graph, introduces an oracle for ordering, and describes a simple but impractical SC multiprocessor with a shared L1 cache, noting scalability issues. It then outlines implementing weak consistency via fences and pipeline stalls, summarizes memory consistency implementation challenges, and introduces multithreaded processors as an alternative design.

nodes.title: Memory Consistency Implementation and Multithreaded Processors
key_items: Summary of the Discussion on Implementing a Memory Consistency Model
nodes.summary: The text first argues that proving sequential consistency in complex multiprocessor systems is difficult, leading designers to use weak memory models where fence instructions must be verified. It then details implementing weak consistency via an access graph without same-thread program-order edges, using causality and coherence edges, and avoiding cycles by stalling fence instructions until prior instructions complete. A summary notes that implementing consistency models requires pipeline modifications and memory acknowledgements, with many subtle corner cases. Finally, it introduces multithreaded processors, which run multiple threads on a single pipeline instead of separate pipelines.

This section covers implementing a memory consistency model, focusing on sequential consistency (SC). It details cache coherence protocols and then introduces access graphs for reasoning about concurrent systems, defining nodes, edges (program-order, store-to-load, coherence), and happens-before. It presents proofs that acyclic access graphs imply SC, including a proof by contradiction for systems waiting for memory requests. It describes a simple but impractical SC machine with a shared L1 cache, noting scalability issues. It then outlines implementing weak consistency using fences and pipeline stalls, summarizes implementation challenges, and introduces multithreaded processors as an alternative design.

nodes.title: Multithreaded Processors
nodes.summary: The text discusses implementing weak consistency via access graphs without cycles, using fence instructions stalled in the MA stage until prior instructions complete. It summarizes that modifying pipelines and memory acknowledgements enables consistency models. Then, it introduces multithreaded processors, including coarse-grained multithreading (round-robin thread switching with saved contexts), fine-grained multithreading (switching every 1-2 cycles), and simultaneous multithreading (SMT) that dynamically partitions issue slots among threads for higher IPC. It distinguishes software vs. hardware threads, notes implementation complexities, and mentions SMT examples like Intel hyperthreading. Finally, it briefly introduces SIMD multiprocessors for scientific and graphics applications.

The section on MIMD multiprocessors covers logical and physical perspectives. It discusses SPMD and MPMD paradigms, then details shared memory, thread stacks, and data sharing challenges. nodes.title: SIMD Multiprocessors
SIMD Multiprocessors (intro)
nodes.summary: The text explains simultaneous multithreading (SMT), which dynamically partitions issue slots among threads to improve IPC, comparing it with coarse- and fine-grained multithreading and noting challenges like instruction selection, memory bandwidth, and fetch complexity. It mentions Intel's hyperthreading and IBM's Power 7. Then it introduces SIMD multiprocessors, covering their use in scientific and graphics applications, historical systolic arrays, vector processors, and modern SIMD functional units, with a background on array addition and superscalar limitations.

nodes.title: SIMD – Vector Processors
nodes.summary: The text outlines multithreading types (simultaneous, fine-grained, coarse-grained) via Figure 12.18, then discusses SIMD processors' history from systolic arrays to modern use in supercomputers and gaming. It explains vector processors, including their definition, array addition example, scalability limits of superscalar, and iconic Cray 1. It notes late-90s adoption in PCs and supercomputers, Intel MMX/SSE, AMD 3DNow!, ARM Neon. Finally, it covers the software interface, specifically vector registers like x86 SSE's XMM0-15 and their data packing.

nodes.title: Software Interface
nodes.summary: The text explains why wide-issue scalar processors are not scalable, leading to vector processors that operate on arrays. It defines vector processors and instructions, citing Cray 1 and scientific uses, and later adoption for gaming and commodity supercomputers. It details vector ISAs like MMX, SSE, 3DNow!, and Neon. The software interface covers vector registers, contiguous and scatter-gather load/store instructions, arithmetic operations, data lanes, and scalar-vector transfers. A practical SSE example using gcc intrinsics for array addition is also discussed.

nodes.title: A Practical Example using SSE Instructions
nodes.summary: This text covers vector instruction set architecture concepts: an example of vector addition; the definition of data lanes in vector instructions; vector operations like multiplication, division, and logical operations; scalar-vector operations; storing vector registers contiguously or non-contiguously; and transferring data between scalar and vector registers. It then presents a practical SSE example using gcc intrinsics to add two floating point arrays, with C code, explaining strip mining and performance gains compared to scalar code. Finally, it introduces predicated instructions for conditional execution in vector processors, with an example of applying a conditional increment.

nodes.title: Predicated Instructions
nodes.summary: The text covers vector instruction usage, including loading floating point values into 128-bit registers, vector addition with SSE intrinsics, and pointer updates, with performance comparison against scalar code. It introduces predicated instructions for conditional vector operations, defining v.cmp and predicated vector add with conditions like lt, gt, and eq. It discusses vector processor design, including pipeline stages, cache interactions, and forwarding logic. nodes.title: Design of a Vector Processor
nodes.summary: The text explains predicated vector instructions, showing how v.cmp and v.lt.add implement conditional element-wise addition. nodes.title: Interconnection Networks
Overview
nodes.summary: The text discusses predicated vector instructions, design of vector processors including pipeline stages and cache integration, and interconnection networks. nodes.title: Bisection Bandwidth and Network Diameter
nodes.summary: The text covers network-on-chip (NOC) properties and topologies in multicore processors. It defines bisection bandwidth as the minimum link failures needed to split a network into two equal parts, serving as a reliability and bandwidth measure. Network diameter is defined as the longest shortest path between node pairs, indicating worst-case latency. It then reviews topologies: chain (bisection bandwidth 1, diameter N-1), ring (bisection bandwidth 2, diameter N/2), and introduces fat trees used in cluster computers.

nodes.title: Network Topologies
Chain and Ring
nodes.summary: The text defines bisection bandwidth as the minimum link failures to split a network into two equal parts. It then discusses network diameter as the longest shortest path between any node pair, representing worst-case latency. It introduces network topologies, assuming N nodes and N divisible by 2 for analysis. It compares chain topologies (bisection bandwidth 1, diameter N-1) and ring topologies (bisection bandwidth 2, diameter N/2). It defines a cluster computer as loosely coupled processors on a LAN and introduces the fat tree topology used in clusters.

nodes.title: Fat Tree
nodes.summary: The text defines cluster computers as loosely coupled processors on a LAN and details fat tree topology, where internal nodes are routers, messages route via common ancestors, link density increases toward the root to reduce congestion, with network diameter 2log(N) and bisection bandwidth N/2, though practical designs use fewer links. It also introduces mesh and torus topologies for multicores, noting corner nodes have two neighbors and rim nodes three.

nodes.title: Mesh and Torus
nodes.summary: The text explains fat tree topology, where internal router switches connect leaf nodes, with link density increasing toward the root to reduce congestion; it covers diameter (2log N) and bisection bandwidth (N/2), noting practical link reduction. It then details mesh topology: nodes in a matrix, diameter 2√N - 2, bisection bandwidth √N, and asymmetry. Torus adds cross links, giving diameter √N and bisection bandwidth 2√N. Folded torus avoids long cross links while maintaining diameter and bisection bandwidth, preferred for multicores. Hypercube is introduced with figures.

nodes.title: Hypercube
nodes.summary: The text explains network diameter assumptions and the need for revised definitions with long links, proposing folded torus to avoid long cross links while maintaining bandwidth and diameter. It introduces hypercubes: their recursive construction, node labeling, routing, log(N) diameter, bisection bandwidth N/2, and O(log(N)) diameter, though unsuitable for multicores. Finally, it mentions the butterfly network with O(log(N)) diameter as suitable for multicores.

nodes.title: Butterfly
nodes.summary: The text discusses hypercube and butterfly network topologies. It explains hypercube construction recursively, labeling, properties like node count 2^k, diameter log(N), and bisection bandwidth N/2. For the butterfly network, it describes the structure with columns of switches, routing based on matching bits, and properties such as additional switches Nlog(N)/2, diameter log(N), and bisection bandwidth N/2. It ends with a comparison of topologies based on internal nodes, links, diameter, and bisection bandwidth, and notes processor frequency saturation.

nodes.title: Comparison of Topologies
nodes.summary: The text explains routing in a butterfly network, detailing how prefix bits match switch labels across k columns to reach the correct destination, and notes the strategy's similarity to hypercube routing. It derives network properties for N nodes (power of 2): requiring log(N) columns and N/2 switches per column, yielding diameter log(N) and bisection bandwidth N/2. It also introduces a comparison of topologies based on switches, links, diameter, and bisection bandwidth, and includes a summary noting processor frequency and performance saturation.

nodes.title: Multithreading

nodes.title: I/O and Storage Devices
I/O and Storage Devices (intro)
nodes.summary: The text introduces I/O and storage devices in computer architecture. It explains the need for an I/O system to communicate with the processor and run programs. It describes typical computer components: processor, memory, and peripherals like keyboard, mouse, monitor, printer, and generic I/O ports (pins and port controller). It highlights storage devices (hard disks, flash drives) for permanent data storage, including files, configuration, and swap space, emphasizing their importance in architecture. It covers standard interfaces (USB, DVI) for device compatibility, and the role of network cards for external communication.

nodes.title: I/O System – Overview
Overview
nodes.summary: The text covers I/O system architecture, defining I/O ports and controllers, and highlighting storage devices' importance. It explains standard interfaces (e.g., USB, DVI) for peripheral compatibility, and differentiates software (OS, drivers) and hardware roles, including system calls like read/write and interrupt handling. It details I/O device bandwidth requirements via a table, noting graphics cards for displays and network cards, and defines a 'card' as a PCB. nodes.title: Requirements of the I/O System
nodes.summary: Table 13.1 lists I/O devices like graphics cards, hard disks, network cards, USB, DVD, audio, keyboard, and mouse, along with their bus technologies and bandwidth requirements. It highlights that graphics cards and main memory need the highest bandwidth, while other devices require less. The text defines a 'card' as a PCB for specific functionality, such as graphics, sound, or network. It explains why multiple bus types exist, such as USB, PCI Express, and SATA, due to varying bandwidth needs and historical reasons, and defines a bus as a set of wires connecting devices for data and control signals.

nodes.title: Design of the I/O System

It details I/O bandwidth hierarchies, from high-speed main memory and graphics to low-speed peripherals. It defines buses, explaining varied types like USB, PCI Express, and SATA due to bandwidth and historical reasons. It describes bus structure and controllers. It notes trends like integrated memory controllers, on-chip graphics, and SOCs. Finally, it introduces the need for layering in I/O systems.

nodes.title: Layers in the I/O System

nodes.title: Physical Layer – Transmission Sublayer
Physical Layer – Transmission Sublayer (intro)
nodes.summary: The text outlines a four-layer I/O system architecture inspired by the OSI model: Physical, Data Link, Network, and Protocol layers. The Physical layer is divided into transmission and synchronization sublayers, covering electrical specifications, bit encoding, and timing. It discusses single-ended signaling, active high/low conventions, and the trade-off between voltage differences and speed due to noise. The Data Link layer handles framing, error checking, and bus access. The Network layer manages frame transmission and addressing (port-based and memory-mapped). The Protocol layer covers end-to-end I/O requests, interrupts, and DMA. A generic I/O link and the need for synchronization due to jitter are also explained.

nodes.title: Single Ended Signaling
nodes.summary: This text covers bus transmission frequencies, noting transmitter clocks may differ from processor clocks. It describes single-ended signaling using active high and active low conventions, but explains its slowness due to large voltage swings and the need to minimize voltage differences for speed, while considering noise limits. It then details Low Voltage Differential Signaling (LVDS), explaining its two-wire circuit, fixed current source, current direction based on input, voltage swing calculation (350 mV with 3.5 mA and 100 Ω), and how the detector infers logical values from voltage difference sign, enabling high-speed operation.

nodes.title: Low Voltage Differential Signaling (LVDS)
nodes.summary: This text covers signaling methods and LVDS. It illustrates active high and active low signaling. It details LVDS: using two wires, monitoring voltage difference, with a 3.5 mA current source and 100 Ω resistor, yielding a 350 mV swing for fast transmission. It discusses challenges of transmitting multiple bits, including variable duty cycles, power consumption, and synchronization issues with strobe lines, leading to ternary signaling with states zero, one, and idle, implementable with LVDS.

nodes.title: Transmission of Multiple Bits
nodes.summary: The text covers the LVDS circuit diagram, then discusses transmitting multiple bits with strobe lines, synchronization challenges, and ternary signaling (zero, one, idle). It defines ternary signaling, explains its LVDS implementation using voltage differences, and details Return to Zero (RZ) protocols. RZ uses positive/negative pulses for 1/0, returning to idle for synchronization. It defines bit period and I/O clock, and notes timing issues. The summary includes all sections: 13.2.3 and 13.2.4, definitions, and circuit references.

nodes.title: Return to Zero (RZ) Protocols
nodes.summary: The text covers voltage-based line state detection using threshold τ for logical 1 and 0, requiring no LVDS changes, and introduces multi-bit physical layer techniques with ternary signaling. It defines bit period and I/O clock, then details Return to Zero (RZ) protocols: positive/negative pulses for 1/0 followed by idle state to aid receiver synchronization, noting bandwidth waste. It distinguishes physical and logical bits, then explains Manchester encoding: 0→1 transition encodes logical 1, 1→0 encodes logical 0, with mid-bit transitions enabling easy decoding and clock synchronization without external strobes.

nodes.title: Manchester Encoding
nodes.summary: The text differentiates physical and logical bits, explaining Manchester encoding where transitions represent logical values, enabling self-clocking but causing power dissipation due to frequent transitions. It contrasts this with Return to Zero (RZ), which uses pauses but wastes bandwidth, and introduces Non Return to Zero (NRZ), which reduces transitions by maintaining voltage for consecutive identical bits, improving speed. Manchester encoding is noted for use in IEEE 802.3 Ethernet, while critics highlight its power inefficiency, motivating NRZ.

nodes.title: Non Return to Zero (NRZ) Protocol
nodes.summary: The text covers self-clocked signals, defining them as allowing the receiver to extract the sender's clock from physical bit transitions, with Manchester encoding as an example used in IEEE 802.3 Ethernet, noting its power dissipation due to transitions. It then describes the NRZ protocol, which reduces transitions by maintaining voltage for consecutive identical bits, improving speed and power efficiency but requiring additional synchronization. Finally, it introduces the NRZI protocol, a variant where transitions encode logical 1s and no transitions encode logical 0s.

nodes.title: Non Return to Zero (NRZI) Inverted Protocol
nodes.summary: The text covers NRZ and NRZI encoding protocols, highlighting NRZ's power efficiency and complexity due to synchronization needs. It introduces the physical layer synchronization sublayer, which determines bit periods and reads frames without timing guarantees. Synchronous buses are discussed, including simple synchronous buses where sender and receiver share a clock and metastability is avoided via setup and hold times. The receiver uses a serial-in-parallel-out register. Mesochronous buses are also mentioned, where a constant phase difference exists between signal and clock.

The section outlines a four-layer I/O architecture inspired by OSI: Physical, Data Link, Network, and Protocol. Low Voltage Differential Signaling (LVDS) is detailed, including its circuit and voltage swing calculation. nodes.title: Physical Layer – Synchronization Sublayer
Synchronous Buses
nodes.summary: This section covers the physical layer synchronization sublayer, explaining how receivers determine bit periods and timing to correctly sample data. It details four bus types: synchronous buses (shared clock, no metastability, serial-in-parallel-out register); mesochronous buses (constant phase difference, needing tunable delay elements); plesiochronous buses (slight clock drift, strobe signals, delay calculators, periodic retuning); and source synchronous buses (sender clock as strobe, delay calculator for phase difference, used in high-performance I/O like Hypertransport). It addresses metastability, keep-out regions, setup/hold times, and resynchronization for frames.

nodes.title: Source Synchronous Bus*
nodes.summary: The text covers three bus types: plesiochronous, source synchronous, and asynchronous. Plesiochronous buses use a tunable delay element, strobe, and delay calculator for clock synchronization. Source synchronous buses address unpredictable delays and jitter by sending the sender clock as a strobe; they use a serial-in parallel-out register with sender clock (xclk), receiver clock (rclk), and a delay calculator for phase differences. Multiple data links can share one strobe. Asynchronous buses lack clock synchronization and strobe; the receiver uses a clock recovery circuit to extract the sender's clock, with a tunable delay element and delay calculator, illustrated using NRZ encoding.

nodes.title: Asynchronous Buses
nodes.summary: The text covers asynchronous bus receivers, including clock detection and recovery using PLL for NRZ encoding, and handling metastability with delay elements. It details strobe-based asynchronous communication and handshaking protocols: 4-phase (set/reset) and 2-phase (toggle) for flow control and acknowledgement. It defines bus types: simple synchronous, mesochronous, plesiochronous, source synchronous, and asynchronous. Finally, it introduces the data link layer, covering framing, buffering, error checking/correction, retransmission, arbitration, and transaction support, with a brief note on parallel links and serial-to-parallel conversion.
