nodes.title: Data Link Layer
Framing and Buffering
nodes.summary: The text covers plesiochronous, source synchronous, and asynchronous bus clocking mechanisms. It then details the data link layer's roles: framing data from physical layer bits, error checking and correction, bus arbitration, and supporting transaction requests. Framing methods discussed include pauses, bit counting, and bit/byte stuffing with special sequences; buffering follows. Error detection and correction are necessitated by electromagnetic interference, crosstalk, and delay variations causing jitter and distortion, requiring redundant information to recover corrupted bits.

nodes.title: Error Detection and Correction
Error Detection and Correction (intro)
nodes.summary: The text covers data link layer framing and error handling. It describes frame sizes varying by device, and three demarcation methods: long pauses (unreliable, wastes bandwidth), bit count (synchronization issues), and bit/byte stuffing using special sequences like 0xDEADBEEF and 0x12345678, with dummy bit insertion for escaping. It then addresses error detection and correction, explaining causes like electromagnetic interference, crosstalk, and temperature changes leading to jitter and distortion. It distinguishes forward error correction (adding bits to detect and recover) from backward error correction (detect and request retransmission). Finally, it details single error detection using parity bits, where XOR of data bits detects single-bit errors, with 12.5% overhead for 8-bit frames.

nodes.title: Single Error Detection
nodes.summary: The text discusses error rates in interconnects, noting that even low probabilities (under 1 in a million) can lead to frequent errors (e.g., 1 per second at 1 million I/O ops/sec), necessitating error handling. It defines forward error correction (adding bits to detect and recover from errors) and backward error correction (detecting errors, discarding, and requesting retransmission). It then details single error detection using parity bits (e.g., 8 data bits plus parity, 12.5% overhead) and single error correction, which requires dlog(n+1)e additional bits, illustrated with an (8,4) code where parity bits are placed at positions 1,2,4,8 and associated with data bits based on binary position patterns.

nodes.title: Single Error Correction
nodes.summary: The text explains single error correction (SEC) using parity bits, covering syndrome calculation and bit arrangements; details SECDED for detecting double errors via an extra parity bit; provides equations for parity bits, tables mapping data-parity relationships and error positions to syndromes; and describes transmission, detection, and correction algorithms.

nodes.title: Single Error Correction, Double Error Detection (SECDED)
nodes.summary: The text explains error-correcting codes: SEC (single error correction) using syndrome to identify single erroneous bits, and SECDED, which adds a parity bit to distinguish single from double errors. It covers Hamming codes and Hamming distance, noting minimum distances for parity, SEC, and SECDED codes. It then introduces Cyclic Redundancy Check (CRC) codes for detecting burst errors, detailing a modulo-2 division example for a 4-bit CRC with an 8-bit message and generator polynomial.

nodes.title: Hamming Codes
nodes.summary: The text explains error detection and correction codes: single-bit error correction and double-bit error detection via SECDED, which has a minimum Hamming distance of 3. It defines Hamming codes and Hamming distance, noting SEC codes have distance 2. It then introduces Cyclic Redundancy Check (CRC) codes for detecting burst errors, including an example of computing a 4-bit CRC for an 8-bit message using modulo-2 division with a 5-bit generator polynomial.

nodes.title: Cyclic Redundancy Check (CRC) Codes
nodes.summary: The text covers error detection and correction codes, starting with SECDED codes that detect double-bit and correct single-bit errors, and Hamming codes based on Hamming distance, noting minimum distances for SEC and SECDED. It then details Cyclic Redundancy Check (CRC) codes for detecting burst errors, including a step-by-step example of computing a 4-bit CRC using modulo-2 division. Finally, it introduces bus arbitration for multidrop buses, explaining the need to select one transmitter when multiple devices contend for the bus, contrasting with point-to-point buses.

The section covers data link layer framing and error handling, including frame demarcation methods (long pauses, bit count, bit/byte stuffing) and causes of errors like interference and crosstalk. It distinguishes forward error correction from backward error correction. It details single error detection using parity bits, single error correction with syndrome calculation, and SECDED for double error detection. Hamming codes and Hamming distance are explained. Cyclic Redundancy Check (CRC) codes for burst error detection are introduced with a modulo-2 division example. Finally, bus arbitration for multidrop buses is discussed.

nodes.title: Arbitration
nodes.summary: The text explains CRC code computation by aligning the divisor with the message, showing an example of a 4-bit CRC code, and appending it for error detection. It then covers bus arbitration, defining the need for fair, priority-based bus allocation among multiple transmitters. It describes centralized arbiter-based star topology, including request/grant/release signals and policies like round-robin, and daisy chain arbitration with token passing, implicit priority, and fairness. Finally, it discusses transaction-oriented buses, contrasting multidrop with point-to-point, half-duplex with full-duplex, and master-slave concepts.

nodes.title: Transaction-Oriented Buses
nodes.summary: This text covers daisy chain bus arbitration, detailing wired-OR request lines, token passing, bus master roles, and token destruction via release signals. It highlights implicit priority and fairness, and ease of adding devices, plus distributed schemes. It then discusses transaction-oriented buses, contrasting multidrop with point-to-point duplex buses, and defines full/half duplex. Using DRAM read timing (RAS/CAS), it explains bus transactions as locked, strongly coupled message sequences with timing and semantic relationships, noting complexity, portability issues, and potential bandwidth waste. Finally, split transaction buses are introduced as a solution, breaking transfers into separate request and response phases with arbitrary intervals.

nodes.title: Split Transaction Buses
nodes.summary: The text explains DRAM read operations where the memory controller sends column addresses and read signals, receives data, and overlaps next row address decoding for lower latency using a duplex bus. It defines bus transactions as tightly coupled, locked sequences of messages with timing and semantic relationships, noting pros like performance but cons like complexity, portability issues, and wasted bandwidth. Split transaction buses are introduced to address these by breaking transfers into separate, unidirectional message sequences, improving simplicity and portability but lacking fine-grained control. Finally, it covers network layer I/O addressing, defining software ports as visible register sets, and routing messages in the chipset.

The Data Link Layer section covers framing and buffering, including clocking mechanisms and methods like pauses and bit stuffing. It details error detection and correction necessitated by interference, covering parity, Hamming codes, and CRC. Bus arbitration is explained, with centralized and daisy chain approaches, policies like round-robin, and fairness. Transaction-oriented buses are discussed, contrasting topologies and duplex modes, with DRAM read timing examples. Split transaction buses are introduced to improve simplicity. Finally, network layer I/O addressing is touched upon.

nodes.title: Network Layer
nodes.summary: The text covers transaction buses and their simplicity and portability, followed by the network layer's I/O addressing, including I/O port addressing, software interfaces, port types (read-only, write-only, read-write), Intel's 64K ports, the I/O address space definition, and ISA support with in/out instructions. It explains routing messages via North and South Bridge chips using I/O routing tables and port-mapped I/O (PMIO). Then, memory-mapped I/O (MMIO) is described, using virtual memory mapping with TLB support, allowing regular load/store instructions. Finally, the protocol layer is introduced for complete I/O requests like printing, involving device drivers and USB port buffers.

nodes.title: Protocol Layer
Protocol Layer (intro)
nodes.summary: The text explains memory-mapped I/O, where I/O address space is mapped to a process's virtual address space, allowing regular load/store instructions instead of dedicated I/O instructions. It details address translation through the TLB and pipeline stages, and notes the programmer's obliviousness to actual I/O port addresses. It then introduces the protocol layer, using a printing example to discuss I/O request handling. It contrasts polling (repeatedly querying device status) with interrupts, and provides a definition of polling along with a SimpleRisc code snippet for its implementation.

nodes.title: Polling
nodes.summary: The text explains I/O device communication using printer examples. It defines polling, where the driver repeatedly queries the printer's status register via I/O ports, with assembly code shown, but notes drawbacks like processor waste. Interrupts are introduced as an alternative, where the device notifies the processor, using vectored interrupts with unique codes. It describes interrupt controllers (PICs/APICs) that buffer and prioritize interrupts, and covers interrupt disabling during critical stages and interrupt masking for selective handling.

nodes.title: Interrupts
nodes.summary: The text explains polling with assembly code, then interrupts as an improvement, covering interrupt identification, vectored interrupts, programmable interrupt controllers (PICs/APICs), buffering, disabling interrupts during critical stages, interrupt masking, priority handling, and definitions. It also introduces DMA by contrasting slow per-instruction I/O transfers (4 bytes each, many instructions for large blocks) with offloading work from the processor, using a grading analogy.

nodes.title: DMA
nodes.summary: The text covers interrupt handling details: interrupt mask vectors enabling/disabling interrupts via bits, priority ordering by PICs, and definitions of vectored interrupts, PIC, and interrupt masking. It then explains DMA for efficient bulk I/O transfers, including the DMA engine's role, transfer procedure, burst vs. cycle stealing modes, and cache coherence issues resolved by DMA snoop circuits. Finally, it introduces case studies on I/O protocols, noting their formal specifications from industry consortia.

The Protocol Layer section covers I/O handling mechanisms. It begins with memory-mapped I/O, address translation via TLB and pipeline stages, and programmer abstraction from I/O port addresses. I/O request handling is illustrated with a printing example, contrasting polling (repeated status checks with code) and interrupts. Polling drawbacks lead to interrupts, covering vectored interrupts, PICs/APICs, buffering, disabling, masking, and priority. DMA is introduced for bulk transfers, detailing the DMA engine, transfer procedures, burst vs. cycle stealing, and cache coherence via snoop circuits. The section concludes with case studies on I/O protocols and their formal specifications.

nodes.title: Case Studies – I/O Protocols
Case Studies – I/O Protocols (intro)
nodes.summary: The text explains DMA engines enabling processors to offload large data transfers between memory and I/O devices, detailing the procedure, use in modern systems, and considerations like bus mastering modes (burst and cycle stealing) and cache coherence via DMA snoop circuits. It then introduces I/O protocols case studies, focusing on PCI Express: its origins, development, and advantages over older buses; its design as a high-speed point-to-point serial interconnect with lanes, striping, and layered architecture for error correction, flow control, and transactions.

nodes.title: PCI Express®
nodes.summary: The text covers PCI Express (PCIe), SATA, and SCSI/SAS I/O protocols. PCIe, a 2004 serial point-to-point standard, replaced older buses like PCI and AGP. It uses lanes with 8b/10b encoding, striping, and a layered architecture (physical, data link, transaction) with features like 32-bit CRC and expansion slots. SATA, a half-duplex serial bus for storage devices, replaced IDE/PATA. It has physical, data link, and transport layers, uses 8b/10b encoding, LVDS signaling, and multipliers for tree topologies. SCSI, originally a parallel multidrop bus for peripherals, evolved into a storage protocol with host/peripheral roles and mutual communication.

nodes.title: SATA
nodes.summary: The text covers SATA and SCSI storage buses. SATA replaced parallel IDE/PATA due to jitter and distortion. It is a point-to-point, half-duplex, asynchronous serial bus with three layers (physical, data link, transport), LVDS signaling, 8b/10b encoding, and a network layer using multipliers for tree topologies. The protocol layer handles sequencing, DMA, buffering, and commands. SATA is a split transaction bus with rich commands for storage, encryption, and device control. SCSI, originally a PCI competitor, became a multidrop parallel bus for storage, connecting hosts and peripherals, with any pair able to communicate.

nodes.title: SCSI and SAS
nodes.summary: The text details the SATA protocol, covering its development from parallel buses, three-layer architecture (physical, data link, transport), half-duplex point-to-point links, 8b/10b encoding, tree topology with multipliers, and protocol layer commands including DMA. It then discusses SCSI, its evolution to serial SAS, and SAS overview: full duplex, expanders (edge and fanout), routing, LUNs, and support for SATA, SCSI, and SMP protocols. Finally, it covers USB: purpose for external devices, speed classifications, versions, generic design, power lines, point-to-point serial topology with hubs, and device limits.

nodes.title: USB
nodes.summary: The text covers SCSI commands and then details USB and FireWire protocols. For USB, it discusses the need for standardization, device speed classifications, versions, backward compatibility, point-to-point serial bus, tree topology with hubs, power limitations, and layers: physical (connectors, signaling, encoding, half-duplex), data link (error checking, frame delimitation, traffic types, arbitration, split transactions), network (device IDs, endpoints, routing), and protocol layer (pipes, token/data/handshake packets). FireWire is described as a high-speed serial bus, IEEE 1394 standard, supporting up to 63 devices, peer-to-peer communication, leader election, tree topology, and physical layer with LVDS links and data strobe encoding.

nodes.title: FireWire Protocol
nodes.summary: The text covers USB protocol layer details: stream and message pipes, token/data/handshake packets, and a summary table. It then introduces FireWire: a high-speed serial bus, IEEE 1394, hybrid peripheral/network bus, supports up to 63 devices, peer-to-peer, tree topology with root election, half-duplex LVDS links, data strobe encoding, CRC error checking, split transactions, 125 μs cycles with isochronous and asynchronous arbitration, network layer I/O ports, memory-mapped I/O, and a summary table. Finally, storage devices are discussed: persistent state, boot process, and file storage.

This section covers DMA engines for offloading data transfers, including bus mastering and cache coherence. It then presents I/O protocol case studies: PCI Express, detailing its serial point-to-point lanes, layered architecture, and error correction; SATA, a half-duplex serial bus for storage with three layers and tree topology; SCSI and SAS, including evolution to serial SAS, expanders, and LUNs; USB, covering speed classifications, versions, tree topology, and protocol layers (pipes, packets); and FireWire (IEEE 1394), a high-speed serial bus with peer-to-peer communication, leader election, and isochronous cycles. Finally, storage devices and the boot process are discussed.

nodes.title: Storage
Storage (intro)
nodes.summary: The text covers FireWire (IEEE 1394) protocol details: 125 μs cycles, root node broadcasting, isochronous and asynchronous transmission scheduling, with 80% cycle time for isochronous, request denial in tree topology, I/O ports, and memory-mapped I/O. It summarizes FireWire in Table 13.8. Then it introduces storage devices: persistent state, boot process, file storage, virtual memory swap space, network-attached storage, and storage technologies—magnetic, optical, and solid-state drives (SSDs), including hybrid solutions. Hard disk physics is explained: ferromagnets, Faraday's law, and permanent magnetism.

nodes.title: Hard Disks
Physics of Data Storage in Hard Disks
nodes.summary: The text covers network-accessible storage and main storage technologies: magnetic, optical, and solid-state drives. It explains hard disk physics using ferromagnets and Faraday's law, encoding bits via magnetic transitions (like NRZI) in sectors. It describes read/write heads, electromagnets, and the platter structure with tracks and sectors, noting platters attach to a spindle. It also compares SSDs (flash, faster, costlier, less capacity) and hybrid server solutions, while referencing further reading.

nodes.title: Structure of the Platter
nodes.summary: The text explains hard disk data storage using magnets, covering read/write heads, magnetic orientation encoding (e.g., NRZI), and sector-based atomic blocks. It details platter structure with tracks and sectors, and challenges of sector allocation, leading to Zoned-Bit Recording (ZBR) that balances capacity and complexity. It describes the physical hard disk assembly: platters, spindle, arms, heads, actuator, and cylinder alignment, including the precision required for track positioning and data access operations.

nodes.title: Structure of the Hard Disk
nodes.summary: The text describes hard disk structure, including platters, spindle, arms, heads, and cylinder alignment, with figures. It explains read/write operations, zone-based spindle motor speed, actuator and servo control for head positioning, and electronic components for data processing, error correction, and bad sector management. It also presents a mathematical model for disk access time, divided into seek time, rotational latency, and transfer time.

nodes.title: Mathematical Model of a Hard Disk Access
nodes.summary: The text covers hard disk internals, including labeled components in Figure 13.32, servo control for head positioning, sector marking and prediction, and electronic components for data transfer, scheduling, and error correction. It presents a mathematical model for disk access time as seek time plus rotational latency plus transfer time, with definitions and a worked example. It then introduces RAID arrays, defining RAID as redundant arrays of inexpensive or independent disks, and notes different RAID levels with varying bandwidth, capacity, and reliability guarantees.

nodes.title: RAID Arrays
nodes.summary: The text defines disk access time as the sum of seek time, rotational latency, and transfer time. It provides an example calculating average access time for 10,000 bytes given seek time, rotation speed, and bandwidth. It then introduces RAID arrays, explaining they are used for high storage, bandwidth, and reliability, defines RAID as Redundant Array of Inexpensive Disks, and notes different RAID levels with varying guarantees for bandwidth, capacity, and reliability.

This section covers hard disk technology in detail. It begins with the physics of magnetic data storage, explaining ferromagnets, Faraday's law, encoding schemes like NRZI, and read/write heads. It describes platter structure with tracks and sectors, Zoned-Bit Recording (ZBR), and the physical assembly of platters, spindle, arms, heads, actuator, and cylinders. It explains read/write operations, servo control, electronic components, error correction, and bad sector management. A mathematical model for disk access time (seek time + rotational latency + transfer time) is presented with an example. Finally, it introduces RAID arrays, defining RAID levels and their trade-offs in bandwidth, capacity, and reliability.

nodes.title: RAID Arrays
nodes.summary: The text covers hard disk access time components—seek, rotational latency, and transfer—with a computation example. It then details RAID levels 0 through 6, explaining data striping, mirroring, bit/byte/block striping, parity distribution, performance, reliability, and use cases. RAID 0 boosts bandwidth; RAID 1 mirrors for reliability; RAID 2-4 use parity but have drawbacks; RAID 5 distributes parity; RAID 6 adds dual parity. Finally, it briefly mentions optical disks (CD, DVD, Blu-ray) as former distribution media, now replaced by USB drives.

nodes.title: Optical Disks – CD, DVD, Blu-ray
nodes.summary: The text covers RAID 4's write contention due to a dedicated parity disk, and RAID 5's distributed parity for better performance and reliability. RAID 6 adds a second parity block for higher reliability using complex functions. It then details optical disks (CD, DVD, Blu-ray), their physics, layers, reader mechanisms, constant linear velocity, and advanced features like write-once and rewritable media, multi-layer and double-sided disks. Finally, it compares CD, DVD, and Blu-ray and introduces flash memory as a more robust portable alternative.

nodes.title: Flash Memory
Advanced Features
nodes.summary: The text discusses constant data transfer rates in optical drives via spindle speed changes and zoning, then covers read-only and write-once optical media using dye layers where lasers create pits and lands. Rewritable disks use phase-change alloys heated to alter reflectivity. Dual-layer disks use partially transparent coatings and fluorescent materials, while double-sided disks require two laser assemblies. A CD/DVD/Blu-ray comparison is referenced, and flash memory is introduced as a more portable, durable alternative to mechanical storage.

nodes.title: Comparison of CDs, DVDs, and Blu-ray Disks
nodes.summary: The text covers optical drive mechanics, including constant data rate via spindle speed adjustment and zoning. It details advanced features like write-once CD-R/DVD-R using dye layers, rewritable media with phase-change alloys, dual-layer disks with fluorescent materials, and double-sided disks. A comparison table highlights CD, DVD, and Blu-ray specifications. It then introduces flash memory as a durable, portable alternative, explaining the floating gate transistor's structure and charge storage mechanism.

nodes.title: The Floating Gate Transistor
nodes.summary: This text compares CD, DVD, and Blu-ray specifications (capacity, laser wavelength, transfer rate) and details flash memory based on floating gate transistors. It explains floating gate operation, charging to store 0 and erasing to 1, and describes NOR flash cells with bit lines, word lines, and sense amplifiers for reading, writing, and erasing data.

nodes.title: NOR Flash
nodes.summary: The text explains floating gate transistors, detailing how stored charge alters threshold voltage to represent binary states (uncharged=1, charged=0). It describes programming (writing 0 by depositing electrons) and erasing (writing 1 by removing electrons) via voltage applications. It then introduces two flash memory cell arrangements: NOR flash, where transistors connect bit lines to ground, enabling unique access and sensing, and NAND flash, featuring series-connected transistors with select lines, requiring specific steps for reading, and notes typical array sizes.

nodes.title: NAND Flash
nodes.summary: The text compares NOR and NAND flash cells, explaining their topologies and read mechanisms. NOR flash is similar to DRAM, while NAND flash uses series-connected floating gate transistors with select transistors, requiring a three-step read process. NAND offers higher density and fewer wires, making it dominant. The text then distinguishes flash as a storage device with block-level access, contrasting it with byte-accessible memory. It discusses operating system caching, synchronization events like sync() and USB eject, and risks of data corruption from uncommitted writes. Finally, it describes NAND flash organization into pages (512-4096 bytes with error correction) and blocks (32-128 pages, 16-512 KB), with erasure at block level.

nodes.title: Blocks and Pages
nodes.summary: The text explains NAND flash memory operation, including reading cells via word line voltages and sensing. It contrasts NAND with NOR, noting NAND's higher density (40-60%) due to fewer wires. Flash is storage, not memory, with block-level access and caching for synchronization. Data is organized into pages (512-4096 bytes) and blocks (32-128 pages). Writing only changes 1s to 0s; erasing is block-level. Program/erase cycles are limited (100,000 to 1 million) due to wear. Wear leveling distributes accesses using logical-to-physical mapping and access counters to extend device lifetime.

nodes.title: Program/Erase Cycles
nodes.summary: The text explains NAND flash memory operations: writing sets bits to 0, erasing to 1, done in blocks due to slow erase. A program/erase (P/E) cycle consists of programming and erasing; reads can occur in between. Flash endures finite P/E cycles (100,000 to 1 million as of 2013) due to silicon dioxide layer wear. Wear leveling distributes accesses evenly across blocks to prevent early faults from temporal and spatial locality. It uses logical-to-physical address mapping, access counters per block, and swapping frequently accessed blocks with less frequently accessed ones when a threshold is exceeded, using a temporary block.

nodes.title: Wear Leveling
nodes.summary: The text covers flash memory reliability. It explains program/erase (P/E) cycles, where writing sets bits to 0, erasing resets to 1, and each cycle damages the oxide layer, limiting endurance. Wear leveling is described to distribute accesses evenly across blocks, using logical-to-physical mapping, access counters, and block swapping to prevent uneven wear. Read disturbance is discussed, where repeated reads program neighboring transistors, mitigated by read counters and data migration. The summary also introduces the I/O system and motherboard components.

nodes.title: Read Disturbance
nodes.summary: The text covers wear leveling in flash memory, detailing a block-swapping process to prevent uneven wear, including copying and erasing blocks and updating logical-to-physical mapping. It defines wear leveling and notes frequent blocks are swapped with less used ones. It then addresses read disturbance, where continuous reads program neighboring transistors, causing errors; mitigation involves read counters and migrating blocks to new locations after thresholds. Finally, it summarizes I/O systems, mentioning the motherboard, chipset, and ports for connecting devices.

The section covers flash memory as a durable, portable alternative to mechanical storage, detailing optical media comparisons (CD/DVD/Blu-ray), floating gate transistors, and NOR vs. NAND flash architectures. It explains NAND's dominance due to higher density, block-level access, and page/block organization. Key reliability topics include program/erase cycle limits, wear leveling techniques with logical-to-physical mapping, and read disturbance mitigation. It concludes with an introduction to the I/O system and motherboard components.

The Storage section covers FireWire (IEEE 1394) protocol details, including cycle times, transmission scheduling, and topology, summarized in a table, before introducing storage devices, their persistent state, boot process, and types like NAS and magnetic/optical/solid-state drives. It explains hard disk physics, encoding, platter structure, access time modeling, and RAID levels 0-6 with trade-offs. Optical disks (CD, DVD, Blu-ray) are detailed with their physics, layers, and features. Flash memory is covered, including floating gate transistors, NOR vs. NAND architectures, reliability, wear leveling, and read disturbance, concluding with an I/O system and motherboard introduction.

nodes.title: Summary and Further Reading
Summary
nodes.summary: The text details flash memory reliability, focusing on wear leveling via block swapping and read disturbance mitigation using read counters and block migration. It summarizes the I/O system, covering motherboard chipsets (North/South Bridge), I/O operations, and four layers: physical (encoding, synchronization), data link (framing, error control, arbitration, transactions), network (port- and memory-mapped I/O), and protocol (polling, interrupts, DMA). Case studies include PCI Express, SATA, SAS, USB, and FireWire. Storage devices are examined: hard disks (encoding, sectors, tracks, access times), optical discs (lands/pits, CD/DVD/Blu-Ray), and flash memory (floating gate transistors, NAND/NOR, programming/erasing). Further reading lists vendor sites, research papers, and books on I/O, error codes, and protocols.

nodes.title: Further Reading
Further Reading (intro)

It details flash memory using floating gate transistors, programming/erasing via voltage pulses, NAND vs. NOR configurations, and design considerations like wear leveling and read disturbance. Further reading recommends vendor websites for motherboard chipsets, research papers for chip architectures, and books on communication, error control, memory systems, and I/O. Official specs for PCI Express, SATA, SCSI, USB, FireWire, and optical disc standards are cited. Data link, network, and protocol layer exercises ask about frame demarcation methods.

nodes.title: Data Link, Network, and Protocol Layer
nodes.summary: The text references CD/DVD/Blu-Ray standards, then lists exercises across seven areas: I/O system overview (North/South Bridge, chipset, layers); physical layer (LVDS, protocols RZ/NRZ/Manchester/NRZI, plesiochronous/source synchronous buses, handshakes, delay elements); data link, network, and protocol layers (framing, SECDED codes, arbiters, split transaction buses, I/O ports, memory-mapped I/O, polling vs interrupts, DMA); and hard disks (zoned recording, operation, performance calculations, parallel head reading).

nodes.title: Hard Disks
nodes.summary: The text presents exercises covering error-correcting codes (SECDED, 3-bit error detection), fully distributed arbiters, split transaction buses, I/O port access, memory-mapped I/O, and I/O communication methods with processor utilization ordering. nodes.title: Optical and Flash Drives
nodes.summary: The text presents exercises (31–43) on storage systems. nodes.title: Design Problems
nodes.summary: The text presents exercises covering hard disk sector arrangement and RAID levels 0-6, including parity computation, RAID 4 example with disk contents, and RAID 5 vs 4 advantages. title: IV Appendix

nodes.title: IV Appendix (intro)
nodes.summary: The text introduces real processor case studies from ARM, AMD, and Intel, emphasizing technical appreciation over comparison. It details ARM's licensing model, where ARM designs cores but does not manufacture chips, and vendors like Qualcomm integrate them into SoCs. It covers the ARMv8 architecture's three processor lines: Cortex-M series for embedded microcontrollers, focusing on power efficiency and cost, with the Cortex-M3 example; and the Cortex-R series for real-time applications, prioritizing reliability and speed.

nodes.title: Case Studies of Real Processors
ARM Processors
ARM Processors (intro)
nodes.summary: The text introduces case studies of real processors from ARM, AMD, and Intel, focusing on embedded and server designs without comparison, to understand practical nuances. It details ARM processors, which license designs rather than manufacture chips. ARM's ARMv8 architecture has three lines: Cortex-M for microcontrollers emphasizing power efficiency and cost, with the Cortex-M3's 3-stage pipeline, ARMv7-M instruction set, and connection via AMBA bus to components like UART, timer, and DMA; Cortex-R for real-time applications prioritizing reliability and speed, lacking virtual memory support; and Cortex-A for high-end devices like smartphones, featuring complex pipelines, vector operations, and virtual memory, specifically Cortex-A8 and A15.

nodes.title: ARM Cortex-M3
nodes.summary: The text covers ARM Cortex processor families: Cortex-R lacks virtual memory support; Cortex-A runs user applications with virtual memory, complex pipelines, and vector operations, focusing on Cortex-A8 and A15. It details Cortex-M3 system design with AMBA bus and components like UART, timer, and DMA; its 3-stage pipeline including fetch, decode, and execute, with units for address generation, branch prediction, and multiply/divide; branch types and handling; and load/store instruction behavior. It introduces Cortex-A8 as a dual-issue superscalar processor with a 13-stage integer pipeline, floating point and SIMD units, and separate caches.

nodes.title: ARM Cortex-A8
nodes.summary: The text discusses ARM processors: Cortex-M3 indirect branch prediction, multiply/divide units, and load/store pipeline stalls. It then covers Cortex-A8 as a dual-issue superscalar processor with a 13-stage pipeline, NEON/VFP units, and detailed pipeline design including fetch, decode, execution, and L1/L2 caches. Finally, it introduces Cortex-A15 as a 3-issue out-of-order multicore processor with deeper pipelines, 40-bit physical addressing, virtualization support, power management, cache coherence via AMBA4, and SECDED error control.

nodes.title: ARM Cortex-A15
nodes.summary: The text details ARM NEON/VFP unit features including register files, pipelines, load/store, and L1/L2 cache configurations. It then covers the ARM Cortex-A15's out-of-order superscalar design, deep pipelines, integrated NEON/VFP, large memory support, multicore clusters, coherence, and power management. Pipeline specifics include branch prediction, loop buffer, reorder buffer, execution units, and cache hierarchy with directory-based MESI protocol. Finally, it introduces AMD processors, contrasting the power-efficient Bobcat for mobile devices with the high-performance Bulldozer for servers, noting Bobcat's out-of-order pipeline, complex micro-ops, and weak memory model.

The section on ARM processors introduces case studies of ARM, AMD, and Intel embedded and server designs, focusing on practical nuances. It covers ARM's licensing model and its ARMv8 architecture with three lines: Cortex-M for power-efficient, cost-effective microcontrollers, detailing the Cortex-M3's 3-stage pipeline, ARMv7-M instruction set, and AMBA bus connections to UART, timer, and DMA; Cortex-R for reliable, fast real-time applications without virtual memory; and Cortex-A for high-end devices like smartphones, featuring complex pipelines, vector operations, and virtual memory, specifically Cortex-A8 (dual-issue superscalar, 13-stage pipeline, NEON/VFP units, L1/L2 caches) and Cortex-A15 (3-issue out-of-order multicore, deeper pipelines, 40-bit physical addressing, virtualization, power management, AMBA4 cache coherence, SECDED error control). It also introduces AMD processors, contrasting the power-efficient Bobcat for mobile with the high-performance Bulldozer for servers.

nodes.title: AMD Processors
AMD Bobcat
nodes.summary: The text describes two processor architectures. It details the Cortex-A15's load/store unit, L1/L2 caches, directory-based MESI coherence, and snoop tag array for I/O and DMA. It then covers AMD processors: the Bobcat, a power-efficient out-of-order core with sophisticated branch prediction, 2-issue pipeline, SIMD support, clock gating, and detailed 16-stage pipeline; and the Bulldozer, a high-performance multithreaded conjoined core sharing fetch and decode across two threads.

nodes.title: AMD Bulldozer
nodes.summary: The text details AMD Bobcat and Bulldozer processors. Bobcat's pipeline includes branch prediction, fetch, decode, scheduling, integer/FP execution, caches, and 16-stage timing. Bulldozer, a high-end conjoined core, features SMT, shared fetch/decode, per-core integer units, shared FPU, branch prediction with BTB, macro-instruction fusion, and caches. It also introduces Intel Atom and Sandy Bridge designs.

The AMD Processors section covers two architectures. The Bobcat is a power-efficient out-of-order core with branch prediction, a 2-issue pipeline, SIMD support, clock gating, and a 16-stage pipeline including fetch, decode, scheduling, and caches. The Bulldozer is a high-performance multithreaded conjoined core featuring SMT, shared fetch and decode across two threads, per-core integer units, a shared FPU, branch prediction with BTB, macro-instruction fusion, and caches. It also briefly introduces Intel Atom and Sandy Bridge designs.

nodes.title: Intel Processors
Intel Processors (intro)
nodes.summary: The text describes AMD Bulldozer and Intel Atom architectures. Bulldozer features branch prediction with a 5500-entry target buffer, decode converting x86 to Cops with macro-instruction fusion, and dispatch to cores with rename, 40-entry scheduler, register file, 128-entry ROB, four pipelines (two ALUs, two address generation), load-store with forwarding and stride prefetching, shared 64KB instruction cache, per-core 16KB write-through L1 (4-cycle loads), shared L2 (1-2MB, 18-cycle), and a shared SMT floating-point unit with FMAC and SIMD pipelines. For Intel Atom, it covers power-efficient design, 2-issue in-order pipeline, direct CISC processing with microcode for complex instructions, a 16-stage pipeline with 6 stages for fetch/decode, and 2-way multithreading.

nodes.title: Intel Atom
nodes.summary: The text covers Intel Atom and Sandy Bridge processors. Atom's design emphasizes power efficiency while maintaining x86 compatibility, featuring a simplified 2-issue in-order pipeline without instruction translation, 2-way multithreading, and a 16-stage pipeline with 6 stages for fetch/decode. It details the fetch, pre-decode, decode stages, branch prediction, instruction length decoder, i-cache size, and execution units. Multithreading trade-offs like increased throughput versus resource contention are discussed. Sandy Bridge overview mentions its GPU, CPUs, cache, and integration with north/south bridges and DDR3 memory.

nodes.title: Intel Sandy Bridge
nodes.summary: This text covers Intel Atom's micro-op translation, integer/FP execution units, and multithreading design, including split instruction queues, shared resource contention, power and throughput trade-offs. It then details Intel Sandy Bridge: goals, on-chip GPU, shared L3, AVX SIMD, power-saving features, ring interconnect, 32nm process, successor Ivy Bridge. Detailed design includes instruction cache, predecoding, decoders, L0 micro-op cache, branch predictor trade-offs, physical register file, out-of-order execution, execution units, caches, ring topology, and turbo mode. Finally, it introduces graphics processors: history, pixel basics, and video refresh.

The section covers Intel processors, focusing on Atom and Sandy Bridge architectures. Atom is described as power-efficient with a 2-issue in-order pipeline, direct CISC processing, microcode for complex instructions, a 16-stage pipeline, 2-way multithreading, and detailed fetch/decode stages, branch prediction, instruction length decoding, cache, execution units, and multithreading trade-offs. Sandy Bridge is detailed with its on-chip GPU, shared L3 cache, AVX SIMD, power-saving features, ring interconnect, 32nm process, successor Ivy Bridge, instruction cache, predecoding, decoders, L0 micro-op cache, branch predictor, physical register file, out-of-order execution, execution units, caches, ring topology, and turbo mode. Graphics processors are introduced with history, pixel basics, and video refresh. AMD Bulldozer architecture is also briefly covered, including branch prediction, decode, dispatch, scheduler, register file, ROB, pipelines, load-store, caches, and shared SMT floating-point unit.

The section covers case studies of ARM, AMD, and Intel processors. ARM's licensing and ARMv8 architecture with Cortex-M (3-stage pipeline, ARMv7-M, AMBA), Cortex-R (real-time), and Cortex-A (Cortex-A8: superscalar, NEON; Cortex-A15: out-of-order, virtualization). AMD: Bobcat (power-efficient, 16-stage) and Bulldozer (multithreaded, shared FPU). Intel: Atom (2-issue, 16-stage, multithreading) and Sandy Bridge (on-chip GPU, AVX, ring interconnect, turbo). Also briefly covers graphics processors and AMD Bulldozer details.

nodes.title: Graphics Processors
Overview
Overview (intro)
nodes.summary: The text covers graphics processors, starting with an overview of high-intensity graphics in modern systems. It explains early rudimentary graphics programming and the need for hardware acceleration. It details monitor pixels, colors, and refresh rates. It distinguishes two graphics applications: automatic image synthesis (e.g., games) using high-level objects and rules, and video display requiring decoding. Graphics libraries break complex structures into triangles, and graphics processors handle operations like collision, movement, lighting, and depth, producing pixel arrays. Video decoding is also offloaded to GPUs due to its compute intensity.

nodes.title: Graphics Applications
nodes.summary: The text covers graphics applications and the graphics pipeline. Graphics applications are divided into automatic image synthesis, where programmers define high-level objects, rules, and lighting, and graphics libraries convert these to basic shapes (triangles) for a GPU to render at 50-100 fps, and video display, where compressed videos are decoded by GPUs. The graphics pipeline stages are vertex processing (transforming vertices and shapes), rasterization (converting triangles to fragments/pixels with parameters), fragment processing (coloring, texturing, shadows, illumination), and framebuffer processing (depth buffering, assembling final pixels). GPUs have many cores for parallel processing, and rendering involves extensive linear algebra.

nodes.title: Graphics Pipeline
nodes.summary: The text covers modern GPUs with many cores for parallel processing. It details the graphics pipeline stages: vertex processing (transformations), rasterization (triangles to fragments), fragment processing (coloring, textures, effects), and framebuffer processing (depth buffering, final image). Rendering is defined as generating pixel scenes via linear algebra. It then discusses the fusion of high-performance computing and graphics, including the rise of shaders and GPGPU with CUDA (General Purpose GPU definition). Finally, it introduces the NVIDIA Tesla architecture, specifically the GeForce 8800, noting clock speeds and its nature as simple inorder cores, with work flowing from host CPU through a dedicated bus.

nodes.title: Fusion of High Performance Computing and Graphics Computing
nodes.summary: The text explains object rotation/translation as parallel matrix operations, then traces graphics growth in the late nineties and the rise of shaders in the early 2000s. By 2006, GPU vendors realized graphics pipelines could handle general-purpose computation, leading to NVIDIA CUDA and GPGPU. GPGPU is defined as a GPU allowing user code via dedicated languages or extensions. The text announces coverage of NVIDIA Tesla architecture, specifically GeForce 8800, noting core speeds of 1.5 GHz and other parts at 600 or 750 MHz. It begins describing Tesla architecture, where host CPU sends commands/data via a dedicated bus to GPU buffers, processing top-to-bottom, and notes GPU as simple inorder cores.

The section covers graphics processors, including high-intensity graphics in modern systems, early rudimentary programming, and hardware acceleration. It explains monitor pixels, colors, and refresh rates, and distinguishes automatic image synthesis (e.g., games) from video display, noting GPUs offload video decoding. Graphics libraries break structures into triangles, and GPUs handle collision, movement, lighting, and depth. The graphics pipeline stages are vertex processing, rasterization, fragment processing, and framebuffer processing. It discusses GPUs' many cores, parallel processing, linear algebra, and the fusion of high-performance computing with graphics via shaders and GPGPU/CUDA. Finally, it introduces the NVIDIA Tesla architecture (GeForce 8800), its clock speeds, simple inorder cores, and host CPU to GPU data flow.

nodes.title: NVIDIA Tesla Architecture
NVIDIA Tesla Architecture (intro)
nodes.summary: The text covers parallelism in graphics operations; the fusion of HPC and graphics computing driven by gaming, visual effects, and engineering software; the evolution to programmable shaders and GPGPU with NVIDIA's CUDA; a definition of GPGPU; the focus on NVIDIA Tesla (GeForce 8800) architecture; clock speeds; and the Tesla architecture's work distribution, including host CPU commands, buffers, multilevel memory hierarchy, specialized units, vertex/pixel/compute work, PTX/SASS instruction sets, and virtual registers.

nodes.title: Work Distribution
nodes.summary: The text describes the NVIDIA Tesla GPU architecture, covering work distribution for vertex, pixel, and compute tasks; GPU compute engines with 128 cores in 8 TPCs, each with 2 SMs containing 8 SPs and dedicated memories; and the interconnection network, L2 caches, DRAM modules, and ROPs handling rasterization. It also details instruction sets, virtual registers, and the layered design separating graphics-specific and generic hardware.

nodes.title: GPU Compute Engines
nodes.summary: The text describes GPU architecture, starting with how CPUs send vertex, pixel, and compute instructions to dedicated GPU units for processing. It then details the GeForce 8800's compute engines: 128 cores in 8 TPCs, each with 2 SMs of 8 SPs, including memory structures and parallel execution. Finally, it covers the interconnection network, L2 caches, DRAM modules (384 pins in 6 groups), and 6 ROPs for rasterization, color interpolation, and blending, with emphasis on SM design.

nodes.title: Interconnection Network, DRAM Modules, L2 Caches, and ROPs
nodes.summary: The text details GPU architecture, starting with instruction processing: GPUs handle vertex, pixel, and compute tasks via dedicated units (vertex processing, pixel processing, compute work distributor) that distribute work to cores. It highlights a two-layer design separating operation-specific pipelines from generic hardware. Then, it describes the GeForce 8800 GPU: 128 cores in 8 TPCs, each with 2 SMs of 8 SPs; SPs are inorder cores with FP ALUs, branch/memory units, and shared memory. It covers the interconnection network, L2 caches, DRAM (384 pins, 6 groups), and 6 ROPs for rasterization. Finally, it explains SM structure: geometry controller, SMC, i-cache, C cache, MT issue unit, and SP features like multiply-add and integer ALU.

The section covers NVIDIA Tesla architecture, focusing on parallelism in graphics and HPC fusion, programmable shaders, and GPGPU with CUDA. It details the GeForce 8800's work distribution for vertex, pixel, and compute tasks via dedicated units. The GPU has 128 cores in 8 TPCs, each with 2 SMs of 8 SPs, plus memory hierarchy, interconnection network, L2 caches, DRAM modules, and 6 ROPs. It also describes instruction sets (PTX/SASS), virtual registers, and the layered design separating graphics-specific and generic hardware. SM structure includes geometry controller, SMC, caches, MT issue unit, and SP features like multiply-add and integer ALU.

nodes.title: Streaming Multiprocessors (SMs)
nodes.summary: The text describes GPU architecture and computation. It details the TPC structure with two SMs, the geometry controller's role in vertex processing, and the SMC's arbitration of resource requests. Each SM contains instruction and constant caches, a multithreaded issue unit, eight SP cores with floating-point and integer ALUs supporting multiply-add and predicated instructions, shared memory, and two SFUs for transcendental and interpolation tasks. A shared texture unit processes threads and fetches texture data. The text also covers NVIDIA's SIMT model, CUDA programming, kernels executing on GPU threads mapped to SPs, and memory types: local, shared, and global, with explicit programmer control.

nodes.title: Computation on a GPU
nodes.summary: The text describes GPU architecture, focusing on SP cores executing integer, logical, memory, and branch instructions with predicated execution, and SFUs handling transcendental and interpolating functions. It details SM components, texture units, and memory types (local, shared, global). It explains NVIDIA's SIMT model, CUDA programming, warps, scheduling, and multithreading. It covers warp execution on SP cores and SFUs, predication, and synchronization. Finally, it introduces CUDA program structure with kernels, threads, blocks, and grids, and provides a code example for array addition.

nodes.title: CUDA Programs
nodes.summary: The text explains GPU warp scheduling, fine-grained multithreading, and SIMD execution, detailing how a 32-thread warp is processed in four cycles across SP cores and SFUs to keep units busy. It describes warp atomicity, independent execution, and synchronization via global memory or primitives. It then covers CUDA programming: kernels, threads, blocks/CTAs, grids, thread IDs, and a vector addition example including host-device memory allocation, copying, kernel invocation, and cleanup. It contrasts GPU thread management with CPU overhead and summarizes the GPU model as SIMD, MPMD, and fine-grained multithreading. The text concludes with an extensive bibliography and index covering computer architecture topics.

The section covers graphics processors, starting with an overview of high-intensity graphics, hardware acceleration, monitor pixels, colors, refresh rates, and the distinction between automatic image synthesis and video display. It details the graphics pipeline stages, GPUs' many cores, parallel processing, linear algebra, shaders, GPGPU/CUDA, and the NVIDIA Tesla architecture. It then focuses on the Tesla architecture, including parallelism, programmable shaders, the GeForce 8800's work distribution, 128 cores in 8 TPCs, memory hierarchy, instruction sets, and the layered design. It describes Streaming Multiprocessors (SMs), their components, SIMT model, CUDA programming, memory types, and warp scheduling. Computation on a GPU is explained with SP cores, SFUs, warps, synchronization, and CUDA program structure. Finally, CUDA programs are detailed with warp scheduling, fine-grained multithreading, SIMD execution, kernels, threads, blocks, grids, and a vector addition example, concluding with a bibliography and index.
